ALPHABET = '123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz'
def b58(data):
    n = int.from_bytes(data, 'big')
    out = ''
    while n:
        n, r = divmod(n, 58)
        out = ALPHABET[r] + out
    zeros = len(data) - len(data.lstrip(b'\x00'))
    return '1' * zeros + out

title: Transactions: chapter 6 of the 3rd edition read byte by byte and recomputed from the standards and Bitcoin Core's sources

nodes.label: What a transaction is
nodes.body: This first branch asks what a Bitcoin transaction is before any of its bytes are read. The book opens with a contrast. Physical cash is a bearer token: Alice pays Bob by handing him some number of tokens, such as dollar bills. Bitcoins do not exist either physically or as digital data, so Alice cannot hand Bob some bitcoins or send them by email. The closer picture is a parcel of land, which cannot be picked up either; a record kept by a local government says who owns it, and the owner transfers it by convincing the government to update that record (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This first branch asks what a Bitcoin transaction is before any of its bytes are read. The book opens with a contrast. Physical cash is a bearer token: Alice pays Bob by handing him some number of tokens, such as dollar bills. Bitcoins do not exist either physically or as digital data, so Alice cannot hand Bob some bitcoins or send them by email. The closer picture is a parcel of land, which cannot be picked up either; a record kept by a local government says who owns it, and the owner transfers it by convincing the government to update that record (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The picture decides everything that follows. There exists a database on every Bitcoin full node that says that Alice controls some number of bitcoins, and Alice pays Bob by convincing full nodes to update their database to say that some of her bitcoins are now controlled by Bob. The data she uses to convince them is called a transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A transaction is therefore not a coin and not a message to Bob; it is an instruction addressed to thousands of independent databases, and every field in it exists because some node needs it to decide whether the update is allowed.

The reader has met transactions already: chapter 2 followed Alice's payment to Bob from her wallet to a confirmed block, and chapter 3 retrieved the very same transaction from Bitcoin Core with the txindex option so that its hexadecimal could be read (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This chapter opens that hexadecimal and reads it field by field. The same bytes are what a wallet signs, what the peer-to-peer network relays, what a block commits to and what an explorer decodes, so the format learned here is met everywhere a transaction is.

The branch has two groups. The first, the idea of a transaction, states what is being transferred - control over outputs recorded in the nodes' database, not tokens - and names the parts every transaction has. The second, serialization formats, explains how that data is written as bytes: Bitcoin Core's format, which is the one used to commit to transactions and to relay them, its extended form for transactions that carry witnesses, the older legacy form, the partially signed format used between programs that cooperate on one transaction, and the byte map the book uses to show the fields in place (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: The idea of a transaction
nodes.body: This group collects the three ideas a reader needs before the bytes make sense: the transaction itself, the ownership record that it asks full nodes to change, and the parts that every transaction is built from. The book's own order is the same: first the comparison with cash and with land, then the statement that a transaction is the data Alice uses to convince full nodes, and only then the serialized bytes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This group collects the three ideas a reader needs before the bytes make sense: the transaction itself, the ownership record that it asks full nodes to change, and the parts that every transaction is built from. The book's own order is the same: first the comparison with cash and with land, then the statement that a transaction is the data Alice uses to convince full nodes, and only then the serialized bytes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Each idea prevents a specific confusion. Thinking of bitcoins as tokens leads a reader to look for the coins inside the transaction, where there are none; thinking of the record as a balance leads a reader to expect an amount to be subtracted from Alice, whereas the record holds whole outputs that are spent entirely; and not knowing the parts makes the byte map in the next group a wall of hexadecimal rather than a list of named fields.

The three sections go from the abstract to the concrete. The transaction is the request; the ownership record is the database every full node keeps and updates when it accepts the request; the parts of a transaction are the top-level fields - version, inputs, outputs, witness structure and lock time, with a marker and a flag in the extended format - each of which gets a branch of its own later in the chapter.

nodes.label: Transaction
nodes.body: A transaction is the data Alice uses to convince full nodes to update their databases so that some of her bitcoins are recorded as controlled by Bob. The book gives the definition after two comparisons: cash, which is a bearer token handed from one person to another, and land, which is transferred by having the keeper of a record change the record. Bitcoin works like the land register, except that the record is kept by every full node, and the transaction is the request that each of them checks and applies (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A transaction is the data Alice uses to convince full nodes to update their databases so that some of her bitcoins are recorded as controlled by Bob. The book gives the definition after two comparisons: cash, which is a bearer token handed from one person to another, and land, which is transferred by having the keeper of a record change the record. Bitcoin works like the land register, except that the record is kept by every full node, and the transaction is the request that each of them checks and applies (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The definition matters because it says who the audience of a transaction is. Bob is not the audience; the full nodes are. Alice's wallet does not send anything to Bob at all - it broadcasts a request to the network, and Bob learns of the payment because his own software watches the same shared record. This is done without using either Alice's or Bob's identities, which the book takes up in the next chapter, and it is why a transaction contains no names, no balances and no account numbers, only references to earlier outputs, new outputs and the proof that spending is authorised (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A transaction works by pointing and by proving. Its inputs point to outputs of earlier transactions that assigned bitcoins to Alice; its outputs assign those bitcoins to new conditions, such as a condition only Bob can satisfy; and its witnesses prove that Alice was allowed to spend what the inputs point to. A full node that receives it looks up each referenced output in its own database, checks that it is unspent, checks the proof and checks the arithmetic, and only then changes its record. Alice's example transaction, the one this chapter reads, is 194 bytes long when serialized, and every one of those bytes belongs to one of the fields that the rest of the chapter names (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The word is used loosely in everyday speech, where a transaction is a payment or a purchase; in this chapter it is a specific data structure with a specific serialization. A second caution is about what is absent: a transaction never states the amount of its inputs, because that amount is read from the referenced outputs, and it never states a fee, because the fee is whatever the inputs are worth beyond what the outputs assign. Both absences are consequences of the definition, and both trip readers who expect a transaction to look like a bank statement.

nodes.example: a request to thousands of databases
nodes.definition: A transaction is the data Alice uses to convince every full node to update its database so that some bitcoins she controls are recorded as controlled by Bob.

nodes.label: The ownership record of a full node
nodes.body: The ownership record is the database that every full node keeps and that says who controls which bitcoins. The book's comparison is with a land register maintained by a local government, with one difference that is the whole point of Bitcoin: there is not one register but thousands of copies, one on every full node, and a transfer happens when the nodes agree to update their copies in the same way (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Chapter 3 introduced the full node as the program that keeps a complete copy of the blockchain and checks every rule for itself, and this chapter shows the database that such a program maintains from the blockchain's transactions.

paras.text: The ownership record is the database that every full node keeps and that says who controls which bitcoins. The book's comparison is with a land register maintained by a local government, with one difference that is the whole point of Bitcoin: there is not one register but thousands of copies, one on every full node, and a transfer happens when the nodes agree to update their copies in the same way (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Chapter 3 introduced the full node as the program that keeps a complete copy of the blockchain and checks every rule for itself, and this chapter shows the database that such a program maintains from the blockchain's transactions.

The record is why Bitcoin needs no trusted keeper. A government can be asked to update a register because it is the only keeper; full nodes cannot be asked, only convinced, because each one applies the rules itself and ignores any request that breaks them. A transaction is thus a proof addressed to strangers, and its format is designed so that a stranger with the record and the rules can check it completely. The book later names what the record holds for each entry: the amount, the conditions for spending, and the height and median time past of the confirming block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The record works as a set of outputs rather than a set of balances. The book describes Bitcoin Core's solution: it keeps a database that stores every unspent transaction output together with essential metadata about it, such as the height of the block that confirmed it, and each time a new block arrives all the outputs the block's transactions spend are removed and all the outputs they create are added (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example is a toy version: an entry for Alice of 100,000 satoshis is removed and an entry for Bob is added, which is what the rest of the chapter does with real fields. The real database has no names in it, only output scripts, which are the subject of the outputs branch.

Two cautions. The record is derived, not primary: a node rebuilds it from the blockchain, so the blockchain is the authority and the database is a cache of its consequences. And the record is not a balance sheet; Alice's bitcoins are a collection of separate outputs of various sizes, and a payment spends whole outputs and makes change, which is why a transaction can look oddly shaped to someone expecting an amount to be debited from an account.

nodes.example: every node keeps the same register
nodes.definition: Every full node keeps its own copy of the database that says which bitcoins are controlled by whom, and a transaction is accepted when the node agrees to update that copy.

nodes.label: The parts of a transaction
nodes.body: The parts of a transaction are its top-level fields, in the order they are serialized: the version, then in the extended format a marker and a flag, then the inputs field, the outputs field, the witness structure for transactions that have one, and finally the lock time. The book's byte map of Alice's transaction shows only these top-level fields, and the chapter examines each of them in the order they appear and describes any additional fields they contain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The parts of a transaction are its top-level fields, in the order they are serialized: the version, then in the extended format a marker and a flag, then the inputs field, the outputs field, the witness structure for transactions that have one, and finally the lock time. The book's byte map of Alice's transaction shows only these top-level fields, and the chapter examines each of them in the order they appear and describes any additional fields they contain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Naming the parts first turns the hexadecimal into a sentence with a grammar. Every byte of a serialized transaction belongs to exactly one field, every field has a fixed position relative to the one before it, and the lengths of the variable fields are stated inside the data, so a reader who knows the order can parse any transaction by hand. The order is also the order of the chapter, and the order of this course's branches follows it with one exception: the sequence field, which lives inside each input, is given a branch of its own because its meaning has changed three times (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The fields divide into the fixed and the counted. The version and the lock time are four bytes each and always present. The inputs and outputs fields each begin with a count, encoded as a compactSize integer, followed by that many items; the witness structure has no count of its own because there is one witness stack per input. The marker and the flag are present only in the extended format, where the marker is zero and the flag is one, and are absent in the legacy format (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The seven names in the worked example are the names the chapter uses for these fields, and the explorer that this course consulted reports the same transaction with exactly these parts (mempool.space, 2026).

The caution is that the parts are not all independent. The number of witness stacks is implied by the number of inputs, the sequence of each input interacts with the lock time of the whole transaction, and the marker only makes sense because a legacy parser would read it as a count of zero inputs. A reader who learns the fields as a list will miss these links, which is why the later branches keep returning to them.

nodes.example: five top-level fields, plus two for segwit
nodes.definition: A serialized transaction has a version, an inputs field, an outputs field, a lock time and, when it spends segwit outputs, a marker, a flag and a witness structure.

nodes.label: Serialization formats
nodes.body: Serialization is the writing of a data structure as a sequence of bytes so that it can be stored, hashed or sent. This group explains the formats a Bitcoin transaction is written in: Bitcoin Core's own format, which the book says is special because it is the format used to make commitments to transactions and to relay them across the peer-to-peer network; its extended form, defined in BIP144, for transactions that carry a witness structure; the original form, now called legacy serialization; and the partially signed bitcoin transaction format, which is the only other widely used format the authors know of (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Serialization is the writing of a data structure as a sequence of bytes so that it can be stored, hashed or sent. This group explains the formats a Bitcoin transaction is written in: Bitcoin Core's own format, which the book says is special because it is the format used to make commitments to transactions and to relay them across the peer-to-peer network; its extended form, defined in BIP144, for transactions that carry a witness structure; the original form, now called legacy serialization; and the partially signed bitcoin transaction format, which is the only other widely used format the authors know of (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The format matters more than a convenience would, because the bytes are hashed. A transaction's identifier is a hash of its serialization, and a block commits to transactions by hashing their serializations into a tree, so two programs that serialized the same transaction differently would compute different identifiers and disagree about which block is valid. That is why the book says programs may use a different format as long as they transmit all of the same data, but why in practice many Bitcoin programs use Bitcoin Core's format: it is reasonably compact and simple to parse (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The five sections go from the general to the particular. The serialized transaction section states what the format is for; the extended format and the legacy format sections explain the two shapes a transaction can take on the network and how a parser tells them apart; the PSBT section describes a format for a transaction that is not yet complete; and the byte map section explains the drawing the book uses to show every field in its place, which this course recomputes from the bytes rather than copies.

nodes.label: Serialized transaction
nodes.body: A serialized transaction is the transaction written as bytes in Bitcoin Core's format. The book retrieves Alice's payment to Bob again with the getrawtransaction command and prints the result as hexadecimal, two characters per byte, noting that it takes 64 hexadecimal characters to display 32 bytes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Chapter 3 introduced that command and the txindex option that lets a node look up any transaction by its identifier (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); this chapter reads what the command returned.

paras.text: A serialized transaction is the transaction written as bytes in Bitcoin Core's format. The book retrieves Alice's payment to Bob again with the getrawtransaction command and prints the result as hexadecimal, two characters per byte, noting that it takes 64 hexadecimal characters to display 32 bytes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Chapter 3 introduced that command and the txindex option that lets a node look up any transaction by its identifier (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); this chapter reads what the command returned.

The serialized form is the canonical form. The book says Bitcoin Core's serialization format is special because it is the format used to make commitments to transactions and to relay them across Bitcoin's peer-to-peer network, and that other programs may use a different format as long as they transmit all of the same data (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A commitment here means a hash that later data can be checked against; because the hash is taken over these bytes, these bytes are what every node must agree on, down to the order of fields and the encoding of each number.

The format works by fixed-width numbers in little-endian order and counted lists. Multi-byte integers are written least significant byte first, which is why the version 1 appears as 01000000; lists are preceded by their length; and variable-length items such as scripts are preceded by their byte count. The worked example counts the characters the book prints and halves them: Alice's transaction is 194 bytes. The explorer this course consulted reports the same size for the same identifier, and the chapter's own library, given these bytes, parses them into the fields the later branches describe (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (mempool.space, 2026).

The caution is that hexadecimal is a display, not the data. A node never handles the text; it handles the 194 bytes, and a program that copies the text must convert it back before hashing, or it will hash the characters and get a meaningless digest. The second caution is that the same transaction can be written in two of the formats of this group, the extended and the legacy, and only one of them is what the identifier is computed over, which the witness branch explains.

nodes.example: the 194 bytes Bitcoin Core returned
nodes.definition: A serialized transaction is the transaction written as the sequence of bytes that Bitcoin Core hashes, relays and stores; the book prints Alice's as 388 hexadecimal characters.

nodes.label: Extended serialization format
nodes.body: The extended serialization format is the layout of a transaction that carries a witness structure. The book says the two fields after the version were added as part of the segregated witness soft fork: the rules were changed according to BIPs 141 and 143, but the extended format itself is defined in BIP144 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In that format the marker must be zero and the flag must be nonzero, and in the current peer-to-peer protocol the flag should always be one, with other values reserved for later upgrades (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016).

paras.text: The extended serialization format is the layout of a transaction that carries a witness structure. The book says the two fields after the version were added as part of the segregated witness soft fork: the rules were changed according to BIPs 141 and 143, but the extended format itself is defined in BIP144 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In that format the marker must be zero and the flag must be nonzero, and in the current peer-to-peer protocol the flag should always be one, with other values reserved for later upgrades (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016).

The format exists so that old and new programs can read the same bytes without a flag day. BIP144 explains that the marker byte is set to zero so that the structure will never parse as a valid transaction in a parser that does not support the proposal: if parsing were to succeed, such a transaction would contain no inputs and a single output, and a transaction cannot have zero inputs (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016). The witness data is thus carried where old nodes never look, which is what lets the identifier exclude it, the theme of the witness branch (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The layout is the legacy layout with three insertions: after the four version bytes come the marker and the flag, then the inputs and outputs exactly as before, then the witness structure, then the lock time. The worked example reads the fifth and sixth bytes of Alice's transaction and finds 00 and 01, the marker and the flag. BIP144 gives the rationale for using two bytes rather than one: a single zero byte would have made an empty transaction, used in some tests, look like new serialized data, and the flag byte can be read as a bit vector that lets more non-committed data be added later (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016).

The caution is that the extended format is not optional for a transaction that has witnesses and not permitted for one that does not. The book states that if the transaction does not need a witness stack, the marker and flag must not be present, and the legacy section at the end of the chapter says that the older format must be used on the network for any transaction with an empty witness structure (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A program that always writes the marker will produce bytes that a peer rejects.

nodes.example: marker 00, flag 01, witness at the end
nodes.definition: The extended serialization format of BIP144 adds a marker byte, a flag byte and a witness structure to the legacy layout, for transactions that spend segwit outputs.

nodes.label: Legacy serialization
nodes.body: Legacy serialization is the original form of Bitcoin's transaction serialization, the one every early transaction used. The book introduces the name when it explains the marker: in legacy serialization, the marker byte would have been interpreted as the number of inputs, zero, and since a transaction cannot have zero inputs the marker signals to modern programs that extended serialization is in use (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter's closing section states that legacy serialization does not include the marker, flag and witness structure fields (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Legacy serialization is the original form of Bitcoin's transaction serialization, the one every early transaction used. The book introduces the name when it explains the marker: in legacy serialization, the marker byte would have been interpreted as the number of inputs, zero, and since a transaction cannot have zero inputs the marker signals to modern programs that extended serialization is in use (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter's closing section states that legacy serialization does not include the marker, flag and witness structure fields (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The legacy format matters for two reasons. It is still used: the book says an older serialization format is still used for many transactions, and it must be used on the Bitcoin peer-to-peer network for any transaction with an empty witness structure, which is only valid if the transaction does not spend any witness programs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). And it is the format the transaction identifier is computed over even for segwit transactions, because segregated witness works precisely by leaving the witness out of the bytes that are hashed, as the witness branch explains (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

The worked example strips Alice's transaction to its legacy form: the four version bytes, everything between the flag and the witness, and the four lock-time bytes, which gives 125 bytes out of 194. The 71 bytes removed at the end are the witness structure, 67 bytes, followed by the lock time, which is put back. Those 125 bytes are what a node without segwit support would see, and the chapter's weight section shows that they are counted four times while the other 69 - the marker, the flag and the witness structure - count once (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

The caution is in the word still. Legacy is not a synonym for obsolete here: a transaction that spends only pre-segwit outputs has no witness and is correctly serialized in the legacy format today. The second caution is that a legacy transaction still has a witness in the abstract sense - the signatures are in its input scripts - and only lacks the separate witness structure; the two uses of the word witness meet in the witness branch.

nodes.example: no marker, no flag, no witness
nodes.definition: Legacy serialization is the original transaction format, without the marker, flag and witness structure; it is still used for every transaction that spends no witness program.

nodes.label: Partially signed bitcoin transaction
nodes.body: The partially signed bitcoin transaction format, PSBT, is the only other widely used transaction serialization format that the authors are aware of, documented in BIPs 174 and 370 with extensions in other proposals. The book says it allows an untrusted program to produce a transaction template that can be verified and updated by trusted programs, such as hardware signing devices, that have the necessary private keys or other sensitive data to fill in the template (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Chapter 5 met the hardware signing device as the holder of keys that signs what a connected application builds; PSBT is the format that crosses that boundary.

paras.text: The partially signed bitcoin transaction format, PSBT, is the only other widely used transaction serialization format that the authors are aware of, documented in BIPs 174 and 370 with extensions in other proposals. The book says it allows an untrusted program to produce a transaction template that can be verified and updated by trusted programs, such as hardware signing devices, that have the necessary private keys or other sensitive data to fill in the template (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Chapter 5 met the hardware signing device as the holder of keys that signs what a connected application builds; PSBT is the format that crosses that boundary.

The format exists because the standard serialization has no room for the information a signer needs. To sign an input, a device must know the amount and the script of the output being spent, which the transaction itself does not carry; to check that change really returns to the wallet, it must know the derivation path of the change key. PSBT stores a significant amount of such metadata about a transaction, which the book says makes it much less compact than the standard serialization format but is why the authors strongly recommend it to developers of wallets that plan to support signing with multiple keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Chow, 2017).

A PSBT is a container of key-value maps: one global map, one map per input and one map per output, each holding typed fields such as the unsigned transaction, the previous output being spent, partial signatures and derivation paths. The format begins with the magic bytes 70736274ff, which spell psbt followed by a separator, as the worked example decodes; BIP174 defines these bytes and the maps, and BIP370 revises the format so that inputs and outputs can be added after creation (Chow, 2017) (Chow, 2021). Roles - creator, updater, signer, finalizer, extractor - each add what they know, and the extractor produces the ordinary serialized transaction at the end.

The caution is scope: the book does not go into detail about PSBT, and neither does this chapter beyond what the format is for; the executed example proves only the magic prefix. A second caution is that a PSBT is not a transaction. It cannot be broadcast, it has no identifier of its own that the network recognises, and the transaction it contains is only valid once every signer has done its part and an extractor has produced the standard bytes.

nodes.example: a template passed between programs
nodes.definition: The partially signed bitcoin transaction (PSBT) format of BIPs 174 and 370 lets an untrusted program build a transaction template that trusted programs holding the keys verify and complete.

nodes.label: Byte map
nodes.body: A byte map is the drawing the book uses to show a serialized transaction as fields rather than as a run of hexadecimal: each field is a box whose width is its length in bytes, placed at the position where its bytes begin. The book replicates Alice's transaction as a byte map that shows only the top-level fields, then draws separate maps for the inputs field, the outputs field and the witness structure, and finally a map in weight units (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A byte map is the drawing the book uses to show a serialized transaction as fields rather than as a run of hexadecimal: each field is a box whose width is its length in bytes, placed at the position where its bytes begin. The book replicates Alice's transaction as a byte map that shows only the top-level fields, then draws separate maps for the inputs field, the outputs field and the witness structure, and finally a map in weight units (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The map is the bridge between the two ways of seeing a transaction. A node sees bytes and offsets; a person sees fields and meanings; the map shows both at once, and it makes visible something a list of fields hides, which is how unequal the fields are. In Alice's transaction the two outputs take 75 bytes and the single witness item 65, while the version, the counts and the lock time together take 11, so most of the transaction is scripts and signatures, and the later weight map shows those proportions change when the witness is discounted (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The worked example recomputes the top-level map from the bytes: the version at offset 0 for 4 bytes, the marker at 4, the flag at 5, the inputs field from 6 for 42 bytes - one input of a 32-byte identifier, a 4-byte index, a one-byte script length, an empty script and a 4-byte sequence, after a one-byte count - the outputs field from 48 for 75 bytes - a one-byte count, then an 8-byte amount, a one-byte script length and a 34-byte script, then an 8-byte amount, a length and a 22-byte script - the witness structure from 123 for 67, and the lock time from 190 for 4, which sums to 194. The chapter's library produces the same spans for every field, down to each witness item, and the deck draws the book's figure beside the recomputed table so that the two can be compared (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The caution is that a byte map is only as right as the parser behind it. Fields with lengths stated inside the data move everything after them, so an error in one count shifts every later box; the book's map of a 194-byte transaction cannot be checked by eye but can be checked by code, which is what this course does. A second caution is that the book's final map is in weight units rather than bytes, so its boxes are not comparable with the first map without the factors of the weight branch.

nodes.example: every field at its offset
nodes.definition: A byte map draws a serialized transaction with each field at its byte position and length, so that the hexadecimal can be read as named parts.

nodes.label: Version, marker and flag
nodes.body: This branch reads the first six bytes of Alice's transaction: the four-byte version and, because her transaction carries a witness, the marker and the flag that announce the extended format. The book says the first four bytes of a serialized Bitcoin transaction are its version, that the original version was 1, written 01000000, and that all transactions in Bitcoin must follow the rules of version 1 transactions, with many of those rules described throughout the book (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This branch reads the first six bytes of Alice's transaction: the four-byte version and, because her transaction carries a witness, the marker and the flag that announce the extended format. The book says the first four bytes of a serialized Bitcoin transaction are its version, that the original version was 1, written 01000000, and that all transactions in Bitcoin must follow the rules of version 1 transactions, with many of those rules described throughout the book (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Six bytes seem too few for a branch, but they decide which rules apply to everything after them. Version 2 transactions were introduced by the BIP68 soft fork, which places additional constraints on the sequence field that apply only to transactions with version 2 or higher, and BIP112 upgraded an opcode that fails when evaluated in a transaction with a version below 2 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The marker and the flag decide whether the bytes that follow are read as the legacy layout or as the extended one, so a parser that misreads them misreads the whole transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016).

The reader meets the version wherever a transaction is decoded - every explorer and every node reports it - and meets it as a decision in any wallet that uses relative timelocks, which must set version 2. The marker and the flag are met in every segwit transaction's hexadecimal as the 0001 after the version, and in the policy of Bitcoin Core, whose source declares version 2 as the current version a new transaction is built with and 3 as the highest version its relay policy treats as standard (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The branch has two groups. The version field group follows the numbers: version 1 and its rules, version 2 and the sequence constraints that came with it, the version 3 proposal that changes relay policy rather than consensus, and the presigned transactions whose safety is the reason version numbers are reserved for upgrades. The marker and flag group explains the two bytes of the extended format, why the marker is a zero that a legacy parser would misread as a count of inputs, and why the flag is a separate byte rather than part of the marker (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016).

nodes.label: The version field
nodes.body: The version field is the four-byte little-endian integer at the start of every transaction. This group covers the three values it has taken or may take and the problem that explains why new values are introduced carefully: version 1, the original; version 2, which the BIP68 soft fork introduced to carry the new meaning of the sequence field; the version 3 proposal that the book says was being widely considered as it was written; and presigned transactions, which can be invalidated by a rule that applies to a version they already use (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The version field is the four-byte little-endian integer at the start of every transaction. This group covers the three values it has taken or may take and the problem that explains why new values are introduced carefully: version 1, the original; version 2, which the BIP68 soft fork introduced to carry the new meaning of the sequence field; the version 3 proposal that the book says was being widely considered as it was written; and presigned transactions, which can be invalidated by a rule that applies to a version they already use (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The group matters because a version number is a promise. Bitcoin's consensus rules can only be tightened by soft fork, and a tightening that applied to every existing transaction could invalidate transactions that were signed long ago and cannot be signed again. Reserving a new version number for the new constraint keeps the old transactions valid under the old number; the book's sidebar on protecting presigned transactions states the problem and this solution, and the sequence branch shows the constraint that BIP68 actually added (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Friedenbach et al., 2015).

The four sections are in historical order. Version 1 is the baseline every transaction must satisfy; version 2 adds BIP68's reading of the sequence field and BIP112's opcode; version 3 is a relay-policy regime under which a transaction accepts topological limits in exchange for protection from a kind of attack the book defers to a later chapter; and the presigned transaction section explains why anyone building a protocol on Bitcoin must avoid features reserved for upgrades and can test a transaction with Bitcoin Core's testmempoolaccept command (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Version 1
nodes.body: Version 1 is the original version of Bitcoin transactions. The book says the first four bytes of a serialized transaction are its version, that the original version was 1, written 0x01000000, and that all transactions in Bitcoin must follow the rules of version 1 transactions, with many of those rules described throughout the book (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Alice's transaction begins with exactly these four bytes, and the worked example reads them as the little-endian integer 1.

paras.text: Version 1 is the original version of Bitcoin transactions. The book says the first four bytes of a serialized transaction are its version, that the original version was 1, written 0x01000000, and that all transactions in Bitcoin must follow the rules of version 1 transactions, with many of those rules described throughout the book (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Alice's transaction begins with exactly these four bytes, and the worked example reads them as the little-endian integer 1.

Version 1 matters as the floor. Later versions do not replace its rules but add to them: a version 2 transaction obeys everything a version 1 transaction obeys and in addition the sequence constraints of BIP68, and the book says that beyond those changes version 2 transactions are identical to version 1 transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Most of what this chapter describes - inputs, outpoints, outputs, amounts, scripts, lock time - are version 1 rules, so a reader who understands version 1 understands the format, and the later versions are a short list of differences.

The number is stored least significant byte first, which is why 1 appears as 01 followed by three zero bytes. Bitcoin Core reads it as a signed 32-bit integer; its CheckTransaction function, the context-free check of a transaction, does not look at the version at all, and the version only matters where a rule names it, in the sequence-lock calculation for version 2 and in the relay policy for version 3 (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Alice's transaction is version 1 even though it spends a segwit output and carries a witness, because segwit changed the serialization and not the version (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The caution is that version 1 is not the version a modern node creates by default. Bitcoin Core's transaction class names 2 as its current version, so a transaction built by a current wallet is usually version 2 even when it uses no relative timelock, and the previous transaction in Alice's chain, the one that paid her, is version 2 as the explorer records it (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (mempool.space, 2026). Version 1 is therefore what old software and some deliberately conservative wallets produce, not what the reader should expect to see most often.

nodes.example: 01000000 in the first four bytes
nodes.definition: Version 1 is the original transaction version, written 01000000 in little-endian order; every transaction must follow its rules, and Alice's transaction uses it.

nodes.label: Version 2 and BIP68
nodes.body: Version 2 is the transaction version introduced by the BIP68 soft fork change to Bitcoin's consensus rules. The book says BIP68 places additional constraints on the sequence field that apply only to transactions with version 2 or higher, that version 1 transactions are unaffected, and that BIP112, part of the same soft fork, upgraded the opcode OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY, which now fails if evaluated as part of a transaction with a version less than 2; beyond those two changes, version 2 transactions are identical to version 1 transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Version 2 is the transaction version introduced by the BIP68 soft fork change to Bitcoin's consensus rules. The book says BIP68 places additional constraints on the sequence field that apply only to transactions with version 2 or higher, that version 1 transactions are unaffected, and that BIP112, part of the same soft fork, upgraded the opcode OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY, which now fails if evaluated as part of a transaction with a version less than 2; beyond those two changes, version 2 transactions are identical to version 1 transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The version gate is what makes the soft fork safe. Before BIP68, the sequence field of a version 1 transaction could hold any value with no consensus meaning, so a transaction signed years earlier with a low sequence number remained valid. Applying the new reading only from version 2 means that no presigned version 1 transaction was invalidated, which is the book's own example of protecting presigned transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Friedenbach et al., 2015). BIP68 states the rule in its own words: the specification defines the meaning of sequence numbers for transactions with a version greater than or equal to 2 (Friedenbach et al., 2015).

A node implements the gate in one comparison. Bitcoin Core's CalculateSequenceLocks computes a relative lock only when the transaction's version is at least 2 and the input's disable flag is clear; otherwise the sequence is ignored for timelock purposes (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The worked example states the same decision as a small function: version 2 with a sequence of 30 means a relative timelock, and the sequence branch explains what a lock of 30 blocks means. The activation height of these rules on the main network, 419,328, is recorded in Bitcoin Core's chain parameters as CSVHeight, the height at which BIP68, BIP112 and BIP113 took effect together (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The caution is that the gate is on the transaction, not on the input. All inputs of a version 2 transaction are read under BIP68, so a wallet cannot opt one input into a relative timelock and leave another with an unrestricted low sequence; it must set the disable flag on the inputs it wants excluded, which is a distinct bit the sequence branch describes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Friedenbach et al., 2015). A second caution is that version 2 does not by itself impose any timelock: with every sequence at its final value the transaction behaves exactly like a version 1 one.

nodes.example: the version that turns sequence into a timelock
nodes.definition: Version 2 transactions were introduced by the BIP68 soft fork; only in a transaction of version 2 or higher is a sequence value below 2 to the 31 a relative timelock, and BIP112's opcode fails below version 2.

io.code: (lambda version, seq: 'relative timelock' if version >= 2 and seq < 2 ** 31 else 'no timelock')(2, 30)

steps.expr: (lambda version, seq: 'relative timelock' if version >= 2 and seq < 2 ** 31 else 'no timelock')(2, 30)

nodes.label: The version 3 proposal
nodes.body: The version 3 proposal is the one the book says was being widely considered as it was written: a proposal to begin using version 3 transactions that does not seek to change the consensus rules but only the policy that Bitcoin full nodes use to relay transactions. Under it, version 3 transactions would be subject to additional constraints in order to prevent certain denial of service attacks that the book discusses under transaction pinning in a later chapter (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The proposal became BIP431, whose title is topology restrictions for pinning (Zhao and Garlick, 2024).

paras.text: The version 3 proposal is the one the book says was being widely considered as it was written: a proposal to begin using version 3 transactions that does not seek to change the consensus rules but only the policy that Bitcoin full nodes use to relay transactions. Under it, version 3 transactions would be subject to additional constraints in order to prevent certain denial of service attacks that the book discusses under transaction pinning in a later chapter (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The proposal became BIP431, whose title is topology restrictions for pinning (Zhao and Garlick, 2024).

The proposal matters as an example of the difference between policy and consensus, a distinction the whole chapter leans on. A consensus rule decides which blocks are valid and binds every node; a policy decides which unconfirmed transactions a node will relay and store, and a node may choose it. Version 3 adds no validity rule - a version 3 transaction in a block is valid under exactly the rules of version 2 - but a node that follows BIP431 refuses to relay a version 3 transaction with more than a small number of unconfirmed relatives, which is what denies an attacker the ability to pin a payment-channel transaction in the memory pool with a large low-fee descendant (Zhao and Garlick, 2024).

BIP431 says a sender signals that a transaction is to be topologically restricted until confirmation by setting its version to 3, and a node applying the policy requires, among other rules, that a version 3 transaction signals replaceability even without the BIP125 signal and that all of its unconfirmed ancestors and descendants are also version 3 (Zhao and Garlick, 2024). Bitcoin Core's documentation records that transactions with version 3 are standard and treated this way as of release 28.0, and its policy source sets the highest standard version to 3 while its transaction class still builds version 2 by default, which is the pair the worked example states (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The caution is that the book's tense is already out of date in one respect and not in another. The proposal was under consideration when the book was written and has since been implemented as policy in Bitcoin Core, so the reader will meet version 3 transactions on the network; but the consensus rules are exactly as the book says, unchanged. A reader should also not expect version 3 from an ordinary wallet, since the restrictions are designed for contract protocols such as payment channels rather than for simple payments (Zhao and Garlick, 2024).

nodes.example: a policy, not a consensus change
nodes.definition: The version 3 proposal, BIP431, changes only the relay policy of full nodes: a version 3 transaction accepts topological restrictions in exchange for protection against pinning attacks; Bitcoin Core treats it as standard since release 28.0.

nodes.label: Presigned transactions
nodes.body: A presigned transaction is a transaction that has been signed but not broadcast. The book's sidebar explains that the last step before broadcasting a transaction for inclusion in the blockchain is to sign it, but that it is possible to sign a transaction without broadcasting it immediately and to save it for months or years in the belief that it can be added to the blockchain later; in the interim the holder may even lose access to the private keys needed to sign an alternative. This is not hypothetical: several protocols built on Bitcoin, including the Lightning Network, depend on presigned transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A presigned transaction is a transaction that has been signed but not broadcast. The book's sidebar explains that the last step before broadcasting a transaction for inclusion in the blockchain is to sign it, but that it is possible to sign a transaction without broadcasting it immediately and to save it for months or years in the belief that it can be added to the blockchain later; in the interim the holder may even lose access to the private keys needed to sign an alternative. This is not hypothetical: several protocols built on Bitcoin, including the Lightning Network, depend on presigned transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Presigned transactions are why consensus upgrades must be careful. Adding a new constraint, as BIP68 did to the sequence field, may invalidate some presigned transactions, and if there is no way to create a new signature for an equivalent transaction, the money being spent in the presigned transaction is permanently lost (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The solution is to reserve some transaction features for upgrades, such as version numbers: anyone creating presigned transactions before BIP68 should have used version 1, so applying BIP68's constraints only to version 2 or higher invalidates none of them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The protection works as a contract between protocol developers and consensus developers. A protocol that uses presigned transactions must not use any feature reserved for future upgrades - unusual version numbers, unused sequence bits, unknown witness versions - and the consensus developers in turn only attach new rules to those reserved features. The book notes that Bitcoin Core's default transaction relay policy does not allow the use of reserved features, and that a developer can test whether a transaction complies with that policy by using Bitcoin Core's testmempoolaccept RPC on the main network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example states the rule as a comparison: a version 1 transaction is untouched by a rule that applies from version 2.

The caution is that relay policy is a weaker guarantee than consensus. A transaction that passes testmempoolaccept today uses no reserved feature today, but policy is a moving target, and what is non-standard now could become a consensus rule later only if it was reserved, which is the reason to test. The second caution is practical: a presigned transaction depends on the previous output it spends staying unspent, so the protocol must also prevent the counterparty from spending that output another way, which is the malleability problem of the witness branch (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: signed now, broadcast years later
nodes.definition: A presigned transaction is signed but not broadcast, perhaps for years; a later rule that applies to its version could make it permanently invalid, so new constraints are reserved for new version numbers.

io.code: (lambda presigned_version, rule_applies_from: 'still valid' if presigned_version < rule_applies_from else 'at risk')(1, 2)

nodes.label: The marker and the flag
nodes.body: The marker and the flag are the two bytes that follow the version in the extended serialization format. The book says that if the transaction includes a witness structure, the marker must be zero and the flag must be nonzero; that in the current peer-to-peer protocol the flag should always be one, with alternative flags reserved for later protocol upgrades; and that if the transaction does not need a witness stack, the marker and flag must not be present (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The marker and the flag are the two bytes that follow the version in the extended serialization format. The book says that if the transaction includes a witness structure, the marker must be zero and the flag must be nonzero; that in the current peer-to-peer protocol the flag should always be one, with alternative flags reserved for later protocol upgrades; and that if the transaction does not need a witness stack, the marker and flag must not be present (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Two bytes carry the whole backward compatibility of segwit's serialization. A legacy parser reads the byte after the version as the count of inputs; a count of zero is impossible, so the zero marker makes an extended transaction unparseable as a legacy one rather than wrongly parseable, and a new parser reads the zero as a signal. The book says the marker signals to modern programs that extended serialization is being used and that the flag provides a similar signal and also simplifies the process of updating the serialization format in the future (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016).

The two sections take one byte each. The marker byte section explains the choice of zero and its collision with the input count; the flag byte section explains why a second byte follows the marker, with BIP144's own rationale that a single zero byte would have made an empty test transaction look like new serialized data, and that the flag can be interpreted as a bit vector for adding more non-committed data later (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016).

nodes.label: Marker byte
nodes.body: The marker is the single byte, always 0x00, that follows the version in a transaction serialized in the extended format. The book explains the choice: in legacy serialization, the marker byte would have been interpreted as the number of inputs, zero; a transaction cannot have zero inputs, so the marker signals to modern programs that extended serialization is being used (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP144 names the field marker and fixes its value at zero (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016).

paras.text: The marker is the single byte, always 0x00, that follows the version in a transaction serialized in the extended format. The book explains the choice: in legacy serialization, the marker byte would have been interpreted as the number of inputs, zero; a transaction cannot have zero inputs, so the marker signals to modern programs that extended serialization is being used (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP144 names the field marker and fixes its value at zero (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016).

The marker matters because it lets one byte stream serve two generations of software without ambiguity. A format change that could be confused with the old format would be dangerous: an old node might accept a mis-parsed transaction, or two nodes might disagree about what a transaction says. Choosing a value that is impossible in the old format removes the ambiguity entirely, and BIP144 states the goal directly: the marker is set to zero so that the structure will never parse as a valid transaction in a parser that does not support the proposal (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016).

A parser reads the marker with a lookahead. After the four version bytes it inspects the next byte; if that byte is zero and the byte after it is nonzero, the transaction is in the extended format and the parser consumes both bytes before reading the real input count; otherwise the byte is the input count itself and the legacy layout follows. The worked example applies exactly this test to Alice's transaction, whose fifth byte is 00 and sixth 01, and reports the extended format. The chapter's library does the same and records the marker and the flag as fields of one byte each in the byte map (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The caution is that the marker is not part of what the transaction identifier commits to. The identifier is computed over the legacy serialization, which has no marker, so two serializations of the same transaction, one with and one without the witness, share a txid while differing in these bytes; the witness branch returns to this. A reader should also note that the rule is strict in both directions: a transaction with a witness must carry the marker and one without a witness must not (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Flag byte
nodes.body: The flag is the byte that follows the marker in the extended format. The book says the flag must be nonzero, that in the current peer-to-peer protocol it should always be one, and that alternative flags are reserved for later protocol upgrades (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP144 lists it after the marker in its table of the format and gives its value as 0x01 (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016).

paras.text: The flag is the byte that follows the marker in the extended format. The book says the flag must be nonzero, that in the current peer-to-peer protocol it should always be one, and that alternative flags are reserved for later protocol upgrades (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP144 lists it after the marker in its table of the format and gives its value as 0x01 (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016).

The flag matters as the room left for the future. BIP144 gives two reasons for having it at all: a single zero byte as marker would lead empty transactions, with no inputs and no outputs and used in some tests, to be interpreted as new serialized data, and the flag byte in between will allow more extra non-committed data to be added to transactions later, such as the outputs being spent, because it can be interpreted as a bit vector (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016). The book summarises the same point: the flag simplifies the process of updating the serialization format in the future (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Read as a bit vector, the flag's lowest bit says that a witness structure follows, and the other seven bits are unassigned; the worked example lists the set bits of 0x01 and finds only bit 0. A future extension could set a second bit to announce a further block of data after the witness, and a parser that recognises only bit 0 would know, from the unknown bit, that it cannot parse the rest, rather than silently misreading it. Non-committed data means data that is not part of what the transaction identifier commits to, which is exactly what a witness is (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016) (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

The caution is that reserved does not mean usable. A transaction with a flag other than 1 is not relayed under current rules, so an application cannot set a bit for its own purposes; this is one of the reserved features the presigned-transaction section says a protocol must avoid (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A second caution: the flag's value is checked only in the extended format, and the whole two-byte pair is absent from the legacy format, so there is no flag of zero anywhere.

nodes.example: one, with other values reserved
nodes.definition: The flag is the byte after the marker; it is 0x01 in the current protocol, other values are reserved for upgrades, and BIP144 reads it as a bit vector for adding non-committed data later.

nodes.label: Inputs
nodes.body: This branch reads the inputs field of a transaction, the 42 bytes of Alice's transaction that say where the bitcoins she spends come from. The book says the inputs field contains several other fields and starts by showing a map of those bytes; the list begins with an integer giving the number of inputs, and each input must contain three fields: an outpoint, a length-prefixed input script and a sequence (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The sequence is given its own branch because its meaning has changed three times.

paras.text: This branch reads the inputs field of a transaction, the 42 bytes of Alice's transaction that say where the bitcoins she spends come from. The book says the inputs field contains several other fields and starts by showing a map of those bytes; the list begins with an integer giving the number of inputs, and each input must contain three fields: an outpoint, a length-prefixed input script and a sequence (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The sequence is given its own branch because its meaning has changed three times.

Inputs are where a transaction connects to the past. A transaction never states how many bitcoins it spends; it points at outputs of earlier transactions, and a full node reads the amount, the spending conditions and the confirmation data from the outputs it finds. Everything a node can refuse - spending an output twice, spending one that does not exist, spending without satisfying its conditions - is decided at the inputs, so the branch is where the rule against double spending lives (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reader meets inputs every time a payment is traced: an explorer shows each input as a link to a previous transaction, and following those links backwards is following outpoints. The compactSize integer met here recurs in every counted field of the chapter, the byte-order confusion recurs in every identifier a user copies, and the empty input script of Alice's transaction is the first visible trace of segregated witness, whose reasons the witness branch gives (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The branch has four groups. The input list explains the count and the compactSize encoding that Bitcoin uses for integers that are usually small; the outpoint group explains the 36 bytes that identify one previous output, what a node obtains from that output, the double-spending rule and the database of unspent outputs; the byte order group explains why the identifier in the outpoint is written backwards from the form a user sees; and the input script group explains the field that legacy transactions fill with signatures and Alice's transaction leaves empty (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: The input list
nodes.body: The input list is the inputs field as a whole: a count followed by that many inputs. The book says the transaction input list starts with an integer indicating the number of inputs, that the minimum value is one, that there is no explicit maximum but restrictions on the size of a transaction effectively limit transactions to a few thousand inputs, and that the number is encoded as a compactSize unsigned integer (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This group explains the count and the encoding, and warns about the other variable-length integers that are not compactSize.

paras.text: The input list is the inputs field as a whole: a count followed by that many inputs. The book says the transaction input list starts with an integer indicating the number of inputs, that the minimum value is one, that there is no explicit maximum but restrictions on the size of a transaction effectively limit transactions to a few thousand inputs, and that the number is encoded as a compactSize unsigned integer (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This group explains the count and the encoding, and warns about the other variable-length integers that are not compactSize.

The count is the first field whose length depends on its value, which is the feature that makes Bitcoin's format compact and makes it necessary to parse in order. A fixed four-byte count would waste three bytes in almost every transaction; a compactSize count costs one byte for up to 252 inputs and grows only when needed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The pizza transaction of this chapter's stories has 131 inputs and still spends one byte on its count, as an executed claim shows (mempool.space, 2026).

The three sections take the field apart. The input count section states the rule of at least one and the effective ceiling; the compactSize section gives the encoding table and the worked arithmetic of its four sizes; and the varint varieties section records the book's warning that several variable-length integers exist in Bitcoin programs, that Bitcoin Core's database uses a different one called VarInts, and that the nBits field of a block header uses yet another encoding called Compact, so the full name compactSize is always used for this one (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Input count
nodes.body: The input count is the integer that opens the inputs field and says how many inputs follow. The book states that the minimum value is one, that there is no explicit maximum value, but that restrictions on the maximum size of a transaction effectively limit transactions to a few thousand inputs, and that the number is encoded as a compactSize unsigned integer (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In Alice's transaction the count is the seventh byte, 01, after the version, the marker and the flag.

paras.text: The input count is the integer that opens the inputs field and says how many inputs follow. The book states that the minimum value is one, that there is no explicit maximum value, but that restrictions on the maximum size of a transaction effectively limit transactions to a few thousand inputs, and that the number is encoded as a compactSize unsigned integer (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In Alice's transaction the count is the seventh byte, 01, after the version, the marker and the flag.

The lower bound is a consensus rule and the reason the marker works. Bitcoin Core's CheckTransaction refuses a transaction whose input list is empty with the error bad-txns-vin-empty, so a count of zero can never appear in a valid legacy transaction, which is why the extended format can use a zero byte in that position as its marker (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The upper bound is indirect: a transaction's legacy serialization times the witness scale factor may not exceed the maximum block weight, and since each input takes at least 41 bytes the arithmetic caps the count in the thousands (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The worked example reads the byte at offset 6 of Alice's transaction as a little-endian integer and gets 1. The count is a compactSize integer, so for up to 252 inputs it is one byte read directly; the pizza transaction of 2010, with 131 inputs, still has a one-byte count of 0x83, and an executed claim parses that transaction and finds the 131 inputs the explorer reports (mempool.space, 2026). A parser must read the count before it can read anything else in the field, because the inputs that follow have no terminator.

The caution is that the count counts inputs, not bitcoins and not addresses. A transaction with one input may spend a large output, and one with hundreds may spend dust; and several inputs may belong to the same key. A second caution is that the count is the number of witness stacks too: the witness structure has no count of its own, so a parser of a segwit transaction uses this number again when it reaches the witness (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: at least one, in practice a few thousand
nodes.definition: The input count is the compactSize integer that opens the inputs field; it must be at least one, and transaction size limits keep it to a few thousand in practice.

nodes.label: CompactSize unsigned integer
nodes.body: A compactSize unsigned integer is Bitcoin's encoding for integers that often have low values but may sometimes have high values. The book says such integers are usually encoded using the compactSize data type, which is a version of a variable-length integer sometimes called var_int or varint, as in the documentation of BIPs 37 and 144, and it gives the table: values from 0 to 252 take one byte, identical to a C uint8_t; otherwise a prefix byte indicates the length and the number follows as a regular little-endian unsigned integer (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A compactSize unsigned integer is Bitcoin's encoding for integers that often have low values but may sometimes have high values. The book says such integers are usually encoded using the compactSize data type, which is a version of a variable-length integer sometimes called var_int or varint, as in the documentation of BIPs 37 and 144, and it gives the table: values from 0 to 252 take one byte, identical to a C uint8_t; otherwise a prefix byte indicates the length and the number follows as a regular little-endian unsigned integer (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The encoding is why most of the counts and lengths in a transaction cost one byte. An input count, an output count, a script length and a witness item length are almost always below 253, so each costs a single byte, and only a rare large value pays for the prefix. The book's table lists the three larger forms: 0xfd followed by a 16-bit number for 253 to 0xffff, 0xfe followed by a 32-bit number up to 0xffffffff, and 0xff followed by a 64-bit number up to 0xffffffffffffffff, for 3, 5 and 9 bytes in all (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The worked example writes the encoder in four lines and runs it on six values: 1 and 252 are single bytes, 253 becomes fd followed by fd00, the largest two-byte value 65535 becomes fdffff, 65536 needs the fe prefix and four bytes, and 2 to the 32 needs ff and eight bytes. Decoding reverses the test: read one byte, and if it is 0xfd, 0xfe or 0xff read two, four or eight more. Bitcoin Core's serialize.h implements exactly this reader and writer, and the chapter's library reproduces the same bytes (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The caution is in the book's warning box: several varieties of variable-length integer are used in different programs, including different Bitcoin programs. Bitcoin Core serializes its UTXO database with a type it calls VarInts, which is different from compactSize, and the nBits field in a block header uses a custom type known as Compact, which is unrelated; the book therefore always uses the full name compactSize for the integers of transaction serialization and the peer-to-peer protocol (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A reader who meets varint in another document should check which one is meant.

nodes.example: 1, 3, 5 or 9 bytes, by value
nodes.definition: A compactSize unsigned integer is one byte for values up to 252 and otherwise a prefix byte 0xfd, 0xfe or 0xff followed by the value as a 2-, 4- or 8-byte little-endian integer.

nodes.label: Other variable-length integers
nodes.body: The other variable-length integers are the encodings that share a family resemblance with compactSize but are not it. The book warns that several varieties of variable length integers are used in different programs, including in different Bitcoin programs: Bitcoin Core serializes its UTXO database using a data type it calls VarInts, which is different from compactSize, and the nBits field in a Bitcoin block header is encoded using a custom data type known as Compact, which is unrelated to compactSize (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The other variable-length integers are the encodings that share a family resemblance with compactSize but are not it. The book warns that several varieties of variable length integers are used in different programs, including in different Bitcoin programs: Bitcoin Core serializes its UTXO database using a data type it calls VarInts, which is different from compactSize, and the nBits field in a Bitcoin block header is encoded using a custom data type known as Compact, which is unrelated to compactSize (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The warning matters because the names collide. A developer who reads varint in one document and compactSize in another may implement the wrong one and produce bytes that no node accepts, and the error is silent until a transaction is rejected. The book resolves it by convention: when talking about the variable-length integers used in Bitcoin transaction serialization and other parts of the peer-to-peer protocol, it always uses the full name compactSize (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example simply lists the three encodings with where each is used.

The three encodings differ in mechanism, not only in name. CompactSize puts the length in a prefix byte, as the previous section shows. Bitcoin Core's VarInts use a continuation bit in each byte so that small numbers take one byte and the encoding grows by one byte at a time, a form suited to a database that stores millions of small values (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The Compact encoding of nBits is not a variable-length integer at all but a base-and-exponent representation of a 256-bit target in four bytes, which chapter 12 of the book explains under mining; it belongs to blocks, not to transactions.

The caution is to let the context decide the encoding rather than the word. Inside a serialized transaction, every count and every length is compactSize, without exception; inside Bitcoin Core's own files other encodings appear, and a program that reads those files needs their rules. A second caution is that the compactSize encoding is not unique in principle - 1 could be written as fd0100 - but Bitcoin Core treats a non-minimal encoding as an error, so a parser should refuse it too (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.definition: Bitcoin programs use several variable-length integers: compactSize in transactions and the P2P protocol, Bitcoin Core's VarInts in its UTXO database, and the unrelated Compact encoding of a block header's nBits field.
