nodes.label: The outpoint
nodes.body: The outpoint is the field with which an input points at the previous output it spends. The book explains it from the definition of a transaction: a transaction is a request for full nodes to update their database of coin ownership information, and for Alice to transfer control of some of her bitcoins she first needs to tell full nodes how to find the previous transfer where she received them; since control is assigned in transaction outputs, Alice points to the previous output using an outpoint, and each input must contain a single outpoint (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The outpoint is the field with which an input points at the previous output it spends. The book explains it from the definition of a transaction: a transaction is a request for full nodes to update their database of coin ownership information, and for Alice to transfer control of some of her bitcoins she first needs to tell full nodes how to find the previous transfer where she received them; since control is assigned in transaction outputs, Alice points to the previous output using an outpoint, and each input must contain a single outpoint (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The outpoint is the whole of what an input says about value. An input carries no amount; the amount is the amount of the output the outpoint names, and all of it is transferred. The book lists what a full node obtains on finding the previous output - its amount, its authorization conditions, the height and median time past of its confirming block, and proof that it exists and has not been spent - and it is from these that every later check proceeds (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The rule that no output may be spent twice is a rule about outpoints: two transactions that name the same one conflict.

The six sections take the 36 bytes and their consequences in turn: the outpoint as a field, the 32-byte transaction identifier it begins with, the 4-byte output index that follows, the rule against double spending, the conflicting transactions that rule produces, and the database of unspent outputs that Bitcoin Core keeps so that the lookup is fast and the rule can be enforced (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Outpoint
nodes.body: An outpoint is the field of an input that points at the output being spent. The book says that since control over bitcoins is assigned in transaction outputs, Alice points to the previous output using an outpoint field, that each input must contain a single outpoint, and that the outpoint contains a 32-byte txid for the transaction where Alice received the bitcoins she now wants to spend, followed by the output index (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The name is a contraction: a point to an output.

paras.text: An outpoint is the field of an input that points at the output being spent. The book says that since control over bitcoins is assigned in transaction outputs, Alice points to the previous output using an outpoint field, that each input must contain a single outpoint, and that the outpoint contains a 32-byte txid for the transaction where Alice received the bitcoins she now wants to spend, followed by the output index (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The name is a contraction: a point to an output.

The outpoint is what makes the ownership record a chain. Chapter 2 drew Alice's payment as a link in a chain of transactions, each spending an output of an earlier one (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); the outpoint is that link written as bytes. Because the identifier is a hash of the previous transaction, an outpoint commits to the whole of the transaction it names, and because the index chooses one output, two inputs that name the same outpoint claim the same bitcoins, which is the double-spending situation the later section describes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The worked example cuts the 36 bytes at offset 7 of Alice's transaction - after the version, the marker, the flag and the input count - and reads them as the transaction identifier, which it reverses into display order, and the index 1. A full node that encounters an outpoint uses the information to find the referenced output, and the book notes that it is only required to look at earlier transactions in the blockchain: within the block that contains the spending transaction, only at transactions placed before it, as determined by the order of leaves in the block's merkle tree (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The explorer that this course consulted reports the same identifier and index for Alice's input (mempool.space, 2026).

The caution is that the identifier in the outpoint is written in Bitcoin's internal byte order, so the 32 bytes read directly do not match what an explorer displays; the byte-order group explains the reversal, which the worked example performs. A second caution is that an outpoint names an output, not a transaction: the previous transaction in Alice's chain had two outputs, and the index 1 chooses the second of them, the one of 100,000 satoshis that chapter 2 followed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (mempool.space, 2026).

nodes.example: 36 bytes: a txid and an index
nodes.definition: An outpoint is the 32-byte txid of a previous transaction followed by the 4-byte index of one of its outputs; every input has exactly one, and a node uses it to find the output being spent.

nodes.label: The previous transaction's identifier
nodes.body: The previous transaction's identifier is the first part of an outpoint: the book says the outpoint contains a 32-byte txid for the transaction where Alice received the bitcoins she now wants to spend, and that this txid is in Bitcoin's internal byte order for hashes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A txid is a digest, the output of a hash function run over the transaction's serialization; chapter 4 introduced hash functions and the double application of SHA-256 that Bitcoin uses for its identifiers, and the foundations group of this chapter returns to how a txid is computed.

paras.text: The previous transaction's identifier is the first part of an outpoint: the book says the outpoint contains a 32-byte txid for the transaction where Alice received the bitcoins she now wants to spend, and that this txid is in Bitcoin's internal byte order for hashes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A txid is a digest, the output of a hash function run over the transaction's serialization; chapter 4 introduced hash functions and the double application of SHA-256 that Bitcoin uses for its identifiers, and the foundations group of this chapter returns to how a txid is computed.

The identifier is what ties the input to exactly one earlier transaction. Because it is a hash of that transaction's bytes, no other transaction has it, and a change of a single byte in the earlier transaction would change it entirely - which is the property that makes malleability dangerous, as the witness branch explains: if the earlier transaction's identifier can change, every outpoint that names it breaks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the book's example the identifier is eb3ae38f... in the bytes, which displays as 4ac54180..., the transaction that paid Alice in block 774,958 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (mempool.space, 2026).

The worked example takes the 32 bytes as they stand in the outpoint, confirms their length, and reverses them to obtain the first sixteen hexadecimal characters of the display form. A full node uses the internal form as a key into its database of unspent outputs; a user uses the display form in an explorer or a command line, and the book's own demonstration of asking Bitcoin Core for the internal form and receiving an error is reproduced in the byte-order group (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The caution is the one the book makes its sidebar about: the same 32 bytes have two spellings, and a program that mixes them looks up a transaction that does not exist. The second caution is that a transaction identifier only commits to the legacy serialization, so for a segwit transaction the signature that authorises the spend is not part of what the identifier covers; that is deliberate and is the subject of the witness branch (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

nodes.example: the first 32 bytes of an outpoint
nodes.definition: The txid in an outpoint is the 32-byte double-SHA-256 identifier of the transaction that created the output being spent, stored in internal byte order.

nodes.label: Output index
nodes.body: The output index is the second part of an outpoint. The book explains that because transactions may contain multiple outputs, Alice also needs to identify which particular output from that transaction to use, called its output index, and that output indexes are 4-byte unsigned integers starting from zero (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In Alice's transaction the index bytes are 01000000, which the worked example reads as 1, the second output of the previous transaction.

paras.text: The output index is the second part of an outpoint. The book explains that because transactions may contain multiple outputs, Alice also needs to identify which particular output from that transaction to use, called its output index, and that output indexes are 4-byte unsigned integers starting from zero (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In Alice's transaction the index bytes are 01000000, which the worked example reads as 1, the second output of the previous transaction.

The index is why an outpoint identifies an output rather than a transaction. Most transactions have at least two outputs, a payment and change, and the one being spent must be named exactly; naming the transaction alone would be ambiguous and would let a spender claim both. The previous transaction in Alice's chain has two outputs, 18,210,494 satoshis at index 0 and 100,000 satoshis at index 1, and her outpoint chooses the second (mempool.space, 2026).

The field is a fixed four bytes in little-endian order, so the value 1 is written as 01 followed by three zero bytes, and the largest possible index is 0xffffffff. That maximal value has a special use: the coinbase transaction of every block, which creates bitcoins rather than spending an output, sets its single outpoint to a null txid and this maximal index, as the coinbase group explains (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For every ordinary input, the index must be smaller than the number of outputs of the referenced transaction, or the output does not exist and the node rejects the transaction.

The caution is that indexes start at zero, so the first output is output 0 and the book's phrase second output means index 1. A reader counting from one will spend the wrong output, and an explorer that labels outputs from zero and a wallet that labels them from one can describe the same outpoint with different numbers.

nodes.example: four bytes counting from zero
nodes.definition: The output index is the 4-byte unsigned integer after the txid in an outpoint; it chooses one output of the previous transaction, counting from zero.

nodes.label: The rule against double spending
nodes.body: The rule against double spending is the consensus rule that forbids any output from being spent more than once within a valid blockchain. The book states it among the things a full node obtains from the previous output - proof that it exists and that no other transaction has spent it - and gives the example: Alice cannot use the same previous output to pay both Bob and Carol in separate transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Chapter 2 introduced the problem that this rule solves; this chapter shows where in the data the rule is checked.

paras.text: The rule against double spending is the consensus rule that forbids any output from being spent more than once within a valid blockchain. The book states it among the things a full node obtains from the previous output - proof that it exists and that no other transaction has spent it - and gives the example: Alice cannot use the same previous output to pay both Bob and Carol in separate transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Chapter 2 introduced the problem that this rule solves; this chapter shows where in the data the rule is checked.

The rule is the reason the outpoint is enough. Because each output can be spent once, the outpoint names a fixed quantity of bitcoins that the spending transaction takes in full, and the node can delete the output from its record after the spend. Without the rule, Bitcoin would be a copyable file rather than a scarce record, which is the problem chapter 1 called the copy problem. The rule is also why conflicting transactions exist as a category: a second transaction naming the same outpoint is not wrong in form, it is simply the one that lost (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A node enforces the rule by lookup rather than by search. The worked example models the simplest form: a set of spent outpoints, and a refusal when the new outpoint is already in it. Bitcoin Core does the converse, keeping the set of unspent outputs and refusing an outpoint that is not in it, and its CheckTransaction additionally refuses a transaction that names the same outpoint twice among its own inputs, with the error bad-txns-inputs-duplicate; the source comment records that this check guards against a crash or an inflation bug depending on the database (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The caution is in the words within a valid blockchain. Two conflicting transactions can both exist in the network at once, and both may be relayed for a time; the rule only says that a chain of blocks containing both is invalid, so one of them, and only one, will ever be confirmed. The second caution is that the rule says nothing about which one, which is the gap that the sequence branch's replacement policies and the witness branch's malleability problems both live in (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: an output is spent at most once
nodes.definition: One of Bitcoin's consensus rules forbids any output from being spent more than once within a valid blockchain: Alice cannot use the same previous output to pay both Bob and Carol.

nodes.label: Conflicting transactions
nodes.body: Conflicting transactions are two transactions that each try to spend the same previous output. The book defines them in the sentence after the double-spending rule and gives their property: they are called conflicting because only one of them can be included in a valid blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example tests two input lists for a shared outpoint and reports the conflict.

paras.text: Conflicting transactions are two transactions that each try to spend the same previous output. The book defines them in the sentence after the double-spending rule and gives their property: they are called conflicting because only one of them can be included in a valid blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example tests two input lists for a shared outpoint and reports the conflict.

The category matters because conflicts are not always attacks. The book's own examples in the sequence branch are deliberate: Alice and Bob sign many versions of one transaction, each spending the same output, and intend only the last to confirm; replace-by-fee is a conflict a sender creates on purpose to raise a fee; and the malleability problems of the witness branch are conflicts created by a third party or a counterparty against the sender's wish (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same data structure covers all of them, and what differs is who created the conflict and why.

A conflict is detected by comparing outpoints. Two transactions conflict if any input of one names an outpoint that any input of the other names, which is what the worked example's set intersection does. A full node that already holds one unconfirmed transaction and receives a conflicting one must choose: the original Bitcoin software chose by sequence number, later software refused the second one, and current software applies replace-by-fee rules, all of which the sequence branch describes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Harding and Todd, 2015). Once one of them is in a block, the choice is made for everyone.

The caution is that a conflicting transaction can have a different identifier while spending the same money, so a payee who watches for a specific txid can miss the payment that actually confirmed. The book's malleability example is exactly this: a mutated copy of Alice's transaction confirms, her original cannot, and Bob's transaction that spent her original output becomes invalid even though nobody acted wrongly (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Watching outpoints rather than identifiers is the defence.

nodes.label: The UTXO database
nodes.body: The UTXO database is the record Bitcoin Core keeps of every unspent transaction output. The book says that different approaches to tracking previous outputs have been tried by different full node implementations, and that Bitcoin Core currently uses the solution believed most effective at retaining all necessary information while minimising disk space: a database that stores every UTXO and essential metadata about it, such as its confirmation block height; each time a new block arrives, all the outputs its transactions spend are removed and all the outputs they create are added (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The UTXO database is the record Bitcoin Core keeps of every unspent transaction output. The book says that different approaches to tracking previous outputs have been tried by different full node implementations, and that Bitcoin Core currently uses the solution believed most effective at retaining all necessary information while minimising disk space: a database that stores every UTXO and essential metadata about it, such as its confirmation block height; each time a new block arrives, all the outputs its transactions spend are removed and all the outputs they create are added (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The database is what turns the double-spending rule from a search into a lookup. Without it, a node checking an outpoint would have to scan the whole blockchain to find the output and then scan again to be sure nothing spent it; with it, the node asks one question of one table. The metadata is what makes the other checks possible: the height is needed for the maturity rule of coinbase outputs and for relative timelocks, which the book names as the reason a node records it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The database is also the reason uneconomical outputs are a public cost, since every entry must be kept by every node, a point the outputs branch takes up.

The worked example runs one update by hand: starting from the two outputs of the transaction that paid Alice, it removes the one her input spends and adds the two her transaction creates, Bob's 20,000 satoshis and her change of 75,000, leaving three entries. A real node does this for every transaction of every block in order, and the book notes that the database is a few gigabytes - it mentions over five gigabytes as of its writing - which a later proposal called Utreexo hopes to replace with a commitment of a kilobyte or two for most nodes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (mempool.space, 2026).

The caution is that the database is a consequence of the blockchain, not a part of it. It can be rebuilt from the blocks and it is not transmitted between nodes; two nodes that have processed the same blocks hold the same set, but neither trusts the other's copy. A second caution is that a UTXO is identified by an outpoint, not by an address, so the database can hold many entries for one address and the balance a wallet shows is a sum the wallet computes, not a value the node stores.

nodes.example: remove what is spent, add what is created
nodes.definition: Bitcoin Core keeps a database of every unspent transaction output with essential metadata; each new block removes the outputs its transactions spend and adds the outputs they create.

nodes.label: Internal and display byte order
nodes.body: This group explains the book's sidebar on the two byte orders of a hash. The book says Bitcoin uses the output of hash functions, called digests, in various ways - as identifiers for blocks and transactions, in commitments, and in proof of work - and that in some cases digests are displayed to users in one byte order but used internally in a different byte order, creating confusion (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It names the two: internal byte order for data within transactions and blocks, display byte order for the form shown to users.

paras.text: This group explains the book's sidebar on the two byte orders of a hash. The book says Bitcoin uses the output of hash functions, called digests, in various ways - as identifiers for blocks and transactions, in commitments, and in proof of work - and that in some cases digests are displayed to users in one byte order but used internally in a different byte order, creating confusion (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It names the two: internal byte order for data within transactions and blocks, display byte order for the form shown to users.

The confusion is real and the book demonstrates it: asked for the transaction whose identifier appears in Alice's outpoint, Bitcoin Core replies that there is no such transaction, and only after the bytes are reversed does it return the transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book calls the behaviour probably an unintentional consequence of a design decision in early Bitcoin software and draws the practical lesson that developers need to remember to reverse the order of bytes in transaction and block identifiers they show to users (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The three sections explain the digest itself, the internal order in which a digest is stored and hashed, and the display order in which it is printed, with the book's own shell pipeline - fold, tac, tr - recomputed in Python so that the reversal can be checked. The alternative names the book gives, little-endian for the internal and big-endian for the display form, are explained in the display section (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Digest
nodes.body: A digest is the output of a hash function. The book's sidebar says Bitcoin uses digests in various ways: they provide unique identifiers for blocks and transactions, they are used in commitments for addresses, blocks, transactions, signatures and more, and they are iterated upon in Bitcoin's proof-of-work function (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Chapter 4 introduced the hash function as a one-way function with a fixed-length output; here the output has a name because its byte order is about to matter.

paras.text: A digest is the output of a hash function. The book's sidebar says Bitcoin uses digests in various ways: they provide unique identifiers for blocks and transactions, they are used in commitments for addresses, blocks, transactions, signatures and more, and they are iterated upon in Bitcoin's proof-of-work function (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Chapter 4 introduced the hash function as a one-way function with a fixed-length output; here the output has a name because its byte order is about to matter.

Digests are the glue of the data structures in this chapter. A transaction identifier is a digest of the transaction, an outpoint carries that digest, and a block commits to its transactions through a tree of digests, so the same 32 bytes travel from the hash function into an outpoint and onto a user's screen. The book's warning is that those bytes are shown in one order and used in another, and a digest is the thing that is reversed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The worked example computes the double SHA-256 of a short byte string and reports its length, 32 bytes, which is the length of every transaction and block identifier. Bitcoin applies SHA-256 twice for these identifiers, a construction the foundations group explains; the first application gives 32 bytes and the second gives 32 bytes again, so the length does not depend on the input. Any change to the input changes the digest unpredictably, which is why a digest can serve as a commitment: showing the digest first and the data later proves the data was fixed in advance.

The caution is that a digest is a value, not a text, and the same value has two hexadecimal spellings in Bitcoin, which the next two sections explain. A second caution is that the uniqueness of a digest as an identifier is practical rather than absolute: two different transactions with the same identifier are astronomically unlikely but not impossible in principle, and BIP30 exists because two early coinbase transactions were in fact identical and therefore had identical identifiers (Wuille, 2012).

nodes.definition: A digest is the output of a hash function; Bitcoin uses digests as identifiers of blocks and transactions, in commitments, and in proof of work.

nodes.label: Internal byte order
nodes.body: Internal byte order is the book's term for the data as it appears within transactions and blocks. The book introduces the term in its sidebar, after the demonstration that the identifier in Alice's outpoint has to be reversed before Bitcoin Core recognises it, and offers the alternative pair of names: little-endian byte order for the internal version and big-endian byte order for the display version (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The 32 bytes of an outpoint's txid are in internal order.

paras.text: Internal byte order is the book's term for the data as it appears within transactions and blocks. The book introduces the term in its sidebar, after the demonstration that the identifier in Alice's outpoint has to be reversed before Bitcoin Core recognises it, and offers the alternative pair of names: little-endian byte order for the internal version and big-endian byte order for the display version (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The 32 bytes of an outpoint's txid are in internal order.

The order matters because it is the one the hash function sees. A node computing a block's merkle tree, a transaction's identifier or the previous-block link of a header hashes digests in internal order, so a program that reversed them would compute different digests and reject valid blocks. The book calls the split probably an unintentional consequence of a design decision in early Bitcoin software, which stored 256-bit numbers as little-endian integers and printed them as numbers, with the most significant byte first (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The worked example takes the display form of the identifier of the transaction that paid Alice and reverses its bytes to obtain the internal form, eb3ae38f..., which is exactly what the outpoint of her transaction contains. Reversal is its own inverse, so the same operation converts in either direction; the chapter's library names both directions for readability but implements one function. The explorer that this course consulted shows the display form, and the byte at offset 7 of Alice's transaction is eb, the first byte of the internal form (mempool.space, 2026).

The caution is to reverse digests and nothing else. The little-endian integers of a transaction - version, amount, index, sequence, lock time - are also stored least significant byte first, but they are read as numbers, not reversed as strings; a reader who reverses a 4-byte sequence as if it were a digest gets a wrong value. Only the 32-byte identifiers have the two spellings the book describes.

nodes.example: the order inside the bytes
nodes.definition: Internal byte order is the order in which a digest's bytes appear within transactions and blocks and are fed to hash functions; the book also calls it little-endian.

nodes.label: Display byte order
nodes.body: Display byte order is the book's term for the form of a digest displayed to users. The sidebar shows the need for it: asking Bitcoin Core for the identifier as it appears in the outpoint returns the error no such mempool or blockchain transaction, and the book then reverses the bytes with a shell pipeline - echo the hex, fold it into two-character pairs, reverse the lines with tac, delete the newlines - and the reversed identifier returns the transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Display byte order is the book's term for the form of a digest displayed to users. The sidebar shows the need for it: asking Bitcoin Core for the identifier as it appears in the outpoint returns the error no such mempool or blockchain transaction, and the book then reverses the bytes with a shell pipeline - echo the hex, fold it into two-character pairs, reverse the lines with tac, delete the newlines - and the reversed identifier returns the transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The display form is the one every user handles: it is what an explorer prints, what a wallet shows as a transaction identifier, what bitcoin-cli accepts, and what this chapter writes when it names a transaction. The book draws the practical consequence for developers, who need to remember to reverse the order of bytes in transaction and block identifiers they show to users, and it fixes its own vocabulary so that the two forms can be named without ambiguity (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The worked example performs the book's pipeline in Python: the internal form is cut into 32 two-character pairs, the pairs are reversed, and the result is the display form 4ac54180..., which the explorer confirms as the identifier of the transaction that paid Alice (mempool.space, 2026). The book notes that another common pair of terms is little-endian for the internal and big-endian for the display version, from the two conventions for writing a multi-byte number; the display form reads like a number with its most significant byte first (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The caution is the one that produced the book's error message: a display-order identifier pasted into a field that expects internal order, or the reverse, names a transaction that does not exist, and the failure is a not-found rather than a format error. A second caution is that block identifiers follow the same convention, and the leading zeros that a user sees at the start of a block hash are, in internal order, trailing zeros - which is why the proof-of-work target is said to require leading zeros in display order.

nodes.example: the order on the screen
nodes.definition: Display byte order is the reversed form in which identifiers are shown to users and accepted by explorers and bitcoin-cli; the book also calls it big-endian.

nodes.label: The input script
nodes.body: The input script is the second field of every input, after the outpoint and before the sequence, and it is length-prefixed. The book calls the field a remnant of the legacy transaction format: Alice's example input spends a native segwit output that does not require any data in the input script, so the length prefix for her input script is zero, and the book takes an input script from a legacy transaction in the most recent block as of its writing to show what a filled one looks like (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The input script is the second field of every input, after the outpoint and before the sequence, and it is length-prefixed. The book calls the field a remnant of the legacy transaction format: Alice's example input spends a native segwit output that does not require any data in the input script, so the length prefix for her input script is zero, and the book takes an input script from a legacy transaction in the most recent block as of its writing to show what a filled one looks like (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The field matters for what it used to hold and for why it is now often empty. In the legacy format signatures and other data are placed in the input script, so it is where a legacy transaction proves it is authorised; and because that data was included in the hash that makes a txid, it is where the malleability problems of the witness branch arose. Segregated witness moved that data out of the field, which is why a modern input often carries only a zero length byte (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The two sections cover the field and its prefix. The input script section explains what a legacy input script contains, using the book's 107-byte example of a signature followed by a public key, and why Alice's is empty; the length prefix section explains the compactSize byte that precedes the script, which is 0x6b for the book's example and 0x00 for Alice's, and why a parser cannot find the sequence without it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Input script
nodes.body: The input script is the field of an input that, in the legacy format, carries the signatures and other data that authorise the spend. The book says the field is a remnant of the legacy transaction format: Alice's example input spends a native segwit output that does not require any data in the input script, so its length prefix is set to zero, and for an example of a length-prefixed input script that spends a legacy output the book takes one from an arbitrary transaction in the most recent block as of its writing, a script of 107 bytes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The input script is the field of an input that, in the legacy format, carries the signatures and other data that authorise the spend. The book says the field is a remnant of the legacy transaction format: Alice's example input spends a native segwit output that does not require any data in the input script, so its length prefix is set to zero, and for an example of a length-prefixed input script that spends a legacy output the book takes one from an arbitrary transaction in the most recent block as of its writing, a script of 107 bytes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The field is where authorisation lived before segregated witness and the reason it moved. Chapter 4 explained that spending requires a signature made with the private key matching the public key an output names; in a legacy transaction that signature and that public key are pushed onto the stack by the input script, and the output script checks them. Because the input script is part of the bytes a txid is computed over, anyone who could rewrite it without invalidating the signature could change the txid, which is the third-party malleability of the witness branch; an empty input script is immune (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The worked example parses the book's 107-byte legacy input script by its own structure: the first byte, 0x48, is a push of 72 bytes, the signature; the byte after the signature, 0x21, is a push of 33 bytes, the compressed public key; and one plus 72 plus one plus 33 is 107, the whole script. The push opcodes are met again in the malleability section, where the same number can be pushed in several ways. The book defers parsing and using scripts to the next chapter; here it is enough to see that the field is data for a stack machine, and that Alice's transaction has none of it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The caution is that an empty input script does not mean an unauthorised spend. Alice's transaction is authorised by the 65-byte signature in its witness structure, which the witness branch reads; the input script is empty because the output she spends is a segwit output, and the book says that for such outputs new nodes require the input script to be empty while old nodes merely allow it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A second caution is that the 107-byte example is not from Alice's transaction and its signature cannot be checked here, since the output it spends is not in the chapter.

nodes.example: 107 bytes for a legacy spend, 0 for segwit
nodes.definition: The input script is the legacy field in which a spending transaction places its signatures and other authorising data; a segwit input leaves it empty.

nodes.label: Script length prefix
nodes.body: The length prefix is the compactSize unsigned integer that precedes an input script and gives its length in bytes. The book explains it on its legacy example: the prefix is a single byte, 0x6b, indicating that the input script is 107 bytes, and on Alice's transaction, where the prefix is zero because a native segwit input needs no input script (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same kind of prefix precedes every output script and every witness item in the chapter.

paras.text: The length prefix is the compactSize unsigned integer that precedes an input script and gives its length in bytes. The book explains it on its legacy example: the prefix is a single byte, 0x6b, indicating that the input script is 107 bytes, and on Alice's transaction, where the prefix is zero because a native segwit input needs no input script (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same kind of prefix precedes every output script and every witness item in the chapter.

The prefix is what makes a variable field parseable. An input script has no terminator and may contain any bytes, so the only way a parser can know where the script ends and the sequence begins is to be told the length first; a wrong prefix shifts every later field and corrupts the whole transaction. The prefix is also counted in the transaction's size and weight - the book's weight table charges Alice's empty input script four weight units, which are the four-times-weighted single byte of its prefix (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The worked example shows the arithmetic the book states: 0x6b is 107, and reading the byte as a little-endian integer gives the same; Alice's prefix is 0x00. Because the prefix is compactSize, a script longer than 252 bytes would need the 0xfd form with two further bytes, which happens for some multisignature input scripts. Bitcoin Core's relay policy caps a standard input script at 1,650 bytes, a limit its policy header names MAX_STANDARD_SCRIPTSIG_SIZE, while consensus allows up to the script size limit of 10,000 bytes (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The caution is that the prefix counts bytes of script, not elements of it: the book's example holds two pushes, a signature and a public key, but the prefix says 107, the total length, and a parser learns the structure inside only by executing the script's push opcodes. A second caution is that the prefix is present even when the script is empty, as Alice's transaction shows; the field is never omitted, only its content.

nodes.example: 0x6b says 107 bytes follow
nodes.definition: The length prefix is the compactSize integer before an input script that says how many bytes of script follow; it is 0x6b for the book's 107-byte example and 0x00 for Alice's empty script.

nodes.label: The sequence field
nodes.body: This branch reads the last four bytes of an input, which the book calls its sequence number, and follows the three meanings the field has carried. The book says the use and meaning of this field has changed over time: it was originally intended to allow creation of multiple versions of the same transaction, with later versions replacing earlier versions as candidates for confirmation; it was later used as the signal for opt-in replace-by-fee; and since BIP68 it is a consensus-enforced relative timelock for transactions of version 2 or higher (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This branch reads the last four bytes of an input, which the book calls its sequence number, and follows the three meanings the field has carried. The book says the use and meaning of this field has changed over time: it was originally intended to allow creation of multiple versions of the same transaction, with later versions replacing earlier versions as candidates for confirmation; it was later used as the signal for opt-in replace-by-fee; and since BIP68 it is a consensus-enforced relative timelock for transactions of version 2 or higher (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The field matters out of proportion to its size because it is the hook on which Bitcoin's contract protocols hang. The book's first use of it is a card game between Alice and Bob that is, in effect, the first payment channel; its second use decides whether an unconfirmed payment can be replaced, which is what a merchant waiting for a payment needs to know; and its third use lets an output be made unspendable until it has aged, which the Lightning Network depends on (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Friedenbach et al., 2015) (Harding and Todd, 2015). Alice's transaction sets it to 0xffffffff, the value that opts out of all three.

The reader meets the field in every input of every transaction, usually as ffffffff, and meets its meanings in three places: in a wallet's choice to make a payment replaceable, which sets the value to 0xfffffffd; in explorers, which flag such transactions as replaceable; and in the construction of any protocol that uses relative timelocks, where BIP68's encoding of blocks and seconds must be computed exactly. Bitcoin Core's transaction header declares the constants - SEQUENCE_FINAL, the disable flag, the type flag, the mask and the granularity - that this branch computes with (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The branch has three groups in the historical order of the book. The first explains the original replacement scheme and the payment channel it enabled: the setup transaction, the refund, the rounds of a card game, and the three problems that led the scheme to be disabled, including a bandwidth attack that the book costs out. The second explains replace-by-fee and the BIP125 signal. The third explains the BIP68 timelock: which sequence values are locks, the type flag that chooses blocks or 512-second units, the disable flag, and the 16-bit mask (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Original sequence-based replacement
nodes.body: The original sequence-based replacement is the first meaning of the field: the book says the sequence field was originally intended to allow creation of multiple versions of the same transaction, with later versions replacing earlier versions as candidates for confirmation, the sequence number tracking the version of the transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This group follows the book's example of Alice and Bob betting on a game of cards, names the kind of protocol it is, and gives the three problems that ended the scheme.

paras.text: The original sequence-based replacement is the first meaning of the field: the book says the sequence field was originally intended to allow creation of multiple versions of the same transaction, with later versions replacing earlier versions as candidates for confirmation, the sequence number tracking the version of the transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This group follows the book's example of Alice and Bob betting on a game of cards, names the kind of protocol it is, and gives the three problems that ended the scheme.

The scheme matters as the ancestor of every payment channel. The book says this type of protocol is what we now call a payment channel, that Bitcoin's creator in an email attributed to him called these high-frequency transactions, and that modern versions of payment channels are increasingly used in Bitcoin today (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Understanding why the original scheme failed - a policy with no incentive, a race that bad luck could lose, and an unlimited free replacement that burdened every node - explains the design of its successors (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The four sections take the story in order. The sequence number section states the field and the final value. The setup and refund section explains the multisignature deposit and the first, refund version of the spend. The payment channel section follows the rounds in which the sequence is incremented and the balances move, and the alternative scenarios in which an old version is broadcast. The replacement attack section costs out the bandwidth attack that led to the scheme being disabled in an early version of the software (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Sequence number
nodes.body: The sequence number is the four-byte unsigned integer that ends each input, after the outpoint and the input script. The book says the final four bytes of an input are its sequence number and that the use and meaning of this field has changed over time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In Alice's transaction the bytes are ffffffff, the maximal value, which the worked example reads as 4,294,967,295; Bitcoin Core names that value SEQUENCE_FINAL (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: The sequence number is the four-byte unsigned integer that ends each input, after the outpoint and the input script. The book says the final four bytes of an input are its sequence number and that the use and meaning of this field has changed over time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In Alice's transaction the bytes are ffffffff, the maximal value, which the worked example reads as 4,294,967,295; Bitcoin Core names that value SEQUENCE_FINAL (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The number matters because it is a per-input field, not a per-transaction one. Each input carries its own, so one transaction can have inputs with different sequence values, which is what lets BIP68 lock some inputs and not others, and what the book notes when it says a transaction may contain any number of timelocked inputs, all of which must have sufficiently aged (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Friedenbach et al., 2015). The maximal value is the one that means nothing special under every rule: no replacement in the original scheme, no BIP125 signal, no relative timelock, and no lock time either, since Bitcoin Core ignores a lock time when every input is final (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The field is read as a little-endian integer, so ffffffff is the maximum and 00000000 the minimum. The original software compared sequence values to choose between versions of a transaction, with the highest winning; BIP125 reads any value up to 0xfffffffd as a signal; BIP68 reads the bits of a value below 2 to the 31 as a timelock; and the lock-time rule reads the value only to see whether it is final (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Harding and Todd, 2015) (Friedenbach et al., 2015) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). All four readings are of the same four bytes, and the later groups give each its own section.

The caution is that the word sequence suggests an order of inputs, which it is not; the inputs are ordered by their position in the list, and the sequence is a per-input number with the meanings above. A second caution is historical: a reader who meets sequence described as a transaction version counter in old material is reading about the first meaning, which the book says was disabled in an early version of the software (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: the last four bytes of an input
nodes.definition: The sequence is the 4-byte field that ends every input; its maximal value 0xffffffff, called final, opts out of replacement, of the BIP125 signal and of any relative timelock.

nodes.label: Setup and refund transactions
nodes.body: The setup transaction is the first transaction of the book's card game. Alice and Bob start by each signing a transaction that deposits some money into an output with a script that requires signatures from both of them to spend, a multisignature script, multisig for short, and this is called the setup transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The first version of the transaction that spends that output, with sequence 0, pays Alice and Bob back the money they initially deposited; this is called a refund transaction, and neither of them broadcasts it, since they only need it if there is a problem (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The setup transaction is the first transaction of the book's card game. Alice and Bob start by each signing a transaction that deposits some money into an output with a script that requires signatures from both of them to spend, a multisignature script, multisig for short, and this is called the setup transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The first version of the transaction that spends that output, with sequence 0, pays Alice and Bob back the money they initially deposited; this is called a refund transaction, and neither of them broadcasts it, since they only need it if there is a problem (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The pair matters because it is the skeleton of every contract between two parties on Bitcoin. A multisignature output is one that neither party can spend alone, which chapter 5 met as the arrangement in which several signers each hold a key and the book's next chapter explains as a script; the refund is what makes depositing into such an output safe, because either party can get their money back if the other disappears (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example models the deposit as two amounts that sum to the output, the state from which every later version of the spend redistributes.

The two transactions are created in a particular order. Both parties must sign the refund before the setup is broadcast, or one of them could lock the other's money forever by refusing to cooperate; the witness branch shows that in the legacy format this ordering is impossible without trust, because the refund must name the setup's identifier, which depends on signatures that are not yet known, a circular dependency (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The sequence field's role is only in the versions of the spend: the refund carries sequence 0 so that any later version, with a higher sequence, replaces it.

The caution is that a refund with sequence 0 could, under the original software, be replaced by any transaction with a higher sequence, so it protected a party only until the other broadcast a later version; the book's alternative scenarios show the race. A second caution is that the setup's multisignature output has nothing to do with the sequence field; the field lives in the spending transactions, and the deposit itself uses a final sequence.

nodes.example: a deposit that needs both signatures
nodes.definition: The setup transaction deposits Alice's and Bob's money into a multisignature output that needs both signatures; the refund transaction, with sequence 0, pays each their deposit back and is kept unbroadcast.

nodes.label: Payment channel
nodes.body: A payment channel is the kind of protocol the book's card game describes: the book says this type of protocol is what we now call a payment channel, and that Bitcoin's creator, in an email attributed to him, called these high-frequency transactions and described a number of features added to the protocol to support them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Alice wins the first round, so the second version of the transaction, with sequence 1, increases her share; Bob wins the second, so the sequence becomes 2 and the shares move back; after many rounds they set the sequence to its maximum, 0xffffffff, finalise, and broadcast only that version (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A payment channel is the kind of protocol the book's card game describes: the book says this type of protocol is what we now call a payment channel, and that Bitcoin's creator, in an email attributed to him, called these high-frequency transactions and described a number of features added to the protocol to support them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Alice wins the first round, so the second version of the transaction, with sequence 1, increases her share; Bob wins the second, so the sequence becomes 2 and the shares move back; after many rounds they set the sequence to its maximum, 0xffffffff, finalise, and broadcast only that version (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The channel matters because it moves value many times with one confirmed transaction. Every version is a complete, signed, valid transaction that spends the setup output, but only the last is broadcast, so the chain records one setup and one settlement no matter how many rounds were played. The book's alternative scenarios show what the replacement rule was for: if Bob broadcasts an earlier version where his balance was higher, full nodes running the original code will not relay it against a version with a higher sequence, and miners using that code will not mine it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The worked example plays two rounds: the refund with sequence 0 and equal balances, Alice winning 10,000, Bob winning 25,000, and then the final version with the maximal sequence, four versions in all, the last paying Alice 35,000 and Bob 65,000. In the original software the rule was simple - a higher sequence replaces a lower one - and the book's second scenario shows its weakness: if Bob's old version is broadcast a few seconds before Alice's final one, nodes relay Bob's and miners try to mine it, and unless Bob gets lucky and a block is found first, Alice's version replaces it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The caution is in the words unless Bob got lucky. The book names three problems with purely sequence-based channels: the replacement rule was only software policy with no incentive for miners to prefer one version, the first transaction sent might get confirmed by luck even when it was not the highest-sequence one, and a security protocol that fails a few percent of the time due to bad luck is not a very effective protocol (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Modern channels fix these with timelocks and penalties, which the book defers to its chapter on second-layer applications.

nodes.example: many versions, one broadcast
nodes.definition: A payment channel is a protocol in which two parties sign many versions of one transaction off the chain, each with a higher sequence, and broadcast only the final one; the book's card game is the original form.

nodes.label: The replacement bandwidth attack
nodes.body: The replacement bandwidth attack is the third problem the book gives with the original scheme: it was possible to replace one version of a transaction with a different version an unlimited number of times, and each replacement would consume the bandwidth of all the relaying full nodes on the network. The book's figures: with about 50,000 relaying full nodes, an attacker creating 1,000 replacement transactions per minute at 200 bytes each would use about 20 KB of their own bandwidth but about 10 GB of full-node network bandwidth every minute (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The replacement bandwidth attack is the third problem the book gives with the original scheme: it was possible to replace one version of a transaction with a different version an unlimited number of times, and each replacement would consume the bandwidth of all the relaying full nodes on the network. The book's figures: with about 50,000 relaying full nodes, an attacker creating 1,000 replacement transactions per minute at 200 bytes each would use about 20 KB of their own bandwidth but about 10 GB of full-node network bandwidth every minute (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The attack matters because it is the reason replacement was removed and then returned in a restricted form. The book says that except for the cost of their 20 KB per minute and the occasional fee when a transaction was confirmed, the attacker would pay nothing for the enormous burden placed on full-node operators, and that to eliminate the risk the original type of sequence-based replacement was disabled in an early version of the software; for several years, nodes would not let an unconfirmed transaction containing a particular input be replaced at all (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The worked example recomputes the book's arithmetic: 1,000 transactions of 200 bytes is 200,000 bytes, which the book rounds to about 20 KB in the attacker's own uplink, and the same bytes relayed to 50,000 nodes is 10 gigabytes a minute across the network. The asymmetry is the whole attack: a replacement costs its sender once and costs the network once per node, and with no fee required for a replacement the ratio is unbounded. BIP125's rule that a replacement must pay more fee than what it replaces, and enough extra to pay for its own relay, is the answer the next group describes (Harding and Todd, 2015).

The caution is in the book's own figure: 1,000 transactions of 200 bytes is 200 KB, not 20 KB, so the text understates the attacker's cost by a factor of ten while the network figure of 10 GB is correct; the worked example shows both. The lesson is unchanged, since the ratio of 50,000 to one is what matters. A second caution is that the attack is about relay, not about blocks: no replacement needs to be confirmed for the damage to be done.

nodes.example: 20 KB in, 10 GB out, every minute
nodes.definition: Unlimited free replacement let an attacker with 1,000 replacements a minute at 200 bytes each cost 50,000 relaying nodes about 10 GB of bandwidth a minute for 20 KB of their own, so the scheme was disabled.

nodes.label: Opt-in replace-by-fee
nodes.body: Replace-by-fee is the second meaning of the sequence field. The book says that after the original replacement was disabled for its potential for abuse, a solution was proposed: programming Bitcoin Core and other relaying full-node software to allow a transaction that paid a higher fee rate to replace a conflicting transaction that paid a lower fee rate, called replace by fee or RBF; some users and businesses objected, so a compromise once again used the sequence field as an opt-in signal (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Replace-by-fee is the second meaning of the sequence field. The book says that after the original replacement was disabled for its potential for abuse, a solution was proposed: programming Bitcoin Core and other relaying full-node software to allow a transaction that paid a higher fee rate to replace a conflicting transaction that paid a lower fee rate, called replace by fee or RBF; some users and businesses objected, so a compromise once again used the sequence field as an opt-in signal (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The group matters for anyone who accepts an unconfirmed payment. A payment that signals replaceability can be replaced by a conflicting one before it confirms, so a merchant who sees the signal knows to wait; the book says this let users and businesses that objected to replacement simply ignore unconfirmed transactions containing the BIP125 signal until they became confirmed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It also matters to the sender, who can raise a fee that turned out too low rather than wait indefinitely.

The two sections are the policy and its signal. The opt-in replace-by-fee section explains what a replacement must do - conflict, pay a higher rate, and pay for its own bandwidth - and what Bitcoin Core allowed and disallowed; the BIP125 signal section gives the rule from the proposal, that any input with a sequence below 0xfffffffe signals replaceability, and computes which values do and do not signal (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Harding and Todd, 2015).

nodes.label: Opt-in replace-by-fee
nodes.body: Opt-in replace-by-fee is the policy under which a relaying node allows a transaction that pays a higher fee rate to replace a conflicting transaction that paid a lower fee rate, provided the original signalled that it may be replaced. The book says RBF was proposed after the original replacement was disabled, that some users and businesses objected to adding replacement back into Bitcoin Core, and that the compromise used the sequence field so that replacement is opt-in (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The fee rate is the fee divided by the transaction's size, a quantity the book's chapter on fees develops.

paras.text: Opt-in replace-by-fee is the policy under which a relaying node allows a transaction that pays a higher fee rate to replace a conflicting transaction that paid a lower fee rate, provided the original signalled that it may be replaced. The book says RBF was proposed after the original replacement was disabled, that some users and businesses objected to adding replacement back into Bitcoin Core, and that the compromise used the sequence field so that replacement is opt-in (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The fee rate is the fee divided by the transaction's size, a quantity the book's chapter on fees develops.

The policy matters because it restores a safe form of what the original scheme offered. A sender whose payment is stuck at a fee that miners ignore can issue a replacement; a payment-channel protocol can rely on a later version displacing an earlier one if it pays more; and the bandwidth attack is priced out, because each replacement must pay more than the one it replaces. Bitcoin Core's replacement checks require the replacement to pay more fees than the original transactions and to pay for its own bandwidth at or above the incremental relay fee rate (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Harding and Todd, 2015).

The worked example compares two fee rates for a transaction of 143 virtual bytes, the size of Alice's: 5,000 satoshis is about 35 satoshis per vbyte, 8,000 is about 56, and the replacement both pays more in total and has the higher rate, so it qualifies. The book notes that there is more to modern replacement policies than fee rates and sequence signals, which it takes up under a later chapter's section on replace-by-fee; BIP125 itself adds that a replacement may not add new unconfirmed inputs and may not evict more than a limited number of transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Harding and Todd, 2015).

The caution is that replace-by-fee is policy, not consensus. A node may run a different policy, a miner may mine whichever conflicting version it prefers, and nothing in the blockchain's validity rules refers to the signal; what the policy gives is predictability on the network as it is actually run. A second caution is that replacement works on conflicts, so a replacement must spend at least one of the same outpoints as the original, which is what makes it a replacement rather than a second payment (Harding and Todd, 2015).

nodes.example: a higher fee rate replaces a lower one
nodes.definition: Opt-in replace-by-fee is the relay policy under which a conflicting transaction paying a higher fee rate replaces an unconfirmed one that signalled replaceability; the replacement must also pay for its own relay.

nodes.label: The BIP125 signal
nodes.body: The BIP125 signal is the use of the sequence field as an opt-in flag for replacement. The book says that as documented in BIP125, an unconfirmed transaction with any input that has a sequence set to a value below 0xfffffffe, that is at least two below the maximum value, signals to the network that its signer wants it to be replaceable by a conflicting transaction paying a higher fee rate; Bitcoin Core allowed those unconfirmed transactions to be replaced and continued to disallow other transactions from being replaced (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The BIP125 signal is the use of the sequence field as an opt-in flag for replacement. The book says that as documented in BIP125, an unconfirmed transaction with any input that has a sequence set to a value below 0xfffffffe, that is at least two below the maximum value, signals to the network that its signer wants it to be replaceable by a conflicting transaction paying a higher fee rate; Bitcoin Core allowed those unconfirmed transactions to be replaced and continued to disallow other transactions from being replaced (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The signal matters because it put the choice in the sender's hands and left everyone else able to read it. A wallet that wants the option of raising a fee sets one input's sequence to 0xfffffffd; a merchant who will not accept replaceable payments before confirmation checks for any sequence below 0xfffffffe; and the explorer that this course consulted reports exactly this flag for every transaction it shows (Harding and Todd, 2015) (mempool.space, 2026). Alice's transaction, with every sequence at the maximum, does not signal.

The worked example tests the four interesting values: the maximum and the value one below it do not signal, 0xfffffffd and every lower value do. The threshold is two below the maximum because the value one below, 0xfffffffe, already had a meaning - it is the highest value that still lets the lock-time field apply - and BIP125 chose not to collide with it (Harding and Todd, 2015) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). BIP125 also describes inherited signalling: a transaction that does not signal is nonetheless replaceable while any unconfirmed ancestor of it signals, since replacing the ancestor removes the descendant too (Harding and Todd, 2015).

The caution is one the book itself makes at the end of the timelock group: any transaction that sets a relative timelock using the sequence field also sends the signal for opt-in replace-by-fee, because a timelock value is far below 0xfffffffe (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A second caution is that Bitcoin Core has moved beyond the signal in its default policy: its release notes for version 28.0 record that the default of the mempoolfullrbf option changed from 0 to 1, so a default node now treats every unconfirmed transaction as replaceable; the book's statement describes the policy as the proposal defined it, and a reader should check the policy of the software in use (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.example: below 0xfffffffe means replaceable
nodes.definition: By BIP125 an unconfirmed transaction with any input whose sequence is below 0xfffffffe, at least two below the maximum, signals that it may be replaced by a conflicting transaction paying a higher fee rate.

nodes.label: Sequence as a relative timelock
nodes.body: The relative timelock is the third meaning of the sequence field and the only one enforced by consensus. The book says the BIP68 soft fork added a new constraint to transactions with version numbers 2 or higher, that the constraint applies to the sequence field, and that inputs with sequence values less than 2 to the 31 are interpreted as having a relative timelock: such a transaction may only be included in the blockchain once the previous output referenced by the outpoint has aged by the relative timelock amount (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Friedenbach et al., 2015).

paras.text: The relative timelock is the third meaning of the sequence field and the only one enforced by consensus. The book says the BIP68 soft fork added a new constraint to transactions with version numbers 2 or higher, that the constraint applies to the sequence field, and that inputs with sequence values less than 2 to the 31 are interpreted as having a relative timelock: such a transaction may only be included in the blockchain once the previous output referenced by the outpoint has aged by the relative timelock amount (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Friedenbach et al., 2015).

A relative timelock is relative to the confirmation of the output being spent rather than to a fixed height or time, which is what contract protocols need: a party can be given a window after a deposit confirms, however long the deposit takes. BIP68's own motivation names bidirectional payment channels and hashed timelock contracts, the building blocks of the Lightning Network, and the version gate of the version branch is what let the meaning be added without invalidating old transactions (Friedenbach et al., 2015) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The four sections follow the bits of the field as BIP68's figure lays them out: the timelock itself and the rule of aging, the type flag at bit 22 that chooses between a count of blocks and a count of 512-second units, the disable flag at bit 31 that lets an input of a version 2 transaction opt out, and the 16-bit mask that extracts the value, whose maximum of 65,535 is a bit more than a year in either unit (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Friedenbach et al., 2015).

nodes.label: BIP68 relative timelock
nodes.body: The BIP68 relative timelock is the consensus rule that reads a low sequence value as a minimum age of the output being spent. The book states it with an example: a transaction with one input with a relative timelock of 30 blocks can only be confirmed in a block with at least 29 blocks between it and the block containing the output being spent on the same blockchain; and since sequence is a per-input field, a transaction may contain any number of timelocked inputs, all of which must have sufficiently aged for the transaction to be valid (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The BIP68 relative timelock is the consensus rule that reads a low sequence value as a minimum age of the output being spent. The book states it with an example: a transaction with one input with a relative timelock of 30 blocks can only be confirmed in a block with at least 29 blocks between it and the block containing the output being spent on the same blockchain; and since sequence is a per-input field, a transaction may contain any number of timelocked inputs, all of which must have sufficiently aged for the transaction to be valid (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The rule matters because it is enforced by every node rather than by policy. An output can be deposited with the knowledge that whoever spends it along a given path must wait, and no amount of fee or luck shortens the wait; BIP68 says its purpose is to prevent mining of a transaction until a certain age of the spent output in blocks or timespan, allowing among other uses the bidirectional payment channels of BIP112 (Friedenbach et al., 2015). The companion opcode of BIP112 lets an output script demand such a lock, so the restriction can be imposed by the script rather than chosen by the spender.

The worked example applies the book's example to Alice's chain: her input spends an output confirmed at height 774,958, and with a lock of 30 blocks the earliest confirming block is 774,988, leaving 29 blocks strictly between. Bitcoin Core computes the same bound in CalculateSequenceLocks as the output's height plus the masked value minus one, which is the last height at which the spend is still forbidden (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The rule applies only to version 2 or higher and only when the disable flag is clear, as the next sections explain (Friedenbach et al., 2015).

The caution is that a relative timelock is a minimum, never a maximum; it cannot make an output expire, only delay it, and the book's note on the maturity rule of coinbase outputs is the same shape of rule. A second caution is that the lock is measured on the same blockchain: if the output's block is reorganised away, the age is counted again from its new confirmation, which is what the phrase on the same blockchain in the book's example means (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: 30 blocks: confirm 29 blocks after the output
nodes.definition: Under BIP68 a version 2 input with sequence below 2 to the 31 may only be confirmed once the output it spends has aged by the sequence's value: a lock of 30 blocks allows confirmation with at least 29 blocks between the two.
