nodes.label: The type flag
nodes.body: The type flag is the bit of the sequence field that says whether a relative timelock counts blocks or time. The book says the sequence value is specified in either blocks or seconds, that a type flag is used to differentiate between values counting blocks and values counting time in seconds, that the flag is set in the 23rd least-significant bit, value 1 shifted left 22, and that if it is set the sequence value is interpreted as a multiple of 512 seconds, otherwise as a number of blocks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The type flag is the bit of the sequence field that says whether a relative timelock counts blocks or time. The book says the sequence value is specified in either blocks or seconds, that a type flag is used to differentiate between values counting blocks and values counting time in seconds, that the flag is set in the 23rd least-significant bit, value 1 shifted left 22, and that if it is set the sequence value is interpreted as a multiple of 512 seconds, otherwise as a number of blocks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The flag matters because the two units suit different contracts. A lock in blocks is exact in the chain's own terms but uncertain in wall-clock time; a lock in seconds is what a human agreement usually wants. BIP68 explains the choice of 512 seconds: blocks are generated every 600 seconds, so with 512-second units the same number of bits encodes about the same span either way, and converting a sequence number to seconds is a multiplication by 512, which is a shift left by nine bits (Friedenbach et al., 2015).

The worked example computes the flag's value, 4,194,304 or 0x400000, and decodes a sequence with the flag set and a value of 8: the masked value is 8 and the lock is 8 times 512, which is 4,096 seconds. Bitcoin Core names the constant SEQUENCE_LOCKTIME_TYPE_FLAG and the shift SEQUENCE_LOCKTIME_GRANULARITY, nine; its CalculateSequenceLocks compares a time-based lock against the median time past of the output's block rather than against block times, as BIP68 specifies (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Friedenbach et al., 2015).

The caution is the ordinal in the book's sentence: the 23rd least-significant bit is bit 22 when counting from zero, which is why the value is 1 shifted left 22 and not 23. A second caution is that the time-based lock is measured in median time past, which is normally an hour or two behind the clock, so a lock of 4,096 seconds does not expire 4,096 seconds after the output's block was seen but after the chain's median time has advanced that far (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Friedenbach et al., 2015).

nodes.example: bit 22 chooses blocks or 512-second units
nodes.definition: The type flag is bit 22 of the sequence, value 1 shifted left 22; set, the lock counts units of 512 seconds, clear, it counts blocks.

nodes.label: The disable flag
nodes.body: The disable flag is the highest bit of the sequence field. The book says a disable flag allows a transaction to include both inputs with a relative timelock, sequence below 2 to the 31, and inputs without a relative timelock, sequence of 2 to the 31 or more (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The flag is the reason the rule speaks of values below 2 to the 31: any value with bit 31 set is not a timelock, whatever its lower bits hold.

paras.text: The disable flag is the highest bit of the sequence field. The book says a disable flag allows a transaction to include both inputs with a relative timelock, sequence below 2 to the 31, and inputs without a relative timelock, sequence of 2 to the 31 or more (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The flag is the reason the rule speaks of values below 2 to the 31: any value with bit 31 set is not a timelock, whatever its lower bits hold.

The flag matters because it keeps old behaviour available input by input. Without it, every input of a version 2 transaction would carry a lock, and a wallet wanting one locked input would have to lock them all; with it, an input that should be spendable at once simply sets the bit. It is also what keeps the final value harmless: 0xffffffff has the disable flag set, so a version 2 transaction whose inputs are all final has no timelock at all, which the book's sequence of meanings relies on (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Friedenbach et al., 2015).

The worked example tests four values: the final value and 0x80000000 have the bit set and so carry no lock; 0x7fffffff and 30 do not and so are read as locks. Bitcoin Core's CalculateSequenceLocks checks this bit first and skips the input entirely when it is set, before looking at the type flag or the mask, which is the order the book's figure of the encoding suggests (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). BIP68 adds that the new rules are not applied to the sequence field of the input of the coinbase transaction, whatever its bits (Friedenbach et al., 2015).

The caution is that the disable flag disables only the relative timelock. A sequence of 0x80000000 still signals replaceability under BIP125, since it is below 0xfffffffe, and still permits the lock-time field to apply, since it is not final; the three meanings of the field are independent readings of the same bits. A second caution is that version 1 transactions have no timelocks regardless of this bit, since the whole rule is gated on the version (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: bit 31 switches the timelock off
nodes.definition: The disable flag is bit 31 of the sequence; an input with it set has no relative timelock even in a version 2 transaction, so a transaction may mix locked and unlocked inputs.

nodes.label: The 16-bit mask
nodes.body: The mask is the way a node extracts the timelock value from the sequence field. The book says that when interpreting sequence as a relative timelock only the 16 least significant bits are considered: once the flags, bits 32 and 23 in the book's counting, are evaluated, the value is usually masked with a 16-bit mask, sequence and 0x0000FFFF; and because the multiple of 512 seconds is roughly the average time between blocks, the maximum relative timelock in both blocks and seconds from 16 bits is a bit more than one year (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The mask is the way a node extracts the timelock value from the sequence field. The book says that when interpreting sequence as a relative timelock only the 16 least significant bits are considered: once the flags, bits 32 and 23 in the book's counting, are evaluated, the value is usually masked with a 16-bit mask, sequence and 0x0000FFFF; and because the multiple of 512 seconds is roughly the average time between blocks, the maximum relative timelock in both blocks and seconds from 16 bits is a bit more than one year (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The mask matters because it fixes the range of what a relative timelock can express and leaves bits free. Sixteen bits give at most 65,535; in 512-second units that is about 388 days, and at ten minutes a block 65,535 blocks is about 455 days, both a bit more than a year as the book says. The bits between the value and the type flag, and between the type flag and the disable flag, are unused and are among the features reserved for upgrades that a presigned transaction must not set (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Friedenbach et al., 2015).

The worked example computes the three figures: the maximal masked value, its span in days at 512 seconds a unit, and its span in days at 600 seconds a block. Bitcoin Core names the mask SEQUENCE_LOCKTIME_MASK with the value 0x0000ffff, and its time-based computation shifts the masked value left by the granularity of nine bits, which multiplies by 512 (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The chapter's library applies the mask after the two flags, in the order the book describes.

The caution is in the book's bit numbering: it says bits 32 and 23 where the flags are at positions 31 and 22 counting from zero, the same convention as the type flag's 23rd least-significant bit; the values 1 shifted left 31 and 1 shifted left 22 are the unambiguous statement. A second caution is that the one-year ceiling is approximate in both units, because blocks are not exactly ten minutes apart and the 512-second units are measured in median time past.

nodes.example: 65,535 blocks or units, about a year
nodes.definition: Only the 16 least significant bits of the sequence carry the relative timelock, so the mask 0x0000ffff extracts a value of at most 65,535, which in blocks or in 512-second units is a bit more than a year.
