nodes.label: Outputs
nodes.body: This branch reads the outputs field, the 75 bytes of Alice's transaction that assign her bitcoins to new conditions. The book says the outputs field contains several fields related to specific outputs and, as with the inputs, starts from a byte map; the field begins with a count, and each output has an amount followed by a length-prefixed output script, the script that contains the conditions that will need to be fulfilled in order to spend the bitcoins (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Alice's transaction has two outputs: 20,000 satoshis to Bob and 75,000 back to herself as change.

paras.text: This branch reads the outputs field, the 75 bytes of Alice's transaction that assign her bitcoins to new conditions. The book says the outputs field contains several fields related to specific outputs and, as with the inputs, starts from a byte map; the field begins with a count, and each output has an amount followed by a length-prefixed output script, the script that contains the conditions that will need to be fulfilled in order to spend the bitcoins (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Alice's transaction has two outputs: 20,000 satoshis to Bob and 75,000 back to herself as change.

Outputs are where value and conditions are written down. The amount is the only place a transaction states a number of satoshis, and the output script is the only place it states who may spend them, so the whole of what chapter 2 called the UTXO is created here. The branch also carries a public cost: every output a node must remember until it is spent burdens every full node, which is why the book spends a section on outputs that are not worth spending and on the dust policy that discourages them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reader meets outputs as the lines of a payment an explorer shows, with an amount and an address; the address is the human form of the output script, which chapter 4 explained, and the amount is the satoshi count the book defines here. The dust limit of 546 satoshis is met as the smallest payment most wallets will make, and the standard templates are met as the handful of address types a wallet offers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The branch has three groups. The output list explains the count, the amount field, the satoshi as a unit and the consensus range of an amount. The dust group explains uneconomical outputs, the policy against creating them and the one exception, the data-carrier output. The output script group explains the script field, its minimum and maximum sizes, the anyone-can-spend scripts on which upgrades are built, and the standard templates that relay policy limits outputs to (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: The output list
nodes.body: The output list is the outputs field as a whole: a compactSize count greater than zero, then that many outputs, each an 8-byte amount and a length-prefixed script. The book says the count is identical in form to the start of the inputs section, that it must be greater than zero, and that the example transaction has two outputs; the amount is an 8-byte signed integer of satoshis, and there are 100 million satoshis in a bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The output list is the outputs field as a whole: a compactSize count greater than zero, then that many outputs, each an 8-byte amount and a length-prefixed script. The book says the count is identical in form to the start of the inputs section, that it must be greater than zero, and that the example transaction has two outputs; the amount is an 8-byte signed integer of satoshis, and there are 100 million satoshis in a bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The list matters because it is where arithmetic is checked. The sum of the outputs may not exceed the sum of the inputs' previous outputs, the difference being the fee that a miner may claim, and each amount must lie within the range consensus allows; Bitcoin Core refuses negative values, values above the maximum and a sum that overflows the range, naming each refusal (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The amount of a single output is bounded above by the total that can ever exist, 21 million bitcoins, which the book gives as 2.1 quadrillion satoshis (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The four sections take the field in order: the count and its lower bound, the amount field and its 8-byte little-endian encoding, the satoshi as the unit the amount counts, and the range from zero to 21 million bitcoins that consensus permits, with Bitcoin Core's constants COIN and MAX_MONEY and the history of why a check against overflow exists (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: Output count
nodes.body: The output count is the integer that opens the outputs field and says how many outputs follow. The book says it is identical to the start of the inputs section: a count indicating the number of outputs, a compactSize integer that must be greater than zero, and the example transaction has two outputs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example reads the byte at offset 48 of Alice's transaction, immediately after her single input, and finds 02.

paras.text: The output count is the integer that opens the outputs field and says how many outputs follow. The book says it is identical to the start of the inputs section: a count indicating the number of outputs, a compactSize integer that must be greater than zero, and the example transaction has two outputs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example reads the byte at offset 48 of Alice's transaction, immediately after her single input, and finds 02.

The lower bound is a consensus rule: Bitcoin Core's CheckTransaction refuses a transaction with no outputs with the error bad-txns-vout-empty, just as it refuses one with no inputs (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A transaction must assign its value somewhere, even if only to a fee, and in practice almost every payment has two outputs, the payment and the change, because an input is spent whole and the remainder has to return to the sender; the book's chapter 2 explained change in exactly these terms (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Like the input count, the output count is compactSize, so it is one byte for up to 252 outputs and grows only for larger transactions; some transactions that pay many recipients at once, such as exchange withdrawals, exceed that and use the three-byte form. The count is read before the outputs because the outputs have no terminator, and the number is used again nowhere else - unlike the input count, which also fixes the number of witness stacks.

The caution is that two outputs do not mean two recipients: Alice's second output is her own change, and nothing in the transaction marks it as such, which is a privacy property the book's later chapters discuss. A second caution is that a count of one is common and legal, for a transaction that spends an output exactly or deliberately leaves the remainder as fee, as the pizza transaction of 2010 did with its single output and its fee of 0.99 bitcoins (mempool.space, 2026).

nodes.example: two outputs: a payment and change
nodes.definition: The output count is the compactSize integer that opens the outputs field; it must be greater than zero, and Alice's transaction has two outputs.

nodes.label: Amount
nodes.body: The amount is the first field of a specific output. The book says it is also called value in Bitcoin Core, that it is an 8-byte signed integer indicating the number of satoshis to transfer, that a satoshi is the smallest unit of bitcoin that can be represented in an on-chain transaction, and that there are 100 million satoshis in a bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The first output of Alice's transaction begins with the bytes 204e000000000000, which the worked example reads as 20,000 satoshis, the payment to Bob.

paras.text: The amount is the first field of a specific output. The book says it is also called value in Bitcoin Core, that it is an 8-byte signed integer indicating the number of satoshis to transfer, that a satoshi is the smallest unit of bitcoin that can be represented in an on-chain transaction, and that there are 100 million satoshis in a bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The first output of Alice's transaction begins with the bytes 204e000000000000, which the worked example reads as 20,000 satoshis, the payment to Bob.

The amount is the only place a transaction states value, and it is stated once per output. The inputs carry no amounts, so a node computes the fee as the sum of the referenced outputs' amounts minus the sum of these; a transaction whose outputs total more than its inputs is invalid, and one whose outputs total less has given the difference to the miner. Chapter 2 followed Alice's payment with this arithmetic: she spent 100,000, paid 20,000, took 75,000 back, and left 5,000 as fee, which the explorer records as the fee of her transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (mempool.space, 2026).

Eight little-endian bytes read as a signed integer give the value; the second output of Alice's transaction, f824010000000000, reads as 75,000. Bitcoin Core's type for the field is CAmount, a 64-bit signed integer, and its CheckTransaction refuses an output whose value is negative with bad-txns-vout-negative and one above the maximum with bad-txns-vout-toolarge, and keeps a running total that it refuses if the sum leaves the money range (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The signed type is why the consensus range starts at zero rather than at the smallest representable number.

The caution is in the word signed. A naive reader of eight bytes could obtain a negative number, and an early version of the software did not check the sum of outputs for overflow, which produced the value overflow incident of August 2010, one of this chapter's stories; Bitcoin Core's source cites the identifier of that bug beside its check (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A second caution is units: an explorer may show 0.0002 BTC while the field holds 20,000, and the conversion by 100 million is the only arithmetic between them.

nodes.example: 8 bytes, little-endian, in satoshis
nodes.definition: The amount is the first field of an output: an 8-byte signed little-endian integer of satoshis, called value in Bitcoin Core; Alice's first output carries 20,000.

error.out: OverflowError: int too big to convert

nodes.label: Satoshi
nodes.body: A satoshi is the smallest unit of bitcoin that can be represented in an on-chain Bitcoin transaction. The book defines it in the amount section and gives the ratio: there are 100 million satoshis in a bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Chapter 1 introduced the unit by name as the one bitcoin's amounts are counted in; this chapter shows the field that counts it. Bitcoin Core names the ratio COIN, with the value 100,000,000 (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: A satoshi is the smallest unit of bitcoin that can be represented in an on-chain Bitcoin transaction. The book defines it in the amount section and gives the ratio: there are 100 million satoshis in a bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Chapter 1 introduced the unit by name as the one bitcoin's amounts are counted in; this chapter shows the field that counts it. Bitcoin Core names the ratio COIN, with the value 100,000,000 (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The unit matters because the amount field is an integer, never a fraction. A transaction does not say 0.0002 bitcoins; it says 20,000, and every wallet, explorer and exchange that shows a decimal is dividing by 100 million for display. That makes the arithmetic of fees and change exact - no rounding can occur on the chain - and it fixes a floor: a payment smaller than one satoshi cannot be made on the chain, which is one reason the book's chapter on second-layer applications exists.

The worked example states the ratio and converts Alice's two amounts: 20,000 satoshis are 0.0002 bitcoin and 75,000 are 0.00075. The ratio also sets the scale of the consensus maximum: 21 million bitcoins times 100 million satoshis is 2.1 quadrillion satoshis, which is the number the book gives for the largest amount an output may carry, and which the next section computes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The caution is that the satoshi is the smallest unit on the chain but not in every Bitcoin system: the Lightning Network, which the book's chapter on second-layer applications describes, accounts in thousandths of a satoshi off the chain and rounds when it settles. A second caution is naming: some software shows sat or sats, and a figure given without a unit may be either satoshis or bitcoins, a difference of eight decimal places.

nodes.example: 100 million to a bitcoin
nodes.definition: A satoshi is the smallest unit of bitcoin an on-chain transaction can represent; there are 100 million satoshis in a bitcoin, so 20,000 satoshis are 0.0002 bitcoin.

nodes.label: The consensus range of an amount
nodes.body: The consensus range of an amount is the set of values an output may carry. The book says Bitcoin's consensus rules allow an output to have a value as small as zero and as large as 21 million bitcoins, which is 2.1 quadrillion satoshis (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core states the upper bound as the constant MAX_MONEY, 21 million times COIN, and the function MoneyRange that checks a value is between zero and that bound inclusive (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: The consensus range of an amount is the set of values an output may carry. The book says Bitcoin's consensus rules allow an output to have a value as small as zero and as large as 21 million bitcoins, which is 2.1 quadrillion satoshis (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core states the upper bound as the constant MAX_MONEY, 21 million times COIN, and the function MoneyRange that checks a value is between zero and that bound inclusive (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The range matters because an amount is a 64-bit signed integer, which can hold values far outside it. Without the check, an output could claim a negative amount, which would make a transaction's outputs sum to less than they are, or two outputs could sum past the top of the integer and wrap around to a small negative number, so that the outputs appear to total less than the inputs; the second is exactly what happened in August 2010, when a transaction created two outputs of over 92 billion bitcoins each whose sum overflowed to a small negative value and passed the check of the time (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The source comment on the check cites that incident's identifier.

The worked example computes the maximum, confirms it equals 2.1 quadrillion, and checks Alice's payment of 20,000 against the range. Bitcoin Core applies three refusals in CheckTransaction: bad-txns-vout-negative for a value below zero, bad-txns-vout-toolarge for a value above MAX_MONEY, and bad-txns-txouttotal-toolarge when the running sum of the outputs leaves the range, which is the check that stops a wraparound (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The maximum is deliberately the total supply, since no output can hold more than everything.

The caution is that the range is a consensus bound, not a policy one: a zero-value output is valid under consensus but is the book's first example of an uneconomical output, and the dust policy of the next group refuses to relay it unless it is a data-carrier output (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A second caution is that MAX_MONEY is slightly above the amount that will ever exist, since the subsidy schedule issues a little under 21 million, as the coinbase group computes; the source says the exact value of the constant is consensus-critical only as an upper bound (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.example: from 0 to 2.1 quadrillion
nodes.definition: Consensus allows an output amount from zero to 21 million bitcoins, 2.1 quadrillion satoshis; Bitcoin Core names the maximum MAX_MONEY and refuses negative, oversized and overflowing totals.

error.code: (lambda g: (exec("value = 21_000_000 * 100_000_000 + 1\nassert 0 <= value <= 21_000_000 * 100_000_000, 'the amount is outside the consensus range'\nresult = value", g), g['result'])[1])({})
error.out: AssertionError: the amount is outside the consensus range

nodes.label: Uneconomical outputs and dust
nodes.body: This group explains the outputs that are not worth spending and the relay policy against creating them. The book says a zero-value output can be spent under the same rules as any other, but spending an output increases the size of a transaction and so the fee that must be paid; if the value of the output is less than the cost of the additional fee, it does not make economic sense to spend it, and such outputs are known as uneconomical outputs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The policies against relaying or mining transactions that create them are called dust policies.

paras.text: This group explains the outputs that are not worth spending and the relay policy against creating them. The book says a zero-value output can be spent under the same rules as any other, but spending an output increases the size of a transaction and so the fee that must be paid; if the value of the output is less than the cost of the additional fee, it does not make economic sense to spend it, and such outputs are known as uneconomical outputs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The policies against relaying or mining transactions that create them are called dust policies.

The group matters because an unspent output is a cost to everyone. The need for full nodes to keep track of all UTXOs means that every UTXO makes it slightly harder to run a full node; outputs of significant value will eventually be spent, but there is no incentive for the person controlling an uneconomical UTXO ever to spend it, potentially making it a perpetual burden on operators of full nodes, and since Bitcoin's decentralisation depends on many people running full nodes, several implementations discourage uneconomical outputs by policy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The three sections are the problem, the policy and the exception. Uneconomical outputs explains the arithmetic and why an output that is economical today may not be tomorrow; the dust limit gives Bitcoin Core's threshold and the 546-satoshi figure many programs assume, recomputed from the source; and the data-carrier output explains why a script beginning with OP_RETURN is allowed a value of zero, because it can never be spent and so never burdens the UTXO set (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: Uneconomical output
nodes.body: An uneconomical output is one that does not make economic sense to spend. The book explains the mechanism: despite having no value, a zero-value output can be spent under the same rules as any other output, but spending an output, using it as an input, increases the size of a transaction, which increases the fee that needs to be paid, and if the value of the output is less than the cost of the additional fee it does not make economic sense to spend it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: An uneconomical output is one that does not make economic sense to spend. The book explains the mechanism: despite having no value, a zero-value output can be spent under the same rules as any other output, but spending an output, using it as an input, increases the size of a transaction, which increases the fee that needs to be paid, and if the value of the output is less than the cost of the additional fee it does not make economic sense to spend it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The concept matters because it is relative to fee rates and therefore unstable. The book says a zero-value output is always uneconomical, since it would contribute nothing even at a fee rate of zero, but that many other low-value outputs can be uneconomical as well, even unintentionally: at a typical fee rate today an output might add more value than it costs to spend, but tomorrow fee rates might rise and make it uneconomical (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A wallet that creates small change outputs is creating future dust for its own user.

The worked example runs the arithmetic for a segwit input of about 68 virtual bytes at 10 satoshis per vbyte: spending costs 680 satoshis, so an output of 500 is uneconomical at that rate. The book's chapter on fees develops the fee rate; here it is enough that the cost of an input is its size times the rate, and that the output's value must exceed it to be worth including. Bitcoin Core's dust threshold, the next section, is this calculation made at a fixed, low rate so that a single number can be a policy (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The caution is that uneconomical is not invalid: consensus accepts a zero-value output and a transaction that spends one, and the refusal is a relay policy of some nodes. A second caution is the cost the book names: the owner of an uneconomical output has no reason ever to spend it, so the entry stays in every full node's UTXO database for ever, and that is a cost paid by everyone rather than by the owner (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: worth less than the fee to spend it
nodes.definition: An uneconomical output is one whose value is less than the extra fee that spending it would add to a transaction; a zero-value output is always uneconomical, and others become so when fee rates rise.

io.code: (lambda value, input_vbytes, rate: (input_vbytes * rate, value < input_vbytes * rate))(500, 68, 10)

nodes.label: Dust limit
nodes.body: The dust limit is the value below which a relaying node treats an output as dust and refuses to relay or mine the transaction that creates it. The book says the policies against relaying or mining transactions creating new uneconomical outputs are called dust policies, based on a comparison between outputs with very small values and particles with very small size, that Bitcoin Core's dust policy is complicated and contains several arbitrary numbers, and that many programs simply assume outputs with less than 546 satoshis are dust (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The dust limit is the value below which a relaying node treats an output as dust and refuses to relay or mine the transaction that creates it. The book says the policies against relaying or mining transactions creating new uneconomical outputs are called dust policies, based on a comparison between outputs with very small values and particles with very small size, that Bitcoin Core's dust policy is complicated and contains several arbitrary numbers, and that many programs simply assume outputs with less than 546 satoshis are dust (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The limit matters because it is the smallest payment most software will make and because it is not a consensus rule but a convention that can change. The book notes that there are occasionally proposals to lower dust limits and counterproposals to raise them, and encourages developers using presigned transactions or multiparty protocols to check whether the policy has changed since publication (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core's source explains the figure: if you would pay more in fees than the value of the output to spend it, the output is dust (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The worked example recomputes both figures Bitcoin Core's comment gives. A typical non-segwit output is 34 bytes and needs an input of at least 148 bytes to spend, so dust is anything below 182 times the dust relay fee of 3,000 satoshis per kilobyte, which is 546 satoshis; a P2WPKH output is 31 bytes and needs an input of at least 67 bytes, so its threshold is 98 times the rate, 294 satoshis (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The policy header names the rate DUST_RELAY_TX_FEE, and the chapter's library computes the threshold from any output script; for a taproot output, 43 plus 67 bytes, it gives 330 satoshis.

The caution is that 546 is a legacy figure that many programs apply to every output type, although Bitcoin Core's own threshold for segwit outputs is lower; the book's phrase simply assume is exact. A second caution is that the threshold is in satoshis at a fixed rate, so a 600-satoshi output passes the dust policy and may still be uneconomical to spend at the fee rates of a busy day; dust and uneconomical overlap but are not the same set (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: 546 satoshis, from 182 bytes at 3,000 sat/kvB
nodes.definition: Bitcoin Core's dust threshold is the size of an output plus the smallest input that could spend it, times the dust relay rate of 3,000 satoshis per kilo-vbyte: 546 satoshis for a legacy P2PKH output, 294 for a P2WPKH output.

nodes.label: Data-carrier output
nodes.body: A data-carrier output is an output whose script starts with OP_RETURN. The book says Bitcoin Core's dust policy has one exception: such outputs can have a value of zero, because the OP_RETURN opcode causes the script to immediately fail no matter what comes after it, so these outputs can never be spent; full nodes do not need to keep track of them, which Bitcoin Core uses to let users store small amounts of arbitrary data in the blockchain without increasing the size of its UTXO database (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A data-carrier output is an output whose script starts with OP_RETURN. The book says Bitcoin Core's dust policy has one exception: such outputs can have a value of zero, because the OP_RETURN opcode causes the script to immediately fail no matter what comes after it, so these outputs can never be spent; full nodes do not need to keep track of them, which Bitcoin Core uses to let users store small amounts of arbitrary data in the blockchain without increasing the size of its UTXO database (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The exception matters because it turns the logic of dust on its head. Dust is bad because it stays in the UTXO set for ever; an OP_RETURN output never enters the set at all, since it is provably unspendable, so it costs nodes nothing after the block that contains it. The book adds the second half of the reasoning: since the outputs are unspendable they are not uneconomical, any satoshis assigned to them become permanently unspendable, so allowing the amount to be zero ensures satoshis are not being destroyed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

An opcode is a one-byte instruction of Bitcoin's script language, which the next chapter of the book explains; OP_RETURN is the byte 0x6a, and the worked example checks the byte and the policy's threshold of zero. Bitcoin Core's GetDustThreshold returns zero for any script its IsUnspendable test accepts, which is a script beginning with OP_RETURN or one longer than the maximum script size (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The chapter's library does the same, and the data after the opcode is simply ignored by every node, which is why it can be anything.

The caution is that the data is stored by every archival node even though it is not in the UTXO set: a data-carrier output costs block space once, not database space for ever, and relay policy limits its size for that reason. A second caution is the one the book makes elsewhere: assigning a positive value to an OP_RETURN output destroys the satoshis, since nothing can ever spend them, and a wallet that does so by mistake has no remedy.

nodes.example: OP_RETURN: unspendable, so not dust
nodes.definition: A data-carrier output is one whose script begins with OP_RETURN; it can never be spent, so nodes need not keep it, and Bitcoin Core's dust policy allows it a value of zero.

nodes.label: The output script
nodes.body: The output script is the last field of an output: the book says the amount is followed by a compactSize integer indicating the length of the output script, the script that contains the conditions that will need to be fulfilled in order to spend the bitcoins, and that according to consensus the minimum size of an output script is zero (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The group covers the field, its size limits, the empty and other anyone-can-spend scripts, and the standard templates.

paras.text: The output script is the last field of an output: the book says the amount is followed by a compactSize integer indicating the length of the output script, the script that contains the conditions that will need to be fulfilled in order to spend the bitcoins, and that according to consensus the minimum size of an output script is zero (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The group covers the field, its size limits, the empty and other anyone-can-spend scripts, and the standard templates.

The output script is where authorization is written, which the book says it only briefly looks at here and makes the subject of the next chapter. For this chapter the field matters as a byte field with rules: its length is prefixed, its maximum depends on when it is checked, a script that anyone can satisfy is valid and is the raw material of soft forks, and relay policy limits outputs to a few templates that wallets recognise as address types (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The four sections take the field, its sizes, its degenerate cases and its usual cases. The output script section reads Alice's two scripts, a 34-byte taproot script and a 22-byte pay-to-witness-public-key-hash script; the size limit section gives the zero minimum and the 10,000-byte spending maximum; the anyone-can-spend section explains the empty script and why upgrades are built on such scripts; and the standard outputs section explains the templates and why Bitcoin Core keeps the restriction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Output script
nodes.body: The output script is the script that contains the conditions that will need to be fulfilled in order to spend the bitcoins of an output. The book says the output amount is followed by a compactSize integer indicating the length of the output script, and that parsing and using scripts is the subject of the next chapter; this chapter reads the field as bytes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Alice's transaction has two: a 34-byte script beginning 51 20 for Bob and a 22-byte script beginning 00 14 for her change.

paras.text: The output script is the script that contains the conditions that will need to be fulfilled in order to spend the bitcoins of an output. The book says the output amount is followed by a compactSize integer indicating the length of the output script, and that parsing and using scripts is the subject of the next chapter; this chapter reads the field as bytes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Alice's transaction has two: a 34-byte script beginning 51 20 for Bob and a 22-byte script beginning 00 14 for her change.

The script is the modern form of what the whitepaper called a public key, the thing that says who is authorised to spend. Chapter 4 showed how an address encodes a script of this kind - a bech32m address for a taproot script, a bech32 address for a version 0 witness script - so the two scripts of Alice's transaction are the two addresses the payment was made to, decoded (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Which conditions a script imposes is for the next chapter; which bytes it occupies and what they cost is for this one.

The worked example cuts both scripts out of the bytes: the first output's length byte at offset 57 says 34, and its script begins 5120, which is the opcode for the number 1 followed by a push of 32 bytes, a segwit version 1 script, the taproot template; the second output's length byte says 22, and its script begins 0014, the number 0 followed by a push of 20 bytes, a segwit version 0 script paying a public key hash. Both are witness programs in the sense of the witness branch: a version number from 0 to 16 followed by 2 to 40 bytes of data (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo et al., 2015). The explorer labels them v1_p2tr and v0_p2wpkh (mempool.space, 2026).

The caution is that a script is not an address: the address is a human encoding of the script with a checksum, and the transaction carries only the script. A second caution is that the two outputs look different only because they pay different script types; the taproot output to Bob costs 136 weight units for its script and the change output 88, as the weight branch's table shows, which is one of the ways a script type affects the fee (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: 34 bytes to Bob, 22 bytes of change
nodes.definition: The output script holds the conditions for spending an output; Alice's first is a 34-byte segwit version 1 script for Bob, her second a 22-byte segwit version 0 script for her change.

nodes.label: Script size limits
nodes.body: The script size limits are the bounds on how long an output script may be. The book says that according to consensus the minimum size is zero, that the maximum varies depending on when it is being checked - there is no explicit limit on the size of an output script in the output of a transaction, but a later transaction can only spend a previous output with a script of 10,000 bytes or smaller - and that implicitly an output script can be almost as large as the transaction containing it, and a transaction almost as large as the block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The script size limits are the bounds on how long an output script may be. The book says that according to consensus the minimum size is zero, that the maximum varies depending on when it is being checked - there is no explicit limit on the size of an output script in the output of a transaction, but a later transaction can only spend a previous output with a script of 10,000 bytes or smaller - and that implicitly an output script can be almost as large as the transaction containing it, and a transaction almost as large as the block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The asymmetry matters because it is a property of where the rule is checked. Creating an output costs block space, which the block weight limit prices; spending it executes the script, which the 10,000-byte limit bounds so that no script can take unbounded work to run. An output with a script above the limit can therefore be created and can never be spent, which makes it a strange kind of data-carrier output. Bitcoin Core names the limit MAX_SCRIPT_SIZE and treats a script above it as unspendable in the same test that catches OP_RETURN (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The worked example states the two bounds and checks that a 10,000-byte script would fit a block by weight. The 10,000-byte limit lives in the script interpreter, which refuses to execute a longer script, so the check happens when the spending transaction is validated; the creating transaction's output passes CheckTransaction regardless of its script's length, as long as the whole transaction fits the block weight limit (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A zero-length script is valid at creation too, and the next section explains what spends it.

The caution is that consensus limits and policy limits differ again here: Bitcoin Core's relay policy will not relay an output whose script is not a standard template, so a 9,000-byte script is valid but will not be relayed by default. A second caution is that these are byte limits on the script as data; the number of operations a script may execute and the size of the elements it pushes are separate limits, which the next chapter of the book treats (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.example: zero at minimum, 10,000 bytes to spend
nodes.definition: Consensus sets the minimum size of an output script at zero and no explicit maximum when it is created, but a later transaction can only spend an output whose script is 10,000 bytes or smaller.

nodes.label: Anyone-can-spend scripts
nodes.body: An anyone-can-spend script is an output script that anyone can satisfy. The book's example is the empty one: an output script with zero length can be spent by an input script containing OP_TRUE, and anyone can create that input script, so anyone can spend an empty output script; there are an essentially unlimited number of such scripts, and Bitcoin protocol developers know them as anyone can spends (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). OP_TRUE is the opcode 0x51, the same byte that the taproot script of Alice's first output begins with.

paras.text: An anyone-can-spend script is an output script that anyone can satisfy. The book's example is the empty one: an output script with zero length can be spent by an input script containing OP_TRUE, and anyone can create that input script, so anyone can spend an empty output script; there are an essentially unlimited number of such scripts, and Bitcoin protocol developers know them as anyone can spends (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). OP_TRUE is the opcode 0x51, the same byte that the taproot script of Alice's first output begins with.

The category matters because it is how Bitcoin upgrades its script language without a hard fork. The book says upgrades often take an existing anyone-can-spend script and add new constraints to it, making it spendable only under the new conditions; the witness branch shows segwit doing exactly this, since to an old node a segwit output script is a number followed by data that anyone could spend, while new nodes require a witness (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo et al., 2015). That is why Alice's taproot output begins with 0x51: to a pre-taproot node it is an anyone-can-spend output.

The worked example states the three facts: the empty script has length zero, 0x51 is OP_TRUE, and the name. The mechanism is that a script's conditions are whatever its opcodes impose, and an empty script imposes none, so the stack left by the input script decides; OP_TRUE leaves a true value, and the spend succeeds. An upgrade that redefines what a particular anyone-can-spend pattern means tightens the rules, which old nodes accept because they would have accepted any spend, which is the definition of a soft fork the witness branch gives (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The caution is the book's own, in strong words: application developers should never need to use an anyone-can-spend script, and anyone who does should loudly announce their plans to Bitcoin users and developers so that future upgrades do not accidentally interfere with their system, since an upgrade may give the pattern a new meaning (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A second caution is that funds sent to such a script are, in practice, a gift to the first miner who notices.

nodes.example: an empty script that OP_TRUE satisfies
nodes.definition: An anyone-can-spend script is one anyone can satisfy, such as the empty output script spent by an input script of OP_TRUE; upgrades take such a script and add constraints to it.

nodes.label: Standard transaction outputs
nodes.body: Standard transaction outputs are the output script templates that Bitcoin Core's policy for relaying and mining transactions allows. The book says the policy effectively limits output scripts to just a few templates, that this was originally implemented after the discovery of several early bugs in Bitcoin related to the script language, and that it is retained to support anyone-can-spend upgrades and to encourage the best practice of placing script conditions in P2SH redeem scripts, segwit version 0 witness scripts and segwit version 1 leaf scripts (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Standard transaction outputs are the output script templates that Bitcoin Core's policy for relaying and mining transactions allows. The book says the policy effectively limits output scripts to just a few templates, that this was originally implemented after the discovery of several early bugs in Bitcoin related to the script language, and that it is retained to support anyone-can-spend upgrades and to encourage the best practice of placing script conditions in P2SH redeem scripts, segwit version 0 witness scripts and segwit version 1 leaf scripts (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The templates matter because they are what wallets, explorers and addresses understand. Each template corresponds to an address type that chapter 4 introduced - pay to public key hash, pay to script hash, the two segwit version 0 forms and taproot - and a transaction whose output matches none of them is valid under consensus but will not be relayed by default nodes, so in practice it cannot be sent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The restriction is also what keeps the anyone-can-spend patterns of future upgrades out of ordinary use.

The worked example lists the templates Bitcoin Core's policy recognises as standard: the five address templates, the bare multisignature template that the source limits to at most three keys, and the data-carrier OP_RETURN template (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Bitcoin Core's IsStandard function classifies a script with its Solver and refuses anything it cannot classify, which is the mechanism; the book defers the templates themselves to the next chapter, where each is parsed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Both of Alice's outputs are standard, one taproot and one version 0 witness public key hash (mempool.space, 2026).

The caution is that standard is a policy word: a non-standard output can be mined if a miner chooses to include it, and standardness has changed as templates were added, so a list is dated. A second caution is that the templates constrain the output script only; what a redeem script, witness script or leaf script inside them may do is far less restricted, which is exactly the point of the best practice the book names (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: a few templates relay policy allows
nodes.definition: Standard transaction outputs are the few output script templates that Bitcoin Core's policy for relaying and mining transactions allows, kept to support upgrades and to encourage putting conditions in redeem, witness and leaf scripts.

nodes.label: Witnesses
nodes.body: This branch explains the witness structure, the 67 bytes near the end of Alice's transaction that prove she was allowed to spend. The book starts from the word: in court a witness is someone who testifies that they saw something important happen; for a math problem such as x plus 2 equals 4, the witness can simply be the value 2, which anyone can check; and when spending bitcoins the important problem is whether the spend was authorised by the people who control them, which full nodes decide by accepting witnesses that consist entirely of data for solving math problems (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This branch explains the witness structure, the 67 bytes near the end of Alice's transaction that prove she was allowed to spend. The book starts from the word: in court a witness is someone who testifies that they saw something important happen; for a math problem such as x plus 2 equals 4, the witness can simply be the value 2, which anyone can check; and when spending bitcoins the important problem is whether the spend was authorised by the people who control them, which full nodes decide by accepting witnesses that consist entirely of data for solving math problems (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The branch matters because where a witness is stored turned out to decide what contracts Bitcoin can support. In the legacy format signatures and other witness data go in the input script, which is hashed into the transaction identifier; the book shows three problems that follow - a circular dependency between two unsigned transactions, a third party's ability to change the identifier by re-encoding a push, and a counterparty's ability to do the same by re-signing - and explains how segregated witness removes all three by leaving the witness out of the identifier (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

The reader meets witnesses in every segwit transaction's hexadecimal, after the outputs and before the lock time; in the empty input script of such transactions; in the names of address types, where witness program and witness version are the terms chapter 4 used; and in the history of the Mt. Gox exchange, whose February 2014 claim that malleability explained its missing withdrawals is one of this chapter's stories. The 2017 activation of segwit at block 481,824 is recorded in Bitcoin Core's chain parameters (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The branch has four groups. The idea of a witness: the court analogy, the public key and signature as the real problem and its solution, and the contract protocols that need transactions signed out of order. The malleability problems: the circular dependency, third-party malleability through alternative push encodings, second-party malleability through alternative signatures, and the wanted kind that signature hashes allow. Segregated witness: the idea, the hard-fork and soft-fork paths, the witness program and the witness structure. And the serialization of the witness structure, with its stacks and items (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: The idea of a witness
nodes.body: This group explains what a witness is before any byte of it is read. The book's sequence is an analogy, a toy and the real case: a human witness in court, whose testimony must be interrogated; a value that witnesses the solution of a math problem, which can be checked rather than believed; and the public key and signature of a digital signature scheme, where the equation can only be solved by someone holding a secret (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This group explains what a witness is before any byte of it is read. The book's sequence is an analogy, a toy and the real case: a human witness in court, whose testimony must be interrogated; a value that witnesses the solution of a math problem, which can be checked rather than believed; and the public key and signature of a digital signature scheme, where the equation can only be solved by someone holding a secret (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The idea matters because it names the role that signatures play without tying it to any one place in the transaction. A signature in an input script, a signature in a witness item and a solution to the toy script 2 OP_ADD 4 OP_EQUAL are all witnesses in this sense: data that lets a node verify an authorisation without trusting anyone. Giving the role a name is what lets the book ask where witnesses should go, which is the question the rest of the branch answers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The three sections build up. The witness section states the definition and the toy script with its witness of 2. The signature witness section explains the public key and the signature as the identifier and the solution of a problem only the key's holder can solve, and shows the script with a public key and OP_CHECKSIG. The contract protocol section explains why developers building protocols on Bitcoin - the sequence branch's payment channel among them - ran into trouble with witnesses in the input script (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Witness
nodes.body: A witness is data that solves the math problem that protects some bitcoins. The book arrives at the definition through the court: a witness there is someone who testifies that they saw something important happen, and courts interrogate witnesses because humans are not always reliable; for a math problem such as x plus 2 equals 4, a witness need not be a person at all, since the proposed value of x can be checked directly (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Full nodes cannot interrogate humans, but they can accept witnesses that consist entirely of data for solving math problems.

paras.text: A witness is data that solves the math problem that protects some bitcoins. The book arrives at the definition through the court: a witness there is someone who testifies that they saw something important happen, and courts interrogate witnesses because humans are not always reliable; for a math problem such as x plus 2 equals 4, a witness need not be a person at all, since the proposed value of x can be checked directly (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Full nodes cannot interrogate humans, but they can accept witnesses that consist entirely of data for solving math problems.

The definition matters because it separates the proof from the prover. A node does not know or care who provides a witness; it checks whether the data satisfies the script, and a valid witness from a thief is as good as one from the owner. That is why the problem must be one that only the owner can solve, which the next section's digital signature provides, and why the data itself must be protected from alteration in transit, which is the malleability group's subject (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The book's toy script is 2 OP_ADD 4 OP_EQUAL: an input supplies a value, the script adds 2 and checks for equality with 4, so the witness 2 succeeds and any other value fails. The worked example checks the arithmetic. In a real transaction the script is in the output being spent and the witness is supplied by the spending transaction; for Alice's transaction the witness is one 65-byte item, a signature, which satisfies the taproot script of the output she spends (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (mempool.space, 2026). The book notes that letting bitcoins be spent by anyone who can solve a simple equation would not be secure, which motivates the next section.

The caution is that the word has two technical uses in this chapter. In the abstract sense every input script of a legacy transaction contains a witness; in the concrete sense of the serialization, the witness structure is a separate field of segwit transactions, and the book says the abstract name for the data held by an input script is a witness when it introduces segregated witness (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The two senses meet in the segregated witness group.

nodes.example: the value 2 solves 2 OP_ADD 4 OP_EQUAL
nodes.definition: A witness is data that solves the math problem protecting an output, which full nodes check instead of trusting; for the script 2 OP_ADD 4 OP_EQUAL the witness is the value 2.

nodes.label: Public key and signature as witness
nodes.body: The public key and the signature are the identifier and the solution of the problem that really protects bitcoins. The book says an unforgeable digital signature scheme uses an equation that can only be solved by someone in possession of certain data they are able to keep secret, that they reference that secret data using a public identifier called a public key, and that a solution to the equation is called a signature; a script containing a public key and an opcode requiring a corresponding signature makes the signature the witness, like the number 2 in the toy example (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The public key and the signature are the identifier and the solution of the problem that really protects bitcoins. The book says an unforgeable digital signature scheme uses an equation that can only be solved by someone in possession of certain data they are able to keep secret, that they reference that secret data using a public identifier called a public key, and that a solution to the equation is called a signature; a script containing a public key and an opcode requiring a corresponding signature makes the signature the witness, like the number 2 in the toy example (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The section matters because it connects this chapter to chapter 4 and to the book's chapter on digital signatures. Chapter 4 explained how a private key becomes a public key and an address; this chapter shows the public key placed in an output script with OP_CHECKSIG, and a signature placed in the witness, and says that the opcode requires the signature to commit to the data in the spending transaction, which is what prevents a valid signature from being reused on a different payment (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The worked example states the three roles. In the script the book shows, the public key is a push of the key's bytes and OP_CHECKSIG is the opcode that takes a signature and a key from the stack and checks them against the transaction; the signature is the witness because it is the datum the spender supplies. The book defers how the equation works to its chapter on signatures; here the point is structural, that the witness is a solution and the output script is the problem (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The caution is in the word commit: a signature covers the transaction's data, so changing the outputs invalidates it, but in the legacy format the signature cannot cover the input script that contains it, since the signature is part of that script. That gap is exactly where third-party malleability lives, as the next group shows. A second caution is that a signature requires a random number from the signer, and a different random number gives a different valid signature, which is the second-party malleability of the same group (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: a problem only the key holder can solve
nodes.definition: In a digital signature scheme the public key is a public identifier of secret data and the signature a solution to an equation only the holder of that data can produce; a script of a public key and OP_CHECKSIG makes the signature the witness.

io.code: (lambda problem: (problem['identifier'], problem['solver'], problem['witness']))({'identifier': 'public key', 'solver': 'the holder of the private key', 'witness': 'signature'})
io.out: ('public key', 'the holder of the private key', 'signature')

nodes.label: Contract protocols
nodes.body: A contract protocol is a series of transactions between parties arranged so that the parties can rely on each other without trust. The book says that witnesses need to be included in the transactions where they are used so that full nodes can verify them, that in the legacy format signatures and other data are placed in the input script field, and that when developers started to implement contract protocols on Bitcoin, such as the payment channel of the sequence branch, they discovered several significant problems with placing witnesses in the input script field (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A contract protocol is a series of transactions between parties arranged so that the parties can rely on each other without trust. The book says that witnesses need to be included in the transactions where they are used so that full nodes can verify them, that in the legacy format signatures and other data are placed in the input script field, and that when developers started to implement contract protocols on Bitcoin, such as the payment channel of the sequence branch, they discovered several significant problems with placing witnesses in the input script field (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Contract protocols matter because they are where Bitcoin's expressiveness is used: payment channels, the Lightning Network, escrows and swaps are all sequences of transactions whose signatures are exchanged in a particular order. The book's circular-dependency example describes a protocol in which Alice and Bob sign a refund before signing the deposit it refunds, so that neither can trap the other's money; the book calls such a design a trustless protocol (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Whether such designs can be built depends on properties of the transaction format, which is why a chapter on serialization turns to them.

The worked example lists the four stages of the card game as a protocol. In each, a transaction is signed and held rather than broadcast, and the holder relies on being able to broadcast it later; that reliance is sound only if the earlier transactions it spends keep the identifiers it was signed against, which is the property the legacy format cannot guarantee. The three sections of the next group are the three ways that guarantee fails, and the segregated witness group is the repair (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The caution is that trustless means not requiring trust in the counterparty, not requiring no assumptions: such a protocol still assumes that the network relays transactions, that miners include them, and that timelocks are enforced. A second caution is that the book's examples are deliberately minimal - two parties, two or three transactions - while real protocols add penalty transactions and hashed timelocks; the mechanisms are those of the book's chapter on second-layer applications.

nodes.example: transactions signed out of order
nodes.definition: A contract protocol is a series of transactions between parties, often signed out of order so that each party is protected before committing; the payment channel is one, and such protocols exposed the problems with witnesses in the input script.

io.code: ['setup transaction', 'refund transaction', 'rounds of the game', 'final transaction']
io.out: ['setup transaction', 'refund transaction', 'rounds of the game', 'final transaction']

nodes.label: The malleability problems
nodes.body: This group states the three problems that the book found with placing witnesses in the input script: the circular dependency, in which a refund cannot be signed before the deposit whose identifier it needs; third-party transaction malleability, in which anyone can re-encode a push in an input script and change a transaction's identifier; and second-party malleability, in which a counterparty can produce an alternative signature and change it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A fourth section covers the malleability people want, which signature hashes provide.

paras.text: This group states the three problems that the book found with placing witnesses in the input script: the circular dependency, in which a refund cannot be signed before the deposit whose identifier it needs; third-party transaction malleability, in which anyone can re-encode a push in an input script and change a transaction's identifier; and second-party malleability, in which a counterparty can produce an alternative signature and change it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A fourth section covers the malleability people want, which signature hashes provide.

The group matters because the problems are not bugs in any program but properties of the data format, and because they are the reason segregated witness was adopted. Each problem ends the same way, with a presigned transaction made invalid because the identifier it spends has changed; the book's Bob loses his payment to Carol through no fault of Alice, Bob or Carol, and its Alice loses her refund because Bob re-signed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The Mt. Gox story of this chapter shows the third-party problem blamed, rightly or not, for an exchange's losses.

The four sections follow the book's order. The circular dependency explains why the refund in a two-party deposit cannot be constructed until the deposit's signatures are known. Third-party malleability shows the alternative encodings of the number 2 and computes that each gives a different identifier. The push encodings section does the computation on a real transaction. Second-party malleability explains the random number in a signature. And wanted malleability explains that the book prefixes the word unwanted for a reason (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Circular dependency
nodes.body: A circular dependency is the first problem the book names with witnesses in the input script. Many contract protocols involve a series of transactions signed out of order: Alice and Bob deposit funds into a script that needs both signatures, but each wants their money back if the other becomes unresponsive, so they sign the refund transaction before the deposit. The book's problem: in the legacy format every field, including the input script that contains signatures, is used to derive a transaction's identifier, and the deposit's identifier is part of the refund's outpoint (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A circular dependency is the first problem the book names with witnesses in the input script. Many contract protocols involve a series of transactions signed out of order: Alice and Bob deposit funds into a script that needs both signatures, but each wants their money back if the other becomes unresponsive, so they sign the refund transaction before the deposit. The book's problem: in the legacy format every field, including the input script that contains signatures, is used to derive a transaction's identifier, and the deposit's identifier is part of the refund's outpoint (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The dependency matters because it makes a trustless two-party deposit impossible in the legacy format. The book spells it out: there is no way for Alice and Bob to construct the refund until both signatures for the deposit are known, but if they know the signatures for the deposit, one of them can broadcast it before signing the refund, eliminating the guarantee of a refund (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example models the chain of needs: the refund needs the deposit's identifier, which needs the deposit's signatures, which should come last.

The dependency is a consequence of what the identifier covers. If the identifier were computed over everything but the signatures, the deposit's identifier would be known as soon as its outputs were decided, the refund could be built and signed, and only then would the deposit be signed and broadcast; that is exactly the change segregated witness makes, by leaving the witness out of the identifier (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo et al., 2015). The book's examples use two transactions it calls Tx 0 and Tx 1, the deposit and the refund, and the same pair reappears in the second-party section.

The caution is that a more complex series of transactions can sometimes eliminate a circular dependency, as the book says at the start of the next section, but at the price of meeting the next problem; the dependency is the first obstacle, not the only one (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A second caution is that the problem is specific to protocols that presign: an ordinary payment, signed and broadcast at once, never needs the identifier of an unsigned transaction.

nodes.example: the refund needs the deposit's txid first
nodes.definition: A circular dependency arises when Alice and Bob want to sign a refund before the deposit it spends, but in the legacy format the deposit's txid depends on its signatures, so the refund cannot be built until both have signed the deposit.

io.code: (lambda needs: needs['refund'] in needs and needs[needs['refund']] == 'signatures of the deposit')({'refund': 'txid of the deposit', 'txid of the deposit': 'signatures of the deposit'})

nodes.label: Third-party transaction malleability
nodes.body: Third-party transaction malleability is the second problem: it is often possible to solve the same script in different ways. The book returns to the script 2 OP_ADD 4 OP_EQUAL and lists several ways to put the value 2 on the stack - OP_2, OP_PUSH1 0x02, OP_PUSH2 0x0002, and the OP_PUSHDATA1, OP_PUSHDATA2 and OP_PUSHDATA4 forms - each of which produces a slightly different transaction with a completely different txid; all versions spend the same outpoints and so conflict, and only one can be in a valid blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Third-party transaction malleability is the second problem: it is often possible to solve the same script in different ways. The book returns to the script 2 OP_ADD 4 OP_EQUAL and lists several ways to put the value 2 on the stack - OP_2, OP_PUSH1 0x02, OP_PUSH2 0x0002, and the OP_PUSHDATA1, OP_PUSHDATA2 and OP_PUSHDATA4 forms - each of which produces a slightly different transaction with a completely different txid; all versions spend the same outpoints and so conflict, and only one can be in a valid blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The problem matters because of who can exploit it. The book's scenario: Alice creates a transaction with OP_2 in the input script paying Bob, Bob immediately spends that output to Carol, and anyone on the network replaces OP_2 with OP_PUSH1 0x02, creating a conflict; if the conflicting version confirms, Alice's original cannot, and Bob's transaction cannot spend its output, so Bob's payment to Carol is invalid even though neither Alice, Bob nor Carol did anything wrong. Someone not involved in the transaction, a third party, was able to mutate it, which the book calls unwanted third-party transaction malleability (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The worked example builds a minimal legacy transaction body with three encodings of the push and hashes each with double SHA-256: three different identifiers from three byte strings that mean the same thing to the script interpreter. The mutation does not touch the signature, because a legacy signature cannot cover the input script that contains it, so each variant is as valid as the original; the next section does the same computation on a real transaction. BIP62 was an attempt to forbid non-canonical encodings by consensus; its status in the proposals repository is closed, and the book presents it as an attempt that, even if it had entirely eliminated third-party malleability, would have left the second-party kind unsolved (Wuille, 2014).

The caution is in the book's tip: there are cases when people want their transactions to be malleable, and Bitcoin provides features for that, notably the signature hashes of the book's chapter on signatures, so the book occasionally prefixes the word unwanted and means the unwanted variant whenever it uses the shorter term (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A second caution is that the attacker gains nothing directly - the mutated transaction pays the same outputs - but can break anything that depended on the original identifier, which for an exchange tracking withdrawals by identifier can look like a payment that never happened.

nodes.example: a stranger changes the txid, not the payment
nodes.definition: Unwanted third-party transaction malleability is a stranger's ability to change a transaction's txid without invalidating it, for example by re-encoding a push in the input script, so that a conflicting copy confirms and any transaction spending the original's outputs becomes invalid.

nodes.label: Alternative push encodings
nodes.body: The alternative push encodings are the concrete bytes behind third-party malleability. A push is an opcode that places data on the script's stack; Bitcoin's script language has several: the opcodes OP_1 to OP_16 push the small numbers directly, the opcodes 1 to 75 push that many following bytes, and OP_PUSHDATA1, OP_PUSHDATA2 and OP_PUSHDATA4 push data whose length is given in one, two or four following bytes. The book lists these forms for the number 2 and notes that each produces a slightly different transaction with a completely different txid (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The alternative push encodings are the concrete bytes behind third-party malleability. A push is an opcode that places data on the script's stack; Bitcoin's script language has several: the opcodes OP_1 to OP_16 push the small numbers directly, the opcodes 1 to 75 push that many following bytes, and OP_PUSHDATA1, OP_PUSHDATA2 and OP_PUSHDATA4 push data whose length is given in one, two or four following bytes. The book lists these forms for the number 2 and notes that each produces a slightly different transaction with a completely different txid (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The encodings matter because the script interpreter treats them alike while the hash function does not. OP_2 is the single byte 0x52; a one-byte push of 0x02 is the two bytes 01 02; a two-byte push of 0x0002 is 02 02 00; and OP_PUSHDATA1 with a length of one is 4c 01 02. The worked example lists these four byte strings. Since the input script is part of the legacy serialization, any of them changes the identifier, and the previous section's example showed three identifiers from three of them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The chapter's library applies the same substitution to a real transaction: given the first bitcoin transaction of January 2009, which has a legacy input script, replacing that script with each of the four encodings and recomputing the identifier gives four different identifiers, which an executed claim records. The substituted transactions would not actually validate, since the real script needs a signature, but the computation shows what a third party could do to a transaction whose script accepted a bare number (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The caution is that relay policy has long refused non-canonical pushes - Bitcoin Core treats a push that is not the shortest encoding as non-standard - so the simplest mutations are not relayed today; the book's point is that policy is not consensus, and that a miner or a non-standard node could still produce the mutation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A second caution is that the opcode numbers 0x01 to 0x4b are themselves lengths, so a push of 2 bytes written 02 is an opcode, not the number two.

nodes.example: four byte strings for the number 2
nodes.definition: The number 2 can be pushed as OP_2, as a one-byte push, as a two-byte push or with OP_PUSHDATA1; each is a different byte string, so each gives a legacy transaction a different txid while the script result is the same.

nodes.label: Second-party transaction malleability
nodes.body: Second-party transaction malleability is the third problem. The book says that when the legacy format was the only format, developers worked on proposals such as BIP62 to minimise third-party malleability, but that even if third-party malleability were entirely eliminated, users of contract protocols faced another problem: if they required a signature from someone else involved in the protocol, that person could generate alternative signatures and change the txid (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2014).

paras.text: Second-party transaction malleability is the third problem. The book says that when the legacy format was the only format, developers worked on proposals such as BIP62 to minimise third-party malleability, but that even if third-party malleability were entirely eliminated, users of contract protocols faced another problem: if they required a signature from someone else involved in the protocol, that person could generate alternative signatures and change the txid (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2014).

The problem matters because it cannot be fixed by canonical encodings. The book's example: Alice and Bob hold money in a two-signature script with a refund; Alice wants to spend some, so they build a chain in which the deposit's second output returns the remainder to the joint script and a new refund spends it, signed before the deposit. There is no circular dependency, and ignoring third-party malleability it looks trustless; but a signer has to choose a large random number when creating a signature, and a different number produces a different signature even if everything signed stays the same (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The worked example states the property: the same data signed with two different random numbers gives two different valid signatures, and in the legacy format two different identifiers. The book compares it to a handwritten signature, which looks slightly different on two copies of the same contract; the consequence is that if Alice broadcasts the deposit containing Bob's signature, Bob can broadcast a conflicting version with a fresh signature, and if his version confirms Alice cannot use the presigned refund, which the book calls unwanted second-party transaction malleability (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The caution is that the second party is a legitimate signer acting within the rules; nothing in the legacy format can distinguish the signature the protocol expected from the one the counterparty substituted, so the only remedy is to take signatures out of the identifier altogether. A second caution is terminological: the book counts the sender as the first party, so a second party is a counterparty in the protocol and a third party is a stranger (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: a counterparty re-signs and changes the txid
nodes.definition: Unwanted second-party transaction malleability is a counterparty's ability to produce an alternative signature, because a signer chooses a random number each time, and so a conflicting transaction with a different txid that invalidates a presigned refund.
