nodes.label: Wanted malleability
nodes.body: Wanted malleability is the kind the book's tip describes: there are cases when people want their transactions to be malleable, and Bitcoin provides several features to support that, most notably the signature hashes, or sighash, of the book's chapter on signatures. The example is Alice using a sighash to allow Bob to help her pay some transaction fees, which mutates Alice's transaction but only in a way that Alice wants (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Wanted malleability is the kind the book's tip describes: there are cases when people want their transactions to be malleable, and Bitcoin provides several features to support that, most notably the signature hashes, or sighash, of the book's chapter on signatures. The example is Alice using a sighash to allow Bob to help her pay some transaction fees, which mutates Alice's transaction but only in a way that Alice wants (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The distinction matters because it fixes the vocabulary of the whole branch. The book says that for this reason it occasionally prefixes the word unwanted to the term transaction malleability, and that even when it and other technical writers use the shorter term, they are almost certainly talking about the unwanted variant (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A reader who takes malleability to mean any change to a transaction will misread both the problems and the remedy, since segregated witness removes only the unwanted kinds.

A signature hash is a flag attached to a signature that says which parts of the transaction the signature commits to; the default commits to everything, and other values leave some inputs or outputs uncommitted so that others may add to them. The worked example sorts the three kinds and keeps the one that is permitted. Wanted malleability survives segregated witness untouched, because it works through what the signature covers rather than through the identifier (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The caution is that a wanted mutation still changes the identifier in the legacy format and still changes the witness identifier in the segwit format, so a protocol that allows one must not presign transactions against the mutated transaction's identifier. A second caution is that sighash flags are a sharp tool: a signature that commits to nothing but one input can be attached to any transaction that spends that input, which is why the book treats them in a chapter of their own.

nodes.example: mutation the sender allows
nodes.definition: Some malleability is wanted: with a signature hash the sender can allow others to change parts of a transaction, as when Bob adds an input to help pay Alice's fee; the book says unwanted when it means the other kind.

io.code: (lambda kinds: [k for k in kinds if kinds[k]])({'unwanted third-party': False, 'unwanted second-party': False, 'sender-permitted (sighash)': True})

nodes.label: Segregated witness
nodes.body: Segregated witness, segwit, is the idea of separating the rest of the data in a transaction from its witness for the purpose of generating a txid. The book says that as early as 2011 protocol developers knew how to solve circular dependence and both malleabilities by avoiding the input script in the calculation that produces a txid, and that the idea took its name from this separation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This group explains the idea, the two ways of deploying it, and the two new fields it introduced.

paras.text: Segregated witness, segwit, is the idea of separating the rest of the data in a transaction from its witness for the purpose of generating a txid. The book says that as early as 2011 protocol developers knew how to solve circular dependence and both malleabilities by avoiding the input script in the calculation that produces a txid, and that the idea took its name from this separation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This group explains the idea, the two ways of deploying it, and the two new fields it introduced.

The group matters because segwit is the format Alice's transaction uses and the reason her input script is empty. It also matters as the clearest example in the book of how Bitcoin changes its rules: the obvious implementation needed a hard fork, an alternative in late 2015 used a soft fork built on anyone-can-spend scripts, and the result is that old nodes allow what new nodes require (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The weight branch shows the second thing segwit changed, the way transaction size is measured.

The five sections go from idea to fields. Segwit itself: the separation and what it eliminates. Hard fork: the incompatible change the obvious design needed. Soft fork: the backward-compatible change and its rule that new nodes may reject but not accept more. Witness program: the output script template of a version number and data that old nodes see as anyone-can-spend. Witness structure: the new field that holds what the input script no longer may, and the book's table of terms for authorization and authentication across the whitepaper, legacy and segwit (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Segregated witness
nodes.body: Segregated witness is the idea of separating the rest of the data in a transaction from its witness for the purpose of generating a txid. The book says the abstract name for the data held by an input script is a witness, that protocol developers knew as early as 2011 that avoiding the input script in the txid calculation solved circular dependence and both malleabilities, and that the idea of the separation is called segregated witness, segwit for short (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP141 is the consensus layer of the design and BIP144 its serialization (Lombrozo et al., 2015) (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016).

paras.text: Segregated witness is the idea of separating the rest of the data in a transaction from its witness for the purpose of generating a txid. The book says the abstract name for the data held by an input script is a witness, that protocol developers knew as early as 2011 that avoiding the input script in the txid calculation solved circular dependence and both malleabilities, and that the idea of the separation is called segregated witness, segwit for short (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP141 is the consensus layer of the design and BIP144 its serialization (Lombrozo et al., 2015) (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016).

Segwit matters because it made the contract protocols of this branch possible. The book states the effect in one sentence: an empty input script keeps witnesses from affecting the txid, eliminating circular dependencies, third-party transaction malleability and second-party transaction malleability (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A refund can now be signed against a deposit whose identifier is fixed before anyone signs the deposit, and no re-encoding or re-signing by anyone can change that identifier, because the identifier no longer covers the data being changed.

The worked example proves the separation on Alice's transaction: hashing the legacy serialization - the bytes without the marker, the flag and the witness structure - with double SHA-256 and reversing the result gives 46620030..., the identifier the book, the explorer and Bitcoin Core all report for her transaction, although the serialization they return includes the witness (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (mempool.space, 2026). BIP141 defines a second identifier, the wtxid, over the whole extended serialization, which does change with the witness and which blocks commit to separately (Lombrozo et al., 2015). An executed claim shows that altering a witness item changes the wtxid and leaves the txid unchanged.

The caution is that segwit is a property of outputs, not of transactions as a whole: a transaction that spends a legacy output still has a witness in its input script and is still malleable in that input, and the book's closing section says a transaction with an empty witness structure must use the legacy format (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A second caution is historical: the design was described in late 2015, activated on the main network at block 481,824 in August 2017, and the book's as early as 2011 refers to the idea rather than the deployment (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: Hard fork
nodes.body: A hard fork is a change to Bitcoin's consensus rules that would not be compatible with older full nodes. The book introduces the term when it explains that the obvious method for implementing segwit - changing the serialization and the identifier for every node at once - requires such a change, and it says hard forks come with a lot of challenges, which it discusses in a later chapter (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Chapter 1 and chapter 2 introduced consensus rules as the rules every full node enforces identically; a hard fork is a change that makes new rules accept something old rules reject.

paras.text: A hard fork is a change to Bitcoin's consensus rules that would not be compatible with older full nodes. The book introduces the term when it explains that the obvious method for implementing segwit - changing the serialization and the identifier for every node at once - requires such a change, and it says hard forks come with a lot of challenges, which it discusses in a later chapter (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Chapter 1 and chapter 2 introduced consensus rules as the rules every full node enforces identically; a hard fork is a change that makes new rules accept something old rules reject.

The term matters because it names the cost of the obvious design. A hard fork requires every node to upgrade or be left on a different chain, since old nodes would reject blocks containing the new transactions; for a change whose benefit is felt mainly by contract protocols, demanding that of every participant was judged too much, and the book says an alternative approach was described in late 2015 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example states the test: if the new rules accept something the old rules reject, the change is a hard fork.

The mechanics follow from how nodes validate. An old node applies the old rules to every block; if a block is valid under the new rules and invalid under the old, old nodes reject it and continue on a chain of blocks that new nodes may in turn consider inferior, and the network splits into two chains with two histories. The book's chapter on mining and consensus treats what it takes to coordinate such a change; for this chapter it is enough that segwit chose the other path (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The caution is that hard and soft describe compatibility, not size or importance: a tiny change that lets a new kind of block through is a hard fork, and a large change that only tightens rules is a soft fork. A second caution is that a hard fork is not inherently bad - the book's later chapter discusses cases - but it needs the whole economy to move, which a soft fork does not.

nodes.label: Soft fork
nodes.body: A soft fork is a backward-compatible change to the consensus rules. The book says the alternative approach to segwit described in late 2015 used one, and defines backward compatible: full nodes implementing the change must not accept any blocks that full nodes without the change would consider invalid; as long as they obey that rule, newer full nodes can reject blocks that older full nodes would accept, giving them the ability to enforce new consensus rules, but only if the newer nodes represent the economic consensus among Bitcoin users (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A soft fork is a backward-compatible change to the consensus rules. The book says the alternative approach to segwit described in late 2015 used one, and defines backward compatible: full nodes implementing the change must not accept any blocks that full nodes without the change would consider invalid; as long as they obey that rule, newer full nodes can reject blocks that older full nodes would accept, giving them the ability to enforce new consensus rules, but only if the newer nodes represent the economic consensus among Bitcoin users (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The soft fork matters because it is how every consensus change in this chapter was made: BIP68, BIP112 and BIP113 for the sequence and lock time, BIP34 for the coinbase, BIP141 for segwit, and the earliest known soft fork that made lock time a consensus rule at block 31,000 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Old nodes keep following the chain because every block that new nodes accept is also valid to them; what they lose is the ability to check the new rules, so they accept on trust what new nodes verify.

The worked example states the test as set inclusion: the set of what new nodes accept must be a subset of what old nodes accept. For segwit, the trick is that a spend of a segwit output is, to an old node, a spend of an anyone-can-spend output with an empty input script, which old rules accept; new rules add the requirement of a valid witness, which only tightens. The book notes the condition in its parenthesis: enforcing new rules this way works only if the upgraded nodes are the economic majority, which its chapter on mining explores (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The caution is that a soft fork can only restrict. A change that gives new meaning to previously forbidden data is impossible as a soft fork, which is why upgrades are built on reserved and anyone-can-spend features that are valid but unused under the old rules; the version branch's presigned-transaction section is the other side of this coin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A second caution is that old nodes after a soft fork are secure only to the extent that the miners enforce the new rules, since the old nodes cannot.

nodes.definition: A soft fork is a backward-compatible change to the consensus rules: full nodes with the change must not accept any block that nodes without it would consider invalid, so new nodes can reject blocks old nodes accept but not the reverse.

nodes.label: Witness program
nodes.body: A witness program is the data part of a segwit output script. The book says the soft-fork segwit approach is based on anyone-can-spend output scripts: a script that starts with any of the numbers 0 to 16 followed by 2 to 40 bytes of data is defined as a segwit output script template, the number indicates its version - 0 is segwit version 0 - and the data is called a witness program; it is also possible to wrap the template in a P2SH commitment, which the chapter does not deal with (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

paras.text: A witness program is the data part of a segwit output script. The book says the soft-fork segwit approach is based on anyone-can-spend output scripts: a script that starts with any of the numbers 0 to 16 followed by 2 to 40 bytes of data is defined as a segwit output script template, the number indicates its version - 0 is segwit version 0 - and the data is called a witness program; it is also possible to wrap the template in a P2SH commitment, which the chapter does not deal with (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

The template matters because it is how segwit became a soft fork. From the perspective of old nodes, the book says, these output script templates can be spent with an empty input script, while from the perspective of a new node any payment to a segwit template must only be spent with an empty input script; old nodes allow it, new nodes require it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Both of Alice's outputs are witness programs - a version 1 program of 32 bytes to Bob and a version 0 program of 20 bytes for her change - and the output she spends is a version 1 program too (mempool.space, 2026).

The worked example decodes Alice's first output script: the first byte 0x51 is the number 1, so the version is 1; the second byte is a push of 32; and 32 bytes follow, the witness program, which for taproot is a public key. For version 0, the book's chapter 4 explained the two program lengths - 20 bytes for a public key hash, 32 for a script hash - and the chapter's library checks the template's bounds of 2 to 40 bytes. The book connects the template to a trend of increasing abstraction: the whitepaper received to public keys and spent with signatures, the original release to output scripts and input scripts, and segwit to witness programs and the witness structure (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The caution is that an unknown version is still anyone-can-spend to every node, including new ones: versions 2 to 16 have no rules yet, so a payment to such a program can be taken by anyone, and wallets refuse to send to them. A second caution is that the version number in the script, 0 to 16, is unrelated to the transaction version of the version branch; both are called version and they count different things.

nodes.label: Witness structure
nodes.body: The witness structure is the field segwit added to the transaction. The book says that with no ability to put data in an input script, users of segwit output script templates need a new field, and that field is called the witness structure (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is serialized after the outputs and before the lock time, it holds one witness stack per input, and it is excluded from the legacy serialization over which the txid is computed (Lombrozo et al., 2015) (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016).

paras.text: The witness structure is the field segwit added to the transaction. The book says that with no ability to put data in an input script, users of segwit output script templates need a new field, and that field is called the witness structure (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is serialized after the outputs and before the lock time, it holds one witness stack per input, and it is excluded from the legacy serialization over which the txid is computed (Lombrozo et al., 2015) (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016).

The field matters because it is where authorisation now lives for most transactions, and because its placement outside the identifier is the whole of segwit's remedy. The book's table of terms lays out the three generations: the whitepaper authorised with a public key and authenticated with a signature, the original release with an output script and an input script, and segwit with a witness program and the witness structure; the worked example reproduces that table. Authorization is who may spend, authentication is proof that they did (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The structure is a sequence of stacks in input order, each stack a count followed by its items with their lengths; the serialization group reads Alice's, which has one stack of one 65-byte item. Because the field is outside the txid, a block cannot commit to witnesses through the ordinary transaction tree, so BIP141 adds a second commitment, a tree of witness identifiers placed in the coinbase transaction, which the coinbase group mentions and the book's chapter on mining explains (Lombrozo et al., 2015) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The caution is that excluded from the txid does not mean uncommitted: the witness is covered by the wtxid and by the block's witness commitment, so it cannot be changed after confirmation; what it cannot do is change the txid before confirmation. A second caution is the book's own observation that the introduction of witness programs and the witness structure complicates Bitcoin, which is why the vocabulary of this branch has so many near-synonyms (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: the new field for what the input script held
nodes.definition: The witness structure is the field added by segwit to hold the data that an input script may no longer carry; it sits after the outputs and before the lock time and is not part of the txid.

nodes.label: Witness structure serialization
nodes.body: This group reads the bytes of the witness structure. The book says that, similar to the inputs and outputs fields, the witness structure contains other fields, and it starts from a map of those bytes in Alice's transaction; unlike those fields, the overall structure does not start with any indication of the total number of witness stacks it contains, because that is implied by the inputs field - there is one witness stack for every input (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This group reads the bytes of the witness structure. The book says that, similar to the inputs and outputs fields, the witness structure contains other fields, and it starts from a map of those bytes in Alice's transaction; unlike those fields, the overall structure does not start with any indication of the total number of witness stacks it contains, because that is implied by the inputs field - there is one witness stack for every input (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The group matters because it is the last variable-length part of the transaction and the one whose count is implicit, which trips parsers. It also shows how legacy inputs coexist with segwit inputs in one transaction: every input has a stack, and a legacy input's stack is the single byte zero. Alice's transaction has one input and one witness item, a 65-byte signature, which is the whole of its authorisation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The three sections read the structure from the outside in: the witness stack, one per input, with its count of items; the witness item, each prefixed by a compactSize length, which the book says it explores in detail in the next chapter; and the legacy input's witness, a count of zero that makes the structure uniform across input types (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Witness stack
nodes.body: A witness stack is the witness of one input: the book says the witness structure for a particular input starts with a count of the number of elements it contains, and that those elements are called witness items (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The number of stacks is not stored; the book says it is implied by the inputs field, since there is one witness stack for every input in a transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In Alice's transaction the structure begins at offset 123 with the byte 01, one item.

paras.text: A witness stack is the witness of one input: the book says the witness structure for a particular input starts with a count of the number of elements it contains, and that those elements are called witness items (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The number of stacks is not stored; the book says it is implied by the inputs field, since there is one witness stack for every input in a transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In Alice's transaction the structure begins at offset 123 with the byte 01, one item.

The stack matters because it is the unit that the output script's witness version interprets. A version 0 program paying a public key hash expects a stack of two items, a signature and a public key; a version 1 taproot key path expects a single item, the signature, which is Alice's case; and a script path expects the script and its control block as the last two items. What the items mean is for the next chapter; this chapter reads the counts (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

The worked example reads the input count at offset 6 and the item count at offset 123 and finds 1 and 1. A parser must therefore remember the input count from the beginning of the transaction and read that many stacks here; the chapter's library does so, and the byte map of the witness structure that the book draws shows the count byte, the length byte and the 65-byte item (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Because each stack is self-delimiting through its counts, stacks for several inputs simply follow one another.

The caution is the one the book makes explicit: there is no count at the start of the structure, and a parser that expects one will read the first stack's item count as a stack count and misread everything after. A second caution is that an item count of zero is a complete stack, which the legacy input section explains; the structure is never shorter than one byte per input.

nodes.example: one stack per input, counted by the inputs
nodes.definition: A witness stack is the part of the witness structure belonging to one input: a compactSize count of items followed by the items; there is one stack per input, so the structure has no count of its own.

nodes.label: Witness item
nodes.body: A witness item is one element of a witness stack. The book says each witness item is prefixed by a compactSize integer indicating its size, that the items are explored in detail in the next chapter, and that Alice's transaction contains one input and one witness item (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example reads the length byte at offset 124, 65, and the item that follows, which begins cf5efe2d and ends with the byte 01.

paras.text: A witness item is one element of a witness stack. The book says each witness item is prefixed by a compactSize integer indicating its size, that the items are explored in detail in the next chapter, and that Alice's transaction contains one input and one witness item (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example reads the length byte at offset 124, 65, and the item that follows, which begins cf5efe2d and ends with the byte 01.

The item is the witness in the concrete sense: for Alice's taproot spend it is a Schnorr signature of 64 bytes followed by one byte, the signature hash flag of the wanted-malleability section, which here is 1, the default that commits to the whole transaction. The explorer labels the output type v1_p2tr and shows this item as the input's witness (mempool.space, 2026). Its 65 bytes are also the largest single field of the transaction and the one most cheaply priced by the weight rules, which the weight branch explains.

The length prefix makes items of any size possible: a signature of 65 bytes, a public key of 33, a script of hundreds, each with its own prefix, and a prefix of 0xfd and two more bytes for an item above 252 bytes. The book's byte map of the witness structure shows the count, the length and the item; the chapter's library records each as a span, and an executed claim parses the item and checks its length and its last byte (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The caution is that a witness item is data, not script: the item is pushed onto the stack as it stands, so the push encodings that caused third-party malleability do not exist here, which is a second, less-noticed reason segwit removes that problem (Lombrozo et al., 2015). A second caution is that the trailing 01 is part of the item - a 64-byte signature with the default flag could in principle omit it, which is why the next chapter treats the flag's encoding.

nodes.example: a 65-byte signature, length-prefixed
nodes.definition: A witness item is one element of a witness stack, prefixed by a compactSize integer giving its size; Alice's single item is a 65-byte signature.

nodes.label: A legacy input's witness
nodes.body: A legacy input's witness is the empty stack. The book says legacy inputs do not contain any witness items, so their witness stack consists entirely of a count of zero, 0x00 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In a transaction that mixes a legacy input and a segwit input, the witness structure therefore has two stacks, one empty and one with items, in the order of the inputs.

paras.text: A legacy input's witness is the empty stack. The book says legacy inputs do not contain any witness items, so their witness stack consists entirely of a count of zero, 0x00 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In a transaction that mixes a legacy input and a segwit input, the witness structure therefore has two stacks, one empty and one with items, in the order of the inputs.

The rule matters because it keeps the structure regular. If legacy inputs had no stack at all, a parser would need to know, for every input, whether the output it spends is a segwit output - information that is in the UTXO database, not in the transaction - before it could parse the witness; with a zero count the parser needs only the input count. The worked example shows the two stacks, of zero and two items.

The zero byte is the compactSize encoding of the count zero, so it is one byte and takes one weight unit. A transaction whose inputs are all legacy would have a structure of nothing but zero bytes, which is why the book's closing section says the legacy format must be used for any transaction with an empty witness structure: the marker and flag would announce a witness that carries nothing (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP144 makes the same rule for the network (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016).

The caution is that a legacy input in a segwit transaction is still malleable: its signature is in its input script, which is in the txid, so a third party can still re-encode its pushes. The protections of this branch apply input by input, and a protocol that needs them must spend only segwit outputs. A second caution is that an empty stack is not an invalid one; the stack of an input spending an anyone-can-spend legacy output is empty and valid.

nodes.example: a stack of zero items
nodes.definition: A legacy input in a segwit transaction has a witness stack consisting entirely of a count of zero, 0x00, so the structure stays one stack per input.

nodes.label: Lock time and the coinbase
nodes.body: This branch covers the last field of every transaction and the first transaction of every block. The book says the final field in a serialized transaction is its lock time, which was part of the original format but initially only enforced by Bitcoin's policy for choosing which transactions to mine, until Bitcoin's earliest known soft fork made it a rule from block 31,000; and that the first transaction in each block is a special case, called a generation transaction in older documentation and a coinbase transaction in newer (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This branch covers the last field of every transaction and the first transaction of every block. The book says the final field in a serialized transaction is its lock time, which was part of the original format but initially only enforced by Bitcoin's policy for choosing which transactions to mine, until Bitcoin's earliest known soft fork made it a rule from block 31,000; and that the first transaction in each block is a special case, called a generation transaction in older documentation and a coinbase transaction in newer (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The two subjects share a theme, time and height as conditions on validity. The lock time says the earliest block or time at which a transaction may be included; the coinbase's maturity rule says how long its outputs must wait before they can be spent; and both rely on the median time past and the block height that the outpoint group said a node records for every output. The coinbase is also where new bitcoins enter, under a schedule this branch computes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The reader meets the lock time as the four zero bytes that end most transactions, and as the field a wallet sets to the current height to discourage fee sniping, which is what the transaction that paid Alice did with a lock time of 774,957 (mempool.space, 2026). The coinbase is met at the top of every block an explorer shows, with its subsidy and its fees, and in the news every four years when the subsidy halves.

The branch has two groups. The lock time group reads the field and its three readings - zero for any block, a value below 500,000,000 as a block height, and a larger value as an epoch time compared with the median time past of eleven blocks. The coinbase group reads the special rules: one input with a null outpoint, a coinbase field of 2 to 100 bytes, outputs that may not exceed the fees plus the subsidy, the subsidy schedule of halvings, the block reward, and the maturity rule of 100 confirmations (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: Lock time
nodes.body: The lock time is the four-byte field that ends every transaction. The book says it was part of Bitcoin's original serialization format but was initially only enforced by policy, and that the earliest known soft fork added a rule that, starting at block height 31,000, forbids the inclusion of a transaction in a block unless its lock time is zero, or is a height the block has reached, or is a time the block's median time past has passed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This group reads the field and each of its three cases.

paras.text: The lock time is the four-byte field that ends every transaction. The book says it was part of Bitcoin's original serialization format but was initially only enforced by policy, and that the earliest known soft fork added a rule that, starting at block height 31,000, forbids the inclusion of a transaction in a block unless its lock time is zero, or is a height the block has reached, or is a time the block's median time past has passed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This group reads the field and each of its three cases.

The lock time matters because it is the oldest timelock in Bitcoin and the one the opcode of BIP65 later built on: a transaction can be made unusable until a date, which is what makes a presigned refund safe to hand over, since it cannot be broadcast early (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Todd, 2014). It is also an example of the chapter's recurring pattern of a feature first enforced by policy and then by consensus, and of a field whose encoding packs two meanings into one number by a threshold.

The four sections take the field, then its two non-zero readings, then the clock those readings compare against. The lock-time field section states the rule and its history; the height lock section computes the book's example of 123,456; the time lock section explains epoch time and the 500,000,000 threshold; and the median time past section computes the median of eleven block times, the quantity BIP113 made the reference for time locks, and explains why it runs an hour or two behind (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo, 2015) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: The lock time field
nodes.body: The lock time field is the final field in a serialized transaction. The book says it was part of Bitcoin's original serialization format but initially only enforced by Bitcoin's policy for choosing which transactions to mine, and that Bitcoin's earliest known soft fork added a rule that, starting at block height 31,000, forbids the inclusion of a transaction in a block unless it satisfies one of three rules, the first being that a lock time of zero makes it eligible for inclusion in any block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Alice's transaction ends with four zero bytes.

paras.text: The lock time field is the final field in a serialized transaction. The book says it was part of Bitcoin's original serialization format but initially only enforced by Bitcoin's policy for choosing which transactions to mine, and that Bitcoin's earliest known soft fork added a rule that, starting at block height 31,000, forbids the inclusion of a transaction in a block unless it satisfies one of three rules, the first being that a lock time of zero makes it eligible for inclusion in any block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Alice's transaction ends with four zero bytes.

The field matters as the simplest way to say not before. A transaction with a lock time in the future is valid in form but cannot be confirmed yet, so it can be signed and handed over without the holder being able to use it early; and because the rule is consensus, no miner can include it ahead of time. Bitcoin Core's IsFinalTx implements the check, with one exception the sequence branch mentioned: if every input's sequence is the final value, the lock time is ignored, a remnant of the original replacement scheme in which a final transaction needed no further waiting (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The worked example reads the four bytes of Alice's lock time as the little-endian integer zero. For a non-zero value the node compares it with the block: the next section's height reading if it is below 500,000,000, the time reading otherwise, and the transaction is final when the lock time is strictly less than the block's height or the block's median time past, which is why a lock time of 123,456 is first satisfied by block 123,456 - the comparison is against the height after it, as the book's example and Bitcoin Core's comparison agree (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The caution is the interaction with the sequence field: a lock time is honoured only if at least one input's sequence is below the final value, so a wallet that wants a lock time must also lower a sequence, which is why many wallets use 0xfffffffe. A second caution is the word earliest: a lock time cannot expire a transaction, only delay it, and the book's note on coinbase maturity makes the same point from the other side (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: zero: eligible for any block
nodes.definition: The lock time is the last 4 bytes of a transaction; zero makes it eligible for any block, and since block 31,000 a non-zero value is a consensus rule restricting which blocks may include it.

nodes.label: Lock time as a block height
nodes.body: A lock time below 500,000,000 is read as a block height. The book's second rule: the transaction indicates that it wants to restrict which blocks it can be included in by setting its lock time to a value less than 500,000,000, and in this case the transaction can only be included in a block that has a height equal to the lock time or higher; a transaction with a lock time of 123,456 can be included in block 123,456 or any later block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A lock time below 500,000,000 is read as a block height. The book's second rule: the transaction indicates that it wants to restrict which blocks it can be included in by setting its lock time to a value less than 500,000,000, and in this case the transaction can only be included in a block that has a height equal to the lock time or higher; a transaction with a lock time of 123,456 can be included in block 123,456 or any later block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The height reading is the precise one, since the chain's height advances by exactly one per block, and it is the one wallets use most. The transaction that paid Alice, confirmed in block 774,958, carries a lock time of 774,957, the height of the chain when it was built; setting the lock time to the current height is a common wallet practice that prevents the transaction from being included in a reorganised earlier block, a defence against what is called fee sniping (mempool.space, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The worked example checks the book's example at the boundary.

Bitcoin Core's IsFinalTx compares the lock time with the height of the block being validated, which is one more than the height of the chain tip when the transaction was built: a lock time of 774,957 is satisfied by block 774,958, because 774,957 is less than 774,958 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The threshold itself is the constant LOCKTIME_THRESHOLD, 500,000,000, which Bitcoin Core's script header annotates with the date it corresponds to as a time, 5 November 1985 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Heights will not reach it for thousands of years, which is what makes the two readings separable.

The caution is the off-by-one that the book's example settles: a lock time of n allows block n, not block n plus one, because the comparison is strict against the block's own height. A second caution is that the height reading has no notion of time at all, so a transaction locked to a height may become valid earlier or later than expected if blocks arrive faster or slower than ten minutes apart.

nodes.example: 123,456 means block 123,456 or later
nodes.definition: A lock time below 500,000,000 is a block height: the transaction can only be included in a block whose height is equal to the lock time or higher, so 123,456 allows block 123,456 and any later one.

nodes.label: Lock time as an epoch time
nodes.body: A lock time of 500,000,000 or more is read as a time. The book's third rule: the transaction indicates that it wants to restrict when it can be included in the blockchain by setting its lock time to a value of 500,000,000 or greater, in which case the field is parsed as epoch time, the number of seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00 UTC, and the transaction can only be included in a block with a median time past greater than the lock time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A lock time of 500,000,000 or more is read as a time. The book's third rule: the transaction indicates that it wants to restrict when it can be included in the blockchain by setting its lock time to a value of 500,000,000 or greater, in which case the field is parsed as epoch time, the number of seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00 UTC, and the transaction can only be included in a block with a median time past greater than the lock time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The time reading matters for agreements made in human terms, a refund valid from a date rather than from a height. Epoch time is the convention of counting seconds from the start of 1970 that most computers use; the block time of Alice's transaction's block, 1,675,559,245, is such a number and the worked example classifies it as a time. The reading is enforced against the median time past, not against the block's own timestamp, a change BIP113 made so that a miner cannot satisfy a lock by writing a later time in a block header (Lombrozo, 2015).

The threshold 500,000,000 separates the two readings because, as a time, it is 5 November 1985, before Bitcoin existed, and as a height it is thousands of years away, so no value is ambiguous (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Bitcoin Core's IsFinalTx chooses the comparison by the threshold and tests that the lock time is less than the block's time or height, with the block's time taken as its median time past when the BIP113 rule is active, which it has been since the same activation as BIP68 (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The caution is that the median time past is normally an hour or two behind the current time, as the book says, so a time lock set for noon is usually satisfiable only in the early afternoon; a protocol that needs precision must allow for it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A second caution is that the two readings cannot be mixed in one transaction, and BIP65's opcode fails when the lock-time type of its argument differs from that of the transaction's field (Todd, 2014).

nodes.example: 500,000,000 or more is a timestamp
nodes.definition: A lock time of 500,000,000 or more is an epoch time, seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00 UTC; the transaction can only be included in a block whose median time past is greater than the lock time.

io.code: (lambda lt: 'epoch time' if lt >= 500_000_000 else 'block height')(1675559245)

nodes.label: Median time past
nodes.body: The median time past is the quantity a time lock is compared against. The book introduces it in the third lock-time rule - a transaction with a time lock can only be included in a block with a median time past greater than the lock time - and says MTP is normally about an hour or two behind the current time, deferring the rules to its chapter on the blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core computes it in GetMedianTimePast as the median of the timestamps of the last eleven blocks (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: The median time past is the quantity a time lock is compared against. The book introduces it in the third lock-time rule - a transaction with a time lock can only be included in a block with a median time past greater than the lock time - and says MTP is normally about an hour or two behind the current time, deferring the rules to its chapter on the blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core computes it in GetMedianTimePast as the median of the timestamps of the last eleven blocks (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The median matters because block timestamps are chosen by miners and are only loosely constrained. A single block's time can be early or late, so a lock compared against it could be satisfied early by a miner who writes a later time; the median of eleven is much harder to move, since a miner would need to control six of the last eleven blocks. BIP113 made the median the endpoint of lock-time calculations for exactly this reason, and BIP68 uses the same median for time-based relative locks (Lombrozo, 2015) (Friedenbach et al., 2015).

The worked example sorts eleven timestamps and takes the sixth, the median; Bitcoin Core walks back eleven blocks from the tip, sorts their times and returns the middle element (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Because a block's time must exceed the median of the eleven before it, the median is monotonic even when individual timestamps are not, which is why it is a safe clock for consensus. The hour-or-two lag follows from the arithmetic: the median of eleven blocks is about six blocks old, which at ten minutes a block is about an hour.

The caution is that the median time past is a property of the chain, not of the world: it can be well behind real time when blocks come slowly and can never run ahead of the latest block times. A second caution is that the lag means a time lock expressed in wall-clock time is honoured conservatively, later rather than earlier, which is the right direction for a lock but a surprise to someone expecting the clock on the wall.

nodes.example: the middle of eleven block times
nodes.definition: The median time past (MTP) of a block is the median of the timestamps of the last eleven blocks; time locks are compared with it, and it is normally an hour or two behind the clock.

nodes.label: Coinbase transactions
nodes.body: The coinbase transaction is the first transaction in each block. The book says it is a special case, that most older documentation calls it a generation transaction and most newer documentation a coinbase transaction, not to be confused with the company of that name, and that it is created by the miner of the block that includes it, giving the miner the option to claim any fees paid by transactions in that block and, up until block 6,720,000, a subsidy of bitcoins that have never been circulated (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The coinbase transaction is the first transaction in each block. The book says it is a special case, that most older documentation calls it a generation transaction and most newer documentation a coinbase transaction, not to be confused with the company of that name, and that it is created by the miner of the block that includes it, giving the miner the option to claim any fees paid by transactions in that block and, up until block 6,720,000, a subsidy of bitcoins that have never been circulated (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The group matters because the coinbase is the only transaction that creates bitcoins, and every rule that limits creation is a rule about it: the subsidy schedule, the sum of its outputs, and the maturity that keeps freshly created coins from being spent until the block is secure. It also uses the fields of this chapter in a special way, which the book lists: one input, a null outpoint, a coinbase field in place of an input script, and since segwit an output that commits to the block's witnesses (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The six sections follow the book's list of special rules. The coinbase transaction section states the role and the names; the null outpoint section reads the all-zero txid and maximal index; the coinbase field section explains the 2-to-100-byte field that gives the transaction its name and the BIP34 height it must begin with; the block subsidy section computes the halving schedule; the block reward section adds the fees; and the maturity rule section explains the 100 confirmations (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: Coinbase transaction
nodes.body: The coinbase transaction is the first transaction in each block, a special case that the book says most older documentation calls a generation transaction and most newer documentation a coinbase transaction, not to be confused with transactions created by the company named Coinbase. It is created by the miner of the block that includes it and gives the miner the option to claim any fees paid by transactions in that block, and additionally, up until block 6,720,000, a subsidy of bitcoins that have never previously been circulated (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The coinbase transaction is the first transaction in each block, a special case that the book says most older documentation calls a generation transaction and most newer documentation a coinbase transaction, not to be confused with transactions created by the company named Coinbase. It is created by the miner of the block that includes it and gives the miner the option to claim any fees paid by transactions in that block, and additionally, up until block 6,720,000, a subsidy of bitcoins that have never previously been circulated (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The coinbase matters as the source of every bitcoin: every output that any transaction has ever spent traces back, through chains of outpoints, to a coinbase output, which is why the book says the maturity rule and the subsidy schedule are enforced on it. It is also the one transaction a node cannot check against previous outputs, since it spends none, so its validity is a matter of the block it sits in - its fees and its height - rather than of the UTXO database (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The book lists the special rules: a coinbase may only have one input; that input's outpoint must have a null txid and the maximal index; the field that would hold an input script is the coinbase field, between 2 and 100 bytes, not executed but subject to the legacy limits on signature-checking operations, and since BIP34 beginning with the block height; the sum of the outputs must not exceed the fees plus the subsidy; and since the 2017 segwit soft fork a block that contains a segwit spend must have a coinbase output committing to all the transactions including their witnesses (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example lists its three defining properties.

The caution is the book's closing remark: most Bitcoin software does not need to deal with coinbase transactions, but their special nature means they can occasionally cause unusual problems in software not designed to expect them - a parser that assumes every outpoint names a real output, or a wallet that counts an immature output as spendable (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A second caution is that Bitcoin Core refuses a coinbase outside a block entirely: as a loose transaction it is invalid with the single word coinbase as its reason (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.example: first in the block, made by the miner
nodes.definition: The coinbase transaction is the first transaction of a block, created by its miner to claim the block's fees and, until the subsidy runs out, newly created bitcoins; older documents call it a generation transaction.

io.code: ['the first transaction in the block', 'created by the miner', 'claims the fees and the subsidy']
io.out: ['the first transaction in the block', 'created by the miner', 'claims the fees and the subsidy']

nodes.label: The null outpoint
nodes.body: The null outpoint is the outpoint of a coinbase transaction's only input. The book says the single input must have an outpoint with a null txid, consisting entirely of zeros, and a maximal output index, 0xffffffff, and that this prevents the coinbase transaction from referencing a previous transaction output, which would at the very least be confusing given that the coinbase pays out fees and subsidy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core's IsCoinBase test is exactly this: one input whose previous outpoint is null (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: The null outpoint is the outpoint of a coinbase transaction's only input. The book says the single input must have an outpoint with a null txid, consisting entirely of zeros, and a maximal output index, 0xffffffff, and that this prevents the coinbase transaction from referencing a previous transaction output, which would at the very least be confusing given that the coinbase pays out fees and subsidy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core's IsCoinBase test is exactly this: one input whose previous outpoint is null (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The null outpoint matters because it is how the format marks the one transaction that creates rather than transfers. Every other transaction's inputs name outputs that exist; the coinbase's input names nothing, and a node recognises the coinbase by that. Bitcoin Core's CheckTransaction enforces the converse too: for a transaction that is not a coinbase, any input with a null outpoint is refused with bad-txns-prevout-null, so a null outpoint can appear nowhere else (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The worked example states the two parts, 32 zero bytes and the maximal four-byte index, and the index as a number. The chapter's library's is_coinbase test reads a parsed transaction and checks all three conditions - one input, a zero txid, a maximal index - and an executed claim confirms that neither Alice's transaction nor the first bitcoin transaction is a coinbase, while a transaction constructed with the null outpoint is. The maximal index is also the value an outpoint can never legitimately hold, since no transaction has four billion outputs.

The caution is that the null outpoint's 36 bytes are still serialized and still weigh: a coinbase input is the same shape as any other, which is why the book lists the rule as a constraint on the outpoint rather than as its absence. A second caution is that the input's sequence field exists too and is exempt from BIP68, as the sequence branch noted; miners use it, together with the coinbase field, as extra space for the numbers they vary while searching for a valid block (Friedenbach et al., 2015).

nodes.example: 32 zero bytes and index 0xffffffff
nodes.definition: A coinbase transaction's single input must have an outpoint with a null txid of all zeros and the maximal output index 0xffffffff, so that it cannot reference a previous output.

nodes.label: The coinbase field
nodes.body: The coinbase field is the field that would contain an input script in a normal transaction. The book says it is called a coinbase, that it is this field that gives the coinbase transaction its name, that it must be at least two bytes and not longer than 100, that it is not executed but legacy limits on the number of signature-checking operations apply to it so arbitrary data should be prefixed by a data-pushing opcode, and that since a 2013 soft fork defined in BIP34 its first few bytes must follow additional rules (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Andresen, 2012).

paras.text: The coinbase field is the field that would contain an input script in a normal transaction. The book says it is called a coinbase, that it is this field that gives the coinbase transaction its name, that it must be at least two bytes and not longer than 100, that it is not executed but legacy limits on the number of signature-checking operations apply to it so arbitrary data should be prefixed by a data-pushing opcode, and that since a 2013 soft fork defined in BIP34 its first few bytes must follow additional rules (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Andresen, 2012).

The field matters as the only free space in a block that a miner may fill: it carries the block height, extra nonce values the miner varies, and often a text tag naming the mining pool, which is how explorers know who mined a block. BIP34 requires the height so that no two coinbase transactions can be identical, which closes the duplicate-transaction problem that BIP30 addressed after two early coinbases were found to be byte-for-byte the same (Andresen, 2012) (Wuille, 2012). Bitcoin Core enforces the length with bad-cb-length (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The worked example builds a field of a three-byte push of the height 780,000 followed by a tag, and checks its length, its bounds, the push length and the height. BIP34 specifies the height as a script number pushed by the usual push opcode, which is the 03 followed by the three little-endian bytes e0 e6 0b in the example (Andresen, 2012). Bitcoin Core's chain parameters record that the BIP34 rule became mandatory on the main network at block 227,931, which its documentation dates to March 2013 (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The caution is in the book's phrase not executed: the field is never run as a script, so it can contain anything, but the sigop counting of the legacy rules still scans it for opcodes, which is why data should sit behind a push opcode that the scanner skips. A second caution is that the field's 100-byte limit is for the field alone; the extra nonce and the tag share it with the height.

nodes.example: 2 to 100 bytes, beginning with the height
nodes.definition: The coinbase field is the coinbase transaction's input-script field, 2 to 100 bytes long, not executed, and since BIP34 beginning with a push of the block height; it gives the transaction its name.

io.code: (lambda field: (len(field), 2 <= len(field) <= 100, field[0], int.from_bytes(field[1:1 + field[0]], 'little')))(bytes.fromhex('03e0e60b') + b'/example miner/')

error.code: (lambda g: (exec("field = bytes.fromhex('03e0e60b') + b'/' + b'x' * 100\nassert 2 <= len(field) <= 100, 'the coinbase field must be 2 to 100 bytes'\nresult = len(field)", g), g['result'])[1])({})
