nodes.label: Block subsidy
nodes.body: The block subsidy is the part of a coinbase's claim that consists of bitcoins that have never previously been circulated. The book says the subsidy started at 50 BTC per block and halves every 210,000 blocks, approximately every four years, with values rounded down to the nearest satoshi, and it dates the subsidy to block 6,720,000 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core's GetBlockSubsidy computes it as 50 times COIN shifted right once per 210,000 blocks, and zero once the shift would be undefined after 64 halvings (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: The block subsidy is the part of a coinbase's claim that consists of bitcoins that have never previously been circulated. The book says the subsidy started at 50 BTC per block and halves every 210,000 blocks, approximately every four years, with values rounded down to the nearest satoshi, and it dates the subsidy to block 6,720,000 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core's GetBlockSubsidy computes it as 50 times COIN shifted right once per 210,000 blocks, and zero once the shift would be undefined after 64 halvings (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The subsidy matters because it is the only source of new bitcoins and the reason the total is bounded. Halving a quantity repeatedly sums to twice its first value, so 210,000 blocks of 50 bitcoins, halved for ever, approach 21 million; the rounding down to a satoshi at each halving makes the actual total slightly less, and the chapter's library sums the whole schedule to 20,999,999.9769 bitcoins, which an executed claim records. Chapter 1 gave the 21 million figure; this is the arithmetic behind it.

The worked example writes the formula in one line and evaluates it at five heights: 50 at the start, 3.125 after the fourth halving at block 840,000, and one satoshi at block 6,720,000, where the 32nd halving leaves 5,000,000,000 shifted right 32 places. The subsidy is still one satoshi at block 6,929,999 and becomes zero at block 6,930,000, the 33rd halving, so the last block with any subsidy is 6,929,999; the book's figure of 6,720,000 is the height from which the subsidy is a single satoshi, not the height at which it ends, a difference an executed claim measures (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The caution is that the schedule is enforced on the coinbase's outputs rather than written in them: a miner may claim less than the subsidy, and some have, by mistake, leaving satoshis uncreated for ever, which is a second reason the total will be below 21 million. A second caution is the word approximately in every four years: the halving is a count of blocks, and blocks arrive faster or slower than ten minutes apart, so the dates drift.

nodes.example: 50 BTC, halved every 210,000 blocks
nodes.definition: The block subsidy is the newly created bitcoin a coinbase may claim: 50 BTC at first, halved every 210,000 blocks and rounded down to the satoshi, so that the total issued is just under 21 million.

io.code: (lambda g: (exec('subsidy = lambda h: (50 * 100_000_000) >> (h // 210_000) if h // 210_000 < 64 else 0\nresult = (subsidy(0) / 1e8, subsidy(840_000) / 1e8, subsidy(6_720_000), subsidy(6_929_999), subsidy(6_930_000))', g), g['result'])[1])({})

nodes.label: Block reward
nodes.body: The block reward is the total amount a miner can claim for a block, which the book defines as the combination of fees and subsidy, and the rule on it is one of the coinbase's special rules: the sum of the outputs must not exceed the value of the fees collected from all the transactions in that block plus the subsidy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core computes the reward as the fees plus GetBlockSubsidy and refuses a block whose coinbase pays more with bad-cb-amount, the message saying coinbase pays too much (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: The block reward is the total amount a miner can claim for a block, which the book defines as the combination of fees and subsidy, and the rule on it is one of the coinbase's special rules: the sum of the outputs must not exceed the value of the fees collected from all the transactions in that block plus the subsidy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core computes the reward as the fees plus GetBlockSubsidy and refuses a block whose coinbase pays more with bad-cb-amount, the message saying coinbase pays too much (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The reward matters because it is where the fees of this chapter's transactions go. Alice's transaction left 5,000 satoshis unassigned; that difference is not lost but is claimable by the miner of block 775,072 in that block's coinbase, together with the fees of every other transaction in the block and the subsidy of the time, 6.25 bitcoins at that height (mempool.space, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The reward is a ceiling, not a floor: a miner may claim less, and the book's chapter on mining explains why a miner would never want to.

The worked example adds three fees to a subsidy of 3.125 bitcoins and checks a claim against the sum. A node computes the fees as the sum over the block's transactions of inputs minus outputs, which requires the UTXO database for every input, so the reward check is the last step of validating a block rather than the first. The reward is also why the coinbase has the maximal output index and null txid: its value comes from the block, not from an outpoint (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The caution is that the reward is a property of a block, not of a transaction: the same coinbase transaction would be invalid in a block with fewer fees. A second caution is that the subsidy and the fees are not separated in the coinbase's outputs; the outputs simply sum to at most the reward, and an explorer that shows them separately is computing the fees itself.

nodes.example: fees plus subsidy, as a ceiling
nodes.definition: The block reward is the total a miner can claim for a block, the fees of its transactions plus the subsidy; the coinbase's outputs may sum to no more than it.

io.code: (lambda fees, subsidy, claimed: (fees + subsidy, claimed <= fees + subsidy))(5000 + 12000 + 3000, 312_500_000, 312_520_000)

steps.expr: (lambda fees, subsidy, claimed: (fees + subsidy, claimed <= fees + subsidy))(5000 + 12000 + 3000, 312500000, 312520000)
(lambda fees, subsidy, claimed: (fees + subsidy, claimed <= fees + subsidy))(17000 + 3000, 312500000, 312520000)

nodes.label: Maturity rule
nodes.body: The maturity rule is the rule that a transaction spending one of a coinbase's outputs cannot be included in any block until after the coinbase transaction has received 100 confirmations. The book says a coinbase may have any other outputs that would be valid in a normal transaction, but that this restriction applies to spending them, and that coinbase outputs that do not yet have 100 confirmations are called immature (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core names the constant COINBASE_MATURITY, 100, and checks it in its input verification (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: The maturity rule is the rule that a transaction spending one of a coinbase's outputs cannot be included in any block until after the coinbase transaction has received 100 confirmations. The book says a coinbase may have any other outputs that would be valid in a normal transaction, but that this restriction applies to spending them, and that coinbase outputs that do not yet have 100 confirmations are called immature (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core names the constant COINBASE_MATURITY, 100, and checks it in its input verification (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The rule matters because a coinbase's value depends on its block staying in the chain. If a block is reorganised away, every transaction in it can be mined again in a later block - except the coinbase, which belongs to that block alone and vanishes with it; anything that had spent its outputs would vanish too. Making the outputs wait 100 blocks makes a reorganisation deep enough to remove them practically impossible, which the book's chapter on consensus develops (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The worked example applies the rule to the first bitcoin transaction of this chapter's stories: it spent the coinbase output of block 9 in block 170, 161 blocks later, which satisfies the rule. Bitcoin Core's check is that the spending height minus the coinbase's height must be at least 100, and the coinbase flag and height of every output are the metadata the UTXO database keeps for this purpose, as the outpoint group noted (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The first bitcoin transaction's input is therefore an outpoint to a coinbase, one the chapter's library parses.

The caution is that maturity is counted in confirmations of the coinbase, not of the spending transaction, and that the spend is invalid rather than merely delayed if included early; a miner who pays itself from a recent coinbase makes an invalid block. A second caution is that explorers and wallets must track the immature state, which the book's remark about software not designed to expect coinbases alludes to (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: 100 confirmations before spending
nodes.definition: The maturity rule says a transaction spending a coinbase output cannot be included in any block until the coinbase has 100 confirmations; outputs with fewer are called immature.

nodes.label: Weight and foundations
nodes.body: This last branch has two jobs. The first is the book's section on weight and vbytes: each Bitcoin block is limited in the amount of transaction data it can contain, so most Bitcoin software needs to be able to measure the transactions it creates or processes, and the modern unit of measurement is called weight, with vbytes as an alternative in which four units of weight equal one vbyte (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The second is to explain the terms the chapter uses throughout without a section of their own: the hash function, double SHA-256, the txid and wtxid, relay policy and consensus.

paras.text: This last branch has two jobs. The first is the book's section on weight and vbytes: each Bitcoin block is limited in the amount of transaction data it can contain, so most Bitcoin software needs to be able to measure the transactions it creates or processes, and the modern unit of measurement is called weight, with vbytes as an alternative in which four units of weight equal one vbyte (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The second is to explain the terms the chapter uses throughout without a section of their own: the hash function, double SHA-256, the txid and wtxid, relay policy and consensus.

Weight matters because it is what a transaction pays for. Fees are quoted per vbyte, blocks are filled by weight, and the factors that make a witness byte cost a quarter of any other byte are what makes segwit cheaper and what the book says was chosen to reduce the weight used when spending a UTXO, discouraging uneconomical outputs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The foundations matter because the chapter's arguments rest on them: malleability is about what a hash covers, and half the rules in the chapter are policy rather than consensus.

The reader meets weight in every fee estimate a wallet shows and in the figure 569 that Bitcoin Core reports for Alice's transaction, which this course recomputes from the bytes field by field. The reader meets the foundations wherever the chapter says txid, hashes, standard or valid; the two kinds of rule are met in the version branch's version 3 proposal, the outputs branch's dust limit and the sequence branch's replacement policy, each a policy, against the consensus rules of lock time, maturity and the subsidy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The branch has two groups. The weight units group explains weight, vbytes, the block limit with its header and transaction-count overhead, and the per-field factors, with the book's table recomputed and summed to 569. The foundations group explains the hash function and its double application, the transaction identifier and the witness transaction identifier as two hashes over two serializations, and the distinction between the relay policy a node chooses and the consensus rules every node must apply (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo et al., 2015) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: Weight and vbytes
nodes.body: Weight is the modern unit in which the size of a transaction or a block is measured, and vbytes are weight divided by four. The book says blocks are limited to 4 million weight, that the block header takes up 240 weight and the transaction count 4 or 12, that all the remaining weight may be used for transaction data, and that to calculate the weight of a field its serialized size in bytes is multiplied by a factor, with the weight of a transaction the sum over its fields (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Weight is the modern unit in which the size of a transaction or a block is measured, and vbytes are weight divided by four. The book says blocks are limited to 4 million weight, that the block header takes up 240 weight and the transaction count 4 or 12, that all the remaining weight may be used for transaction data, and that to calculate the weight of a field its serialized size in bytes is multiplied by a factor, with the weight of a transaction the sum over its fields (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The unit matters because it replaced the byte as the measure of block capacity when segwit activated, and because the replacement is uneven on purpose: a byte of witness data weighs one unit and any other byte weighs four, so the same transaction is cheaper in the segwit format than it would be with its signatures in the input script. The book says the factors and the fields they apply to were chosen to reduce the weight used when spending a UTXO, which helps discourage the creation of uneconomical outputs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

The four sections cover the unit, its quarter, the limit and the factors. Weight is defined by BIP141's formula and recomputed for Alice's transaction; vbytes are the rounded-up quarter, 143 for her; the block weight limit is Bitcoin Core's constant with the header and count overheads the book lists; and the weight factors section recomputes the book's table of every field of Alice's transaction and sums it to 569, the number Bitcoin Core returns (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: Weight
nodes.body: Weight is the modern unit of measurement for the size of Bitcoin transactions and blocks. The book says each block is limited in the amount of transaction data it can contain, so most software needs to measure the transactions it creates or processes, and that the unit is called weight (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP141 defines a transaction's weight as its base size, the serialization without witness data, times three, plus its total size with the witness, and Bitcoin Core's GetTransactionWeight computes exactly that (Lombrozo et al., 2015) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: Weight is the modern unit of measurement for the size of Bitcoin transactions and blocks. The book says each block is limited in the amount of transaction data it can contain, so most software needs to measure the transactions it creates or processes, and that the unit is called weight (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP141 defines a transaction's weight as its base size, the serialization without witness data, times three, plus its total size with the witness, and Bitcoin Core's GetTransactionWeight computes exactly that (Lombrozo et al., 2015) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Weight matters because it is the number a fee is paid for and the number a block is filled by. The book verifies its own table by asking Bitcoin Core for the weight of Alice's transaction and receiving 569; this course cannot run a node, but it recomputes the number from the bytes and finds the same, and the explorer that this course consulted reports 569 as well (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (mempool.space, 2026). Every fee-rate figure a wallet shows is a fee divided by this number or by its quarter.

The worked example computes both sizes and the formula: the legacy serialization of Alice's transaction, without the marker, the flag and the 67-byte witness structure, is 125 bytes; the full serialization is 194; and three times 125 plus 194 is 569. The same result follows from the per-field factors of the later section, since multiplying the legacy bytes by three and adding every byte once is the same as charging four for a legacy byte and one for a witness byte. A legacy transaction's weight is simply four times its size (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

The caution is that weight is not bytes and is not what the network transmits: Alice's transaction is 194 bytes on the wire and 569 in weight, and a fee rate in satoshis per byte and one in satoshis per vbyte differ by the discount. A second caution is that weight counts the serialized bytes only; the cost of validating a transaction, in signature checks, is bounded by a separate limit that the book's chapter on mining discusses (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.example: 3 times the legacy size plus the full size
nodes.definition: Weight is BIP141's measure of a transaction: the legacy serialization's size times 3 plus the full serialization's size, which is 569 for Alice's transaction, the figure Bitcoin Core reports.

nodes.label: Vbytes
nodes.body: A vbyte, a virtual byte, is an alternative version of weight in which four units of weight equal one vbyte. The book says it provides an easy comparison to the original byte measurement unit used in legacy Bitcoin blocks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP141 defines the virtual transaction size as the weight divided by four, rounded up to the next integer, so a transaction with no witness has as many vbytes as bytes and a segwit transaction has fewer (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

paras.text: A vbyte, a virtual byte, is an alternative version of weight in which four units of weight equal one vbyte. The book says it provides an easy comparison to the original byte measurement unit used in legacy Bitcoin blocks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP141 defines the virtual transaction size as the weight divided by four, rounded up to the next integer, so a transaction with no witness has as many vbytes as bytes and a segwit transaction has fewer (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

The unit matters because it is what most wallets and fee estimators quote: a fee of 10 satoshis per vbyte, not per weight unit, and the old intuition that a block holds a million bytes becomes a million vbytes. The worked example computes Alice's 143 vbytes from 569 weight, shows the unrounded quarter of 142.25, and shows that a legacy transaction's vbytes equal its bytes, which is the comparison the book means.

The rounding is always up, so that fractional weight cannot be hidden: 569 divided by four is 142.25 and the vbyte count is 143. The chapter's library computes it with a negative floor division, the standard way to round up in integer arithmetic. Because a block's limit of 4 million weight is a million vbytes, a fee rate per vbyte and a block's capacity in vbytes are the two numbers a miner uses to fill a block, which the book's chapter on fees develops (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

The caution is that two transactions of the same byte size can have different vbyte sizes, because their witness shares differ: a taproot spend's 65-byte signature is cheap and a legacy spend's 107-byte input script is not. A second caution is the name: a vbyte is a unit of weight, not a kind of byte, and the serialized transaction does not change size when measured in it.

nodes.example: weight divided by four, rounded up
nodes.definition: A vbyte is a quarter of a weight unit, rounded up, so that a legacy transaction's vbytes equal its bytes; Alice's transaction is 143 vbytes.

nodes.label: The block weight limit
nodes.body: The block weight limit is the consensus rule that blocks are limited to 4 million weight. The book says so and adds the overheads: the block header takes up 240 weight, an additional field, the transaction count, uses either 4 or 12 weight, and all of the remaining weight may be used for transaction data (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core names the limit MAX_BLOCK_WEIGHT with the value 4,000,000 and cites BIP141 for it, and BIP141's rule is that block weight is at most 4,000,000 (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

paras.text: The block weight limit is the consensus rule that blocks are limited to 4 million weight. The book says so and adds the overheads: the block header takes up 240 weight, an additional field, the transaction count, uses either 4 or 12 weight, and all of the remaining weight may be used for transaction data (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core names the limit MAX_BLOCK_WEIGHT with the value 4,000,000 and cites BIP141 for it, and BIP141's rule is that block weight is at most 4,000,000 (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

The limit matters because it is the scarce resource every fee competes for. Four million weight is a million vbytes, and the worked example shows that if every transaction were Alice's, a block would hold about 7,029 of them; the book's chapter on fees treats the market this creates. The limit replaced the earlier one-megabyte limit on the block's size at the segwit soft fork, which is why the book speaks of legacy blocks and the original byte unit (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

The weight of a block is computed by the same formula as a transaction's, over the whole serialized block: BIP141 defines block weight as base size times three plus total size, and Bitcoin Core's GetBlockWeight applies it to the block, header included (Lombrozo et al., 2015) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The transaction count is a compactSize integer, one byte for up to 252 transactions and three bytes beyond, which at a factor of four gives the book's 4 or 12 weight; a block with thousands of transactions uses the three-byte form.

The caution is the header figure. An 80-byte header counted by BIP141's formula weighs 80 times three plus 80, which is 320, not 240; 240 is 80 times three, the base-size part alone, so the book's figure appears to omit the header's contribution to the total size, a discrepancy an executed claim of this chapter records (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo et al., 2015). The difference is 80 units out of four million and changes no conclusion, but a reader computing capacity to the byte should use 320.

nodes.example: 4 million weight a block
nodes.definition: Blocks are limited to 4,000,000 weight, Bitcoin Core's MAX_BLOCK_WEIGHT; the header and the transaction count take a small fixed share and the rest is for transactions.

nodes.label: Weight factors
nodes.body: The weight factors are the multipliers applied to each field's size. The book says that to calculate the weight of a particular field the size of that serialized field in bytes is multiplied by a factor, and that the weight of a transaction is the sum of the weights of all its fields; its table gives a factor of 4 for the version, the counts, the outpoint, the input script, the sequence, the amount, the output script and the lock time, and a factor of 1 for the marker and flag, the witness count and the witness items, and totals Alice's transaction at 569 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The weight factors are the multipliers applied to each field's size. The book says that to calculate the weight of a particular field the size of that serialized field in bytes is multiplied by a factor, and that the weight of a transaction is the sum of the weights of all its fields; its table gives a factor of 4 for the version, the counts, the outpoint, the input script, the sequence, the amount, the output script and the lock time, and a factor of 1 for the marker and flag, the witness count and the witness items, and totals Alice's transaction at 569 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The factors matter because they are where the discount lives. The book says they were chosen to reduce the weight used when spending a UTXO, which discourages uneconomical outputs: the signature that spends an output is witness data at a factor of 1, while the output script that creates one is at 4, so creating outputs is relatively dear and spending them relatively cheap (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In Alice's transaction the 66 bytes of witness items weigh 66, while the 58 bytes of her two output scripts weigh 232.

The worked example rebuilds the book's table from the byte counts of each field and the two factors: 16 for the version, 2 for the marker and flag, 4 for the input count, 144 for the 36-byte outpoint, 4 for the one-byte prefix of the empty input script, 16 for the sequence, 4 for the output count, 64 for two 8-byte amounts, 232 for the two output scripts with their length prefixes, 1 for the witness count, 66 for the witness item with its length, and 16 for the lock time, which sum to 569. The chapter's library derives the same rows from its byte spans rather than from a typed table, and an executed claim compares the two (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The caution is that the book's rows group bytes in a way a parser does not: the outpoint row is the 32-byte identifier and the 4-byte index together, the output script row includes each script's length prefix, and the witness items row includes the item's length byte. A second caution is that only three rows carry the factor of 1, so a transaction's discount depends entirely on how much of it is witness, which is why a taproot spend with a 65-byte witness is among the lightest transactions there are.

nodes.example: 4 for most fields, 1 for marker, flag and witness
nodes.definition: Each field's weight is its serialized size times a factor: 4 for the version, inputs, outputs and lock time, 1 for the marker, the flag and the witness structure; summed over Alice's transaction the factors give 569.

nodes.label: Foundations
nodes.body: This group explains the terms the chapter uses on every page without a section of its own. The hash function and its double application are what every identifier and commitment in the chapter is made of; the txid and the wtxid are the two identifiers BIP141 defines over the two serializations; and relay policy and consensus rules are the two kinds of rule the chapter keeps distinguishing, from the dust limit to the standard templates to the version 3 proposal (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

paras.text: This group explains the terms the chapter uses on every page without a section of its own. The hash function and its double application are what every identifier and commitment in the chapter is made of; the txid and the wtxid are the two identifiers BIP141 defines over the two serializations; and relay policy and consensus rules are the two kinds of rule the chapter keeps distinguishing, from the dust limit to the standard templates to the version 3 proposal (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

The group matters because the chapter's hardest ideas are precise statements about these terms. Malleability is the statement that a txid covers the input script; segregated witness is the statement that it covers the legacy serialization only; the book's remark that there is more to replacement than fee rates is a statement about policy; and the maturity rule is a statement about consensus. A reader who has the terms straight can follow each argument as a line of a proof.

The six sections are two triples. The first triple is cryptographic: the hash function, the double SHA-256 that Bitcoin applies to it, and the two identifiers that result. The second is institutional: the relay policy that a node chooses and may change, the consensus rule that every node must apply identically, and the memory pool in which policy is applied, which the book's later chapters treat at length and this chapter needs only as a name (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Hash function
nodes.body: A hash function is a function that maps data of any length to a digest of fixed length, in a way that cannot be run backwards and that changes the digest unpredictably when the input changes. Chapter 4 introduced it for addresses; this chapter relies on it for identifiers and commitments, and the book's sidebar lists the uses: unique identifiers for blocks and transactions, commitments for addresses, blocks, transactions and signatures, and the iteration of proof of work (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin's function is SHA-256, whose digest is 32 bytes.

paras.text: A hash function is a function that maps data of any length to a digest of fixed length, in a way that cannot be run backwards and that changes the digest unpredictably when the input changes. Chapter 4 introduced it for addresses; this chapter relies on it for identifiers and commitments, and the book's sidebar lists the uses: unique identifiers for blocks and transactions, commitments for addresses, blocks, transactions and signatures, and the iteration of proof of work (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin's function is SHA-256, whose digest is 32 bytes.

The function matters here for two properties. Fixed length is why a 32-byte txid can stand for a transaction of any size and sit in a 36-byte outpoint. Sensitivity to the input is why a transaction's identifier changes completely when a single byte of its serialization changes - the property that makes identifiers trustworthy and that makes malleability a problem, since any mutation of the hashed bytes, however meaningless to the script interpreter, produces a new identifier (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The worked example hashes an empty input and a ten-thousand-byte input and finds 32 bytes both times. Python's hashlib provides the function, and every worked example in this chapter that computes an identifier uses it twice in succession, which the next section explains. A commitment uses the function in the order the book describes: the digest is published first, the data later, and anyone can check that the data hashes to the digest, which is how a block commits to its transactions and an outpoint to a previous transaction.

The caution is that a hash function identifies bytes, not meaning: two serializations of the same transaction, one with witness and one without, hash to different values, and two byte strings that push the same number hash differently, which is the whole of the malleability group. A second caution is that the one-way and collision-free properties are the current state of cryptanalysis rather than theorems, as chapter 4 noted.

nodes.example: any input, a fixed 32-byte digest
nodes.definition: A hash function maps input of any length to a fixed-length digest, one-way and unpredictable, so that a digest can identify data and commit to it; Bitcoin's is SHA-256, with a 32-byte output.

nodes.label: Double SHA-256
nodes.body: Double SHA-256 is the hash construction Bitcoin uses for transaction and block identifiers: SHA-256 applied to the output of SHA-256. Chapter 4 met it in base58check, where the first four bytes of a double hash are a checksum; here it is the whole of the identifier. The chapter's library writes it as hash256, the name Bitcoin Core uses, and every identifier the book prints - Alice's 46620030..., the previous transaction's 4ac54180... - is such a double hash reversed into display order (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Double SHA-256 is the hash construction Bitcoin uses for transaction and block identifiers: SHA-256 applied to the output of SHA-256. Chapter 4 met it in base58check, where the first four bytes of a double hash are a checksum; here it is the whole of the identifier. The chapter's library writes it as hash256, the name Bitcoin Core uses, and every identifier the book prints - Alice's 46620030..., the previous transaction's 4ac54180... - is such a double hash reversed into display order (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The construction matters because it is exactly what the word txid means in every sentence of the chapter. When the book says every field of a legacy transaction is used to derive the txid, it means every field is in the bytes that are hashed twice; when BIP141 says the witness is excluded from the txid, it means the bytes hashed are the legacy serialization. Knowing the construction lets a reader recompute any identifier in the chapter, which the worked examples of the witness branch do (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

The worked example double-hashes a short string and shows the reversed digest's first sixteen characters; the same two lines, applied to the 125 legacy bytes of Alice's transaction, give her identifier, as the segregated witness section's example shows. The reversal is the byte-order convention of the inputs branch. Why the function is applied twice is a historical design choice; the book does not explain it, and the practical consequence is only that every identifier costs two hash computations.

The caution is that the double hash is over the serialization, so any program that serializes a transaction differently - a different compactSize encoding, a witness included where it should not be - computes a different identifier and will not find the transaction it is looking for. A second caution is that the chapter's examples compute identifiers from saved bytes, and a saved copy that was edited by hand would hash to something else; the executed claims compare against the explorer's and the book's identifiers for that reason (mempool.space, 2026).

nodes.example: SHA-256 of SHA-256
nodes.definition: Bitcoin's identifiers are double SHA-256: the hash function applied to its own output, so a txid is SHA-256 of SHA-256 of the legacy serialization, shown reversed.

nodes.label: Transaction identifier
nodes.body: The transaction identifier, txid, is the double SHA-256 of a transaction's serialization in display byte order. The book uses the term from the chapter's first listing, where it asks Bitcoin Core for the transaction by its identifier, and makes its definition explicit in the witness branch: in the legacy format every field, including the input script that contains signatures, is used to derive a transaction's identifier (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP141 keeps the identifier as the hash of the serialization without the witness, so that it is unchanged for legacy transactions and witness-independent for segwit ones (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

paras.text: The transaction identifier, txid, is the double SHA-256 of a transaction's serialization in display byte order. The book uses the term from the chapter's first listing, where it asks Bitcoin Core for the transaction by its identifier, and makes its definition explicit in the witness branch: in the legacy format every field, including the input script that contains signatures, is used to derive a transaction's identifier (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP141 keeps the identifier as the hash of the serialization without the witness, so that it is unchanged for legacy transactions and witness-independent for segwit ones (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

The identifier matters because it is how everything refers to a transaction: an outpoint, an explorer, a wallet's history, a block's merkle tree. Its exact scope is the subject of the witness branch - a malleable identifier breaks every outpoint that names it, and segwit fixes the scope so that nothing a third or second party can change is in it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example confirms the identifier's display length, 64 hexadecimal characters for 32 bytes, the count the book gave at the start of the chapter.

A node computes the identifier by serializing the transaction in the legacy format, hashing twice and storing the result; it displays it reversed. The chapter's library's txid function does these steps and an executed claim shows it reproducing the identifiers of all four saved transactions, including the two legacy ones from 2009 and 2010, which have no witness and whose legacy serialization is their whole serialization (mempool.space, 2026). A block's merkle tree, which the book's chapter on the blockchain explains, is built from these identifiers in internal order.

The caution is the one the witness branch exists for: before segwit, the identifier of an unconfirmed transaction was not reliable, and a protocol that stored one could find it changed; after segwit, it is reliable only for inputs that spend segwit outputs. A second caution is that the identifier does not commit to the witness, so two valid transactions with the same identifier and different witnesses are possible, which is why BIP141 adds the next section's identifier (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

nodes.example: double SHA-256 of the legacy bytes, reversed
nodes.definition: The txid is the double SHA-256 of a transaction's legacy serialization, displayed in reversed byte order; for a segwit transaction it therefore excludes the witness.

nodes.label: Witness transaction identifier
nodes.body: The witness transaction identifier, wtxid, is the double SHA-256 of a transaction's full extended serialization, witness included, in display byte order. BIP141 defines it beside the txid: a new data structure, the witness, is committed to by a new identifier, and a block that contains segwit transactions commits to the wtxids of all its transactions through an output of its coinbase (Lombrozo et al., 2015). The book mentions this commitment among the coinbase's special rules and defers its details to the chapter on mining (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The witness transaction identifier, wtxid, is the double SHA-256 of a transaction's full extended serialization, witness included, in display byte order. BIP141 defines it beside the txid: a new data structure, the witness, is committed to by a new identifier, and a block that contains segwit transactions commits to the wtxids of all its transactions through an output of its coinbase (Lombrozo et al., 2015). The book mentions this commitment among the coinbase's special rules and defers its details to the chapter on mining (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The wtxid matters because something must commit to witnesses. Leaving the witness out of the txid is what removes malleability, but a block that committed only to txids would let anyone substitute a different valid witness for a transaction after the fact; the wtxid closes that gap, and the coinbase commitment ties every wtxid to the block. For a legacy transaction, whose serialization has no witness, BIP141 says the wtxid equals the txid (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

The worked example compares Alice's two identifiers, her txid 46620030... and her wtxid f7cdbc7c..., and finds them different, as they must be for a transaction with a witness. The chapter's library computes the wtxid over the 194 extended bytes and the txid over the 125 legacy bytes, and an executed claim shows that replacing the witness item changes the first and not the second. The commitment in the coinbase is a merkle root of wtxids with the coinbase's own entry set to zero, which the book's chapter on mining describes (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

The caution is that the wtxid is not what outpoints use: an input names a previous output by txid, never by wtxid, which is why the txid's stability is what matters for presigned transactions. A second caution is that explorers rarely show the wtxid, so a reader who wants to check one must compute it, which is one reason this chapter's library exists.

nodes.example: the hash of everything, witness included
nodes.definition: The wtxid is the double SHA-256 of the whole extended serialization, witness included; it changes when the witness changes, and blocks commit to it separately from the txid.

nodes.label: Relay policy
nodes.body: Relay policy is the set of rules a full node applies when deciding which unconfirmed transactions to relay to its peers and to keep in its memory pool, the store of transactions waiting for a block. The book names such rules throughout the chapter: Bitcoin Core's default transaction relay policy that refuses reserved features, the dust policies that affect the relay and mining of unconfirmed transactions, the policy that limits output scripts to standard templates, and the policy of replacement (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core's policy sources hold the constants (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: Relay policy is the set of rules a full node applies when deciding which unconfirmed transactions to relay to its peers and to keep in its memory pool, the store of transactions waiting for a block. The book names such rules throughout the chapter: Bitcoin Core's default transaction relay policy that refuses reserved features, the dust policies that affect the relay and mining of unconfirmed transactions, the policy that limits output scripts to standard templates, and the policy of replacement (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core's policy sources hold the constants (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The distinction matters because policy is not validity. A transaction that violates policy can still be included in a block by a miner who chooses to, and the block is valid; a transaction that violates consensus can never be. The book's version 3 proposal is the clearest case, a change that does not seek to change the consensus rules but only the policy that nodes use to relay transactions, and the book's advice to test a transaction with testmempoolaccept is advice about policy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example lists the policies this chapter has met.

A node applies policy in its memory pool: a received transaction is checked against consensus first and then against policy, and one that fails policy is dropped without being relayed, which is why non-standard transactions rarely reach miners. Policy is set by the software's defaults and the operator's options, so it can differ between nodes and change between releases; Bitcoin Core's documentation lists which proposals its policy implements and since which release (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book's phrase as of this writing recurs in this chapter because policy moves.

The caution is to never rely on policy as a guarantee: a presigned transaction that is standard today may be non-standard later, and a dust limit that protects a protocol today may be lowered. A second caution is the reverse: policy is also a protection, as the version 3 and reserved-features rules show, so a developer who routes around it by using a non-default node forfeits that protection (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: what a node chooses to relay and keep
nodes.definition: Relay policy is the set of rules a full node applies to unconfirmed transactions it relays and keeps in its memory pool; it is chosen by the node, can change, and includes dust, standardness, version 3 and replacement rules.

nodes.label: Consensus rule
nodes.body: A consensus rule is a rule that every full node enforces identically to decide whether a block, and each transaction in it, is valid. Chapter 2 introduced the term; this chapter is full of its instances, which the worked example lists: a transaction has at least one input and one output, amounts lie in range, no output is spent twice, the sequence locks of BIP68, the lock time rule since block 31,000, the subsidy and the reward, the maturity of coinbase outputs, and the block weight limit (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: A consensus rule is a rule that every full node enforces identically to decide whether a block, and each transaction in it, is valid. Chapter 2 introduced the term; this chapter is full of its instances, which the worked example lists: a transaction has at least one input and one output, amounts lie in range, no output is spent twice, the sequence locks of BIP68, the lock time rule since block 31,000, the subsidy and the reward, the maturity of coinbase outputs, and the block weight limit (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Consensus rules matter because they are what the ownership record of the first branch is made of: a full node's database is the result of applying them to every block, and two nodes that apply the same rules to the same blocks hold the same record. They can be changed only by the soft forks and hard forks of the witness branch, and the book's care about presigned transactions and reserved features is care about how those changes are made safely (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Bitcoin Core keeps its context-free consensus checks in CheckTransaction, which refuses with named reasons - bad-txns-vin-empty, bad-txns-vout-negative, bad-cb-length and the rest - and its context-dependent ones, which need the UTXO database and the chain, in its input verification and block connection, where the lock time, the sequence locks, the maturity and the reward are checked (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Every executed claim of this chapter that names such a reason reads it from the saved source at the pinned commit.

The caution is that consensus is defined by what the nodes run, not by any document: a proposal describes a rule, but the rule binds only once the economic majority enforces it, which the book says in its soft-fork definition. A second caution is that the boundary moves in one direction in practice - policy rules sometimes become consensus rules, as the lock time did at block 31,000 - and a developer should read a policy rule as a possible future consensus rule (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: what every node must enforce identically
nodes.definition: A consensus rule is a rule every full node enforces identically to decide which blocks and transactions are valid; this chapter's examples are the input and output bounds, the amount range, BIP68, the lock time, the subsidy and the maturity rule.

findings: Background

Chapter 6 reads one real transaction, Alice's payment to Bob, byte by byte. It defines a transaction as the data Alice uses to convince every full node to update its database of coin ownership, then walks the serialization in order: the version, the marker and flag of the extended format, the inputs with their compactSize count, outpoints, input scripts and sequence numbers, the outputs with their amounts and output scripts, the witness structure, and the lock time; it explains the three meanings the sequence field has carried, the problems that placing witnesses in the input script caused for contract protocols and how segregated witness solved them as a soft fork, the special rules of the coinbase transaction, the weight and vbyte units, and the legacy format that transactions without witnesses still use.
Comparative analysis

Every number the chapter prints for its example transaction reproduces from its bytes with the Python standard library alone: the 388 hexadecimal characters are 194 bytes; the marker is 0x00 and the flag 0x01 at offsets 4 and 5; the single input's outpoint is the identifier eb3ae38f... in internal order, 4ac54180... in display order, with output index 1; the sequence is 0xffffffff; the two outputs carry 20,000 and 75,000 satoshis under a 34-byte segwit version 1 script and a 22-byte version 0 script; the witness is one 65-byte item; the lock time is zero; the identifier 46620030... is the double SHA-256 of the 125-byte legacy serialization; and the weight is 569, field by field exactly as the book's table gives it - version 16, marker and flag 2, inputs count 4, outpoint 144, input script 4, sequence 16, outputs count 4, amount 64, output script 232, witness count 1, witness items 66, lock time 16 - which is the figure the book obtained from bitcoin-cli and the figure an independent explorer records.
Comparative analysis

The chapter says Alice's transaction is included in block 774,958. Two independent explorers consulted on 2026-10-08 (mempool.space and blockstream.info) place the transaction 46620030... in block 775,072; block 774,958 is the block of the transaction it spends, 4ac54180..., whose lock time is 774,957. The chapter's statement about where a node looks for the previous output remains correct in substance - the referenced output is in an earlier block - but the height named is that of the previous transaction, not of Alice's own.
Comparative analysis

The chapter says the block header takes up 240 weight. By BIP141's definition, block weight is base size times three plus total size, and Bitcoin Core's GetBlockWeight applies that formula to the whole serialized block, header included; an 80-byte header therefore weighs 320 units, and 240 is 80 times three, the base-size part alone. The difference is 80 units of 4,000,000 and changes no conclusion of the chapter.
Comparative analysis

The chapter says miners may claim a subsidy up until block 6,720,000. Under Bitcoin Core's GetBlockSubsidy - 50 BTC shifted right once per 210,000 blocks - the subsidy at block 6,720,000, the 32nd halving, is one satoshi, and it stays one satoshi until block 6,929,999; it becomes zero at block 6,930,000, the 33rd halving. The last block with a non-zero subsidy is therefore 6,929,999, and 6,720,000 is the height from which the subsidy is a single satoshi. The whole schedule sums to 2,099,999,997,690,000 satoshis, just under 21 million bitcoins.
Comparative analysis

The chapter's arithmetic for the replacement bandwidth attack understates the attacker's own cost: 1,000 transactions of 200 bytes a minute is 200,000 bytes, about 200 KB, not about 20 KB; the network-wide figure of about 10 GB a minute for 50,000 relaying nodes is correct. The ratio of 50,000 to one, which is the point of the example, is unaffected.
Comparative analysis

The chapter numbers the sequence field's flags as the 23rd least-significant bit and bits 32 and 23, counting from one, while giving the values 1 shifted left 22 and, implicitly, 1 shifted left 31; BIP68 and Bitcoin Core name the same bits by their values, 1 << 22 for the type flag and 1U << 31 for the disable flag, and the 16-bit mask 0x0000ffff. The two conventions agree; a reader counting bits from zero should use 22 and 31.
Comparative analysis

The standards' figures all reproduce with the chapter's library: compactSize integers of 1, 3, 5 and 9 bytes with the prefixes 0xfd, 0xfe and 0xff at the thresholds 253, 0x10000 and 0x100000000; BIP68's 512-second units and its rule that a lock of 30 blocks allows confirmation 29 blocks after the spent output's block; BIP125's threshold of 0xfffffffe; BIP141's vbytes as the weight rounded up over four, its witness-independent txid and witness-dependent wtxid, which an executed claim shows by altering a witness item; Bitcoin Core's dust thresholds of 546 satoshis for a legacy output and 294 for a segwit version 0 output at 3,000 satoshis per kilo-vbyte, from the sizes its policy source states; and the four push encodings of the number 2 that give a legacy transaction four different identifiers.
Conclusion

For the course, the chapter's lesson is that a transaction is a request to strangers, and that every one of its fields exists because a stranger needs it to decide: the outpoint to find the money, the witness to check the authorisation, the amounts to check the arithmetic, the sequence and lock time to check the timing, and the version, marker and flag to know which rules apply. The second lesson is the one the witness branch and this chapter's stories carry: what a hash covers decides what can be built on it, and segregated witness is the repair of a scope that was drawn too wide in 2009.
Contemporary developments

Two of the chapter's as-of-this-writing statements have moved. The version 3 proposal the chapter says was being widely considered became BIP431, and Bitcoin Core's list of implemented proposals records that transactions with version 3 are standard and treated as topologically restricted until confirmation as of release 28.0; its policy header names 3 as the highest standard version while its transaction class still builds version 2 by default. And the opt-in replacement policy the chapter describes is no longer the default: the release notes of 28.0 record that the default of the mempoolfullrbf option changed from 0 to 1, so a default node treats every unconfirmed transaction as replaceable whether or not it carries the BIP125 signal.
Contemporary developments

No Bitcoin Core node was available for this chapter, so where chapter 5 matched a running release, this chapter matches the project's sources at the commit pinned for the course (05bc2f5): the consensus constants (MAX_BLOCK_WEIGHT 4,000,000, COINBASE_MATURITY 100, WITNESS_SCALE_FACTOR 4, COIN and MAX_MONEY), the context-free checks of CheckTransaction with their named refusals (bad-txns-vin-empty, bad-txns-vout-negative, bad-txns-vout-toolarge, bad-txns-txouttotal-toolarge, bad-txns-inputs-duplicate, bad-cb-length, bad-txns-prevout-null), the sequence constants of CTxIn, LOCKTIME_THRESHOLD, the eleven-block median time past, GetBlockSubsidy and the block reward check, and the mainnet activation heights 227,931 (BIP34), 419,328 (BIP68, 112, 113) and 481,824 (segwit). The one runtime value the book quotes, the weight 569, is recomputed from the serialization and compared with an explorer's record rather than with a node.
Course notes

The owner's course notes for this chapter, written in 2021 after the 2nd edition, cover the same ground in the older vocabulary that the 3rd edition has replaced: transactions as data structures, the UTXO set and the wallet balance, change, the coinbase transaction, the serialized outputs and inputs of its tables 6-1 and 6-2, the locking and unlocking scripts the 3rd edition now calls output and input scripts, and a long section on transaction fees that the 3rd edition moves to a chapter of its own. Their topics that the 3rd edition keeps are all present in this ontology; the segregated-witness serialization, the weight unit, the BIP68 timelock and the malleability history, which the 2nd edition treated elsewhere or not at all, are the material this chapter adds.
Terms used without definition

An audit of the explanations written for this chapter listed every technical term they use and compared it with the concepts of chapters 1 to 5 and of this chapter. The terms used without a concept of their own were the ownership record a full node keeps, the byte map, the digest and its two byte orders, the satoshi, the hash function and double SHA-256, the txid and the wtxid, relay policy and the consensus rule. Each was added as a concept of this chapter with its own section, so that no term in the document is used before it is explained; the terms earlier chapters define - the full node, the blockchain, the block, the private and public key, the address and its script, the UTXO, the wallet, the hardware signing device, multisignature - are used as they stand.

stories.title: Ten bitcoins to Hal Finney, block 170
stories.who: Satoshi Nakamoto (sender) and Hal Finney, cryptographer and the second person to run the software
stories.where: block 170 of the blockchain; Finney's computer in California, running bitcoin since the day before
stories.story: On 11 January 2009 Hal Finney posted two words, running bitcoin, and the next day the software's author sent him 10 BTC. The transaction, f4184fc5..., sits in block 170 and is the first ever to spend an output: its single input points at the coinbase of block 9, 161 blocks earlier, and its two outputs pay 10 BTC to Finney's public key and 40 BTC back to the sender. It is a legacy transaction - no marker, no flag, no witness - and the chapter's own library parses it and recomputes its identifier from the bytes. Every field this chapter reads was already there, unchanged, in 2009.
stories.lesson: The format you are reading is the one from block 170
stories.source: The transaction f4184fc596403b9d638783cf57adfe4c75c605f6356fbc91338530e9831e9e16 as saved in ch06-evidence from mempool.space on 2026-10-08: block 170, 275 bytes, one input spending output 0 of 0437cd7f..., outputs of 10 BTC and 40 BTC; Finney's post of 2009-01-11 is on Wikimedia Commons as 'First tweet about bitcoin'. Photo: Hal Finney in 1972, Daily News-Post staff photo, public domain.

stories.title: 10,000 bitcoins for two pizzas
stories.who: Laszlo Hanyecz, programmer in Jacksonville, Florida; the pizzas ordered by forum user jercos
stories.where: a Papa John's on Atlantic Avenue, Jacksonville - the shop now carries a plaque
stories.story: Four days after offering 10,000 BTC on the bitcointalk forum to anyone who would send him two pizzas, Laszlo Hanyecz reported that the deal was done. The payment, a1075db5..., confirmed in block 57,043 on 22 May 2010: 131 inputs, because his wallet gathered mining rewards of 50 BTC each, and a single output of 10,000 BTC, with 0.99 BTC left as the fee. The transaction is 23,620 bytes and, as a legacy transaction, weighs exactly four times that. The chapter's library parses all 131 inputs and recomputes its identifier; the bitcoin community marks 22 May as Pizza Day.
stories.lesson: An input count of 131 is what one-output payments can look like
stories.source: The bitcointalk thread 'Pizza for bitcoins?' opened by laszlo on 2010-05-18 and his report of 2010-05-22; the transaction a1075db55d416d3ca199f55b6084e2115b9345e16c5cf302fc80e9d5fbf5d48d saved in ch06-evidence from mempool.space: block 57,043, 131 inputs, 1 output of 1,000,000,000,000 satoshis, fee 99,000,000 satoshis, weight 94,480. Photo: the plaque at Papa John's, Atlantic Ave, Jacksonville, by Sanjev Rajaram, CC0.

stories.title: The block that created 184 billion bitcoins
stories.who: an unknown attacker; Jeff Garzik, who reported the strange block on the forum; Satoshi Nakamoto, who patched the software the same day
stories.where: block 74,638 - and the bitcointalk forum thread Strange block 74638, where the fix was coordinated within hours
stories.story: Block 74,638 contained a transaction with two outputs of 92,233,720,368.54277039 BTC each. Added as 64-bit integers the two amounts overflowed to a small negative number, so the check that outputs do not exceed inputs passed and the chain accepted 184 billion bitcoins out of thin air. Jeff Garzik reported the block within two hours, Satoshi Nakamoto pushed a patch within about five hours and released version 0.3.10 the next day with a check on the sum of the outputs, and the honest chain overtook the bad one at block 74,691, erasing the transaction. Bitcoin Core's tx_check.cpp still cites the bug, CVE-2010-5139, beside the three refusals this chapter reads: a negative value, a value above 21 million, a total that leaves the range.
stories.lesson: A signed amount needs a range check; the chain learned it the hard way
stories.source: The Bitcoin wiki's 'Value overflow incident' page: block 74638 on 2010-08-15, two outputs of 92,233,720,368.54277039 BTC, the 0.3.10 fix and the reorganisation at block 74691; the forum thread 'Strange block 74638' (bitcointalk topic 822) with its timeline of the patch; Bitcoin Core src/consensus/tx_check.cpp at commit 05bc2f5, '(see CVE-2010-5139)', saved in ch06-evidence. Photo: Gavin Andresen, the developer to whom Satoshi handed the project after this era, at Web Summit 2014 - Stephen McCarthy / Web Summit, CC BY 2.0.

imgs.credit: Gavin Andresen, Web Summit 2014 - photo: Stephen McCarthy / Web Summit, CC BY 2.0

stories.title: Mt. Gox blames malleability
stories.who: Mt. Gox, then the largest bitcoin exchange, and its CEO Mark Karpeles; Christian Decker and Roger Wattenhofer of ETH Zurich, who measured the claim
stories.where: Shibuya, Tokyo - and the whole Bitcoin network, whose relayed transactions the researchers recorded
stories.story: On 7 February 2014 Mt. Gox halted bitcoin withdrawals, and on 10 February it issued a press release blaming a bug in the bitcoin software: someone could alter transaction details to make it seem that a sending of bitcoins had not occurred when it had. That is third-party malleability - a stranger re-encodes a push in the input script, the txid changes, and software that tracks payments by txid believes the payment failed. Decker and Wattenhofer, who had recorded the network's transactions for a year, found no widespread malleability attacks before the announcement: about 302,000 BTC were ever involved in such attacks, and only 1,811 BTC of them before the press release. On 28 February the exchange filed for bankruptcy protection, 850,000 BTC short; segregated witness, activated in 2017, took the input script out of the txid for good.
stories.lesson: Track outpoints, not txids - and do not blame the protocol first
stories.source: Decker and Wattenhofer, 'Bitcoin Transaction Malleability and MtGox', arXiv:1403.6676 (ETH Zurich, March 2014; ESORICS 2014): the figures 302,000 BTC ever involved and 1,811 BTC before the press release, and the finding of no widespread attacks before the closure; the Mt. Gox press release of 2014-02-10 and the bankruptcy filing of 2014-02-28 as summarised at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Gox. No free-licence photograph of the exchange or its office could be verified, so the slide shows the story's figures instead.

ndiag.title: Alice and Bob's card game: the original payment channel
ndiag.read_from: chapter 6, Original sequence-based transaction replacement: the setup transaction into a multisignature output, the refund with sequence 0 that neither broadcasts, the rounds of the card game in which the sequence is incremented and the balances move, the final version with sequence 0xffffffff that is broadcast, relayed and confirmed, and the alternative scenario in which Bob broadcasts an earlier version
ndiag.why: the passage is an exchange between Alice, Bob and the network in an order that matters - deposit, refund, rounds, final version, and an old version that nodes refuse: an interaction

messages: the setup transaction: both deposit into a multisignature output
the refund transaction, sequence 0, signed by both and not broadcast
the setup transaction is broadcast and confirmed
round 1: Alice wins, a new version with sequence 1, both sign
round 2: Bob wins, sequence 2, both sign, not broadcast
the final version, sequence 0xffffffff, is broadcast
an earlier version with a lower sequence number
not relayed: a higher-sequence version replaces it
the final version is relayed and confirmed by miners

ndiag.title: The life of a transaction, from signing to confirmation
ndiag.read_from: chapter 6: Protecting presigned transactions (signed but not broadcast, for months or years), Opt-in transaction replacement signaling (an unconfirmed transaction with the BIP125 signal may be replaced by a conflicting one paying a higher fee rate), Lock time (eligible for any block, or only from a height or a time), Sequence as a relative timelock (confirmed only once the spent output has aged), the rule against double spending (only one of two conflicting transactions can be in a valid blockchain)
ndiag.why: the passages describe the states a transaction is in over time and the events that move it - signed, held, broadcast, replaced, confirmed, or refused as a conflict: a life cycle

states.label: Signed: a valid transaction, not yet broadcast
Presigned and held, perhaps for years
Unconfirmed: relayed and kept by full nodes under their policy
Waiting: lock time or relative timelock not yet satisfied
Replaced: a conflicting transaction paying a higher fee rate
Confirmed: included in a block, its outputs in the UTXO database
Refused: it conflicts with a confirmed transaction

transitions: its lock time or a sequence timelock is not yet satisfied
the height or the median time past reaches the lock
it signalled replaceability and a conflicting transaction pays more
a miner includes it in a block
a conflicting transaction spending the same output was confirmed first
the output it spends was spent by another transaction

ndiag.title: Third-party malleability: a stranger changes the txid, Bob's payment to Carol fails
ndiag.read_from: chapter 6, Third-party transaction malleability: Alice creates a transaction with OP_2 in the input script paying Bob, Bob immediately spends that output to Carol, anyone on the network replaces OP_2 with OP_PUSH1 0x02 creating a conflict with a different txid; if the conflicting version is confirmed, Alice's original cannot be, and Bob's transaction cannot spend its output - and Segregated witness: an empty input script keeps witnesses from affecting the txid
ndiag.why: the passage is an exchange between Alice, Bob, Carol, a third party and the network, in an order that decides who loses: an interaction

messages: a transaction that pays Bob, OP_2 in its input script
a transaction that spends that output to Carol, by Alice's txid
the same transaction with OP_PUSH1 0x02: a different txid, a conflict
the conflicting version is in the valid blockchain, the original is not
the output Bob spends does not exist: his transaction is invalid
no output for Carol to spend
segregated witness: the witness is separated from the txid, no conflict

ndiag.title: Who works with a transaction, and for what
ndiag.read_from: chapter 6: a transaction as the data Alice uses to convince full nodes to update their database; the full node that looks up the outpoint, obtains the amount and the conditions, checks for double spending and updates its UTXO database; the miner who creates the coinbase and claims the fees and the subsidy; the software that measures a transaction's weight; the relay policy a node applies to unconfirmed transactions; and the contract protocols that presign transactions
ndiag.why: the chapter tells what the different people and programs do with a transaction - build, sign, relay, validate, mine, measure - a set of uses by actors

usecases.label: Build and sign a transaction that spends her outputs
Look up each outpoint and obtain the amount and the conditions
Refuse a double spend and update the UTXO database
Apply relay policy to an unconfirmed transaction
Create the coinbase and claim the fees and the subsidy
Measure the weight and the fee rate
Presign transactions with lock times and sequence timelocks

ndiag.title: Deploying segregated witness as a soft fork
ndiag.read_from: chapter 6, Segregated witness: the obvious method requires a hard fork, not compatible with older full nodes; the alternative of late 2015 uses a soft fork, a backward-compatible change under which newer nodes may reject blocks older nodes accept but not the reverse; the approach is based on anyone-can-spend output scripts - a number 0 to 16 followed by 2 to 40 bytes is the segwit template; old nodes allow an empty input script, new nodes require one, and the witness goes in the new witness structure
ndiag.why: the passage is a procedure with one decision - change the rules in a way old nodes reject, or in a way they accept - and the steps that follow the second branch: a workflow

nodes.label: The idea: the witness is not part of the data generating the txid
Would older full nodes reject the new blocks?
A hard fork: a change older full nodes reject; every node must upgrade
A soft fork: new nodes reject blocks old nodes accept, not the reverse
The template: a number 0 to 16 and 2 to 40 bytes, anyone-can-spend
Old nodes allow an empty input script and accept the block
New nodes require an empty input script and a valid witness
The witness structure holds the witness, which is not part of the txid

resources.title: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition - Chapter 6: Transactions (the book's source, CC BY-SA 4.0)
resources.why: The chapter itself, free to read: every quotation in this page is re-read from the commit the textbook ontology pins.

resources.title: BIP 141: Segregated Witness (Consensus layer) (status: Deployed)
resources.why: Defines the witness-independent txid, the wtxid, the witness program template, weight as base size times three plus total size, and the 4,000,000 block weight limit this page recomputes.

resources.title: BIP 144: Segregated Witness (Peer Services) (status: Deployed)
resources.why: The extended serialization format: the zero marker, the 0x01 flag read as a bit vector, and the witness structure at the end of the transaction.

resources.title: BIP 68: Relative lock-time using consensus-enforced sequence numbers (status: Deployed)
resources.why: The third meaning of the sequence field, bit by bit: the disable flag, the type flag at 1 << 22, the 16-bit mask and the 512-second units this page decodes.

resources.title: BIP 112: CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY (status: Deployed)
resources.why: The opcode, deployed with BIP68, that lets an output script demand a relative timelock and fails in a transaction below version 2.

resources.title: BIP 113: Median time-past as endpoint for lock-time calculations (status: Deployed)
resources.why: Why a time lock is compared with the median of eleven block times rather than with a block's own timestamp.

resources.title: BIP 125: Opt-in Full Replace-by-Fee Signaling (status: Deployed)
resources.why: The signal of a sequence below 0xfffffffe, the rules a replacement must meet, and inherited signalling.

resources.title: BIP 431: Topology Restrictions for Pinning (status: Draft)
resources.why: The version 3 proposal the chapter says was being considered: a relay policy, not a consensus change, implemented by Bitcoin Core since 28.0.

resources.title: BIP 174: Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction Format (status: Deployed)
resources.why: The only other widely used serialization: the magic bytes, the maps and the roles that pass a transaction template between programs.

resources.title: BIP 34: Block v2, Height in Coinbase (status: Deployed)
resources.why: Why the coinbase field begins with a push of the block height since 2013.

resources.title: BIP 62: Dealing with malleability (status: Closed)
resources.why: The attempt to forbid non-canonical encodings by consensus, which could not have solved second-party malleability.

resources.title: Bitcoin Core: src/consensus/tx_check.cpp (CheckTransaction, the context-free rules)
resources.why: The refusals this page names - empty inputs, empty outputs, negative or oversized amounts, duplicate inputs, a bad coinbase length - with the comment that cites the 2010 overflow bug.

resources.title: Bitcoin Core: doc/bips.md (the proposals the project implements, and since which release)
resources.why: Which of this chapter's standards are in the reference implementation, when each took effect, and the 28.0 note on version 3 transactions.

resources.title: Transactions - Bitcoin (developer reference)
resources.why: The field-by-field reference of the raw transaction format, with the compactSize table and the sequence and lock-time rules.

resources.title: Bitcoin Core :: Segregated Witness Wallet Development Guide
resources.why: The project's own guide to witness programs, the witness structure and transaction weight for wallet developers.

resources.title: Transaction | How Bitcoin Transactions Work (learnmeabitcoin)
resources.why: A drawn walk through a raw transaction's bytes, the same walk this page performs in code.

resources.title: Transaction pinning | Bitcoin Optech
resources.why: The attack the version 3 proposal defends against, explained for developers of contract protocols.

resources.title: Replace-by-fee (RBF) | Bitcoin Optech
resources.why: The history of replacement policy from the original sequence scheme to opt-in and full RBF.

resources.title: Alice's transaction 46620030... on mempool.space
resources.why: The explorer's record of the chapter's transaction: block 775,072, weight 569, the outpoint, the two outputs and the witness - the record this page's checks compare against.

resources.title: Block 170 on mempool.space: the first transaction that spends an output
resources.why: Where the chapter's first story lives: Satoshi's 10 BTC to Hal Finney, spending the coinbase of block 9.

resources.title: Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System (the whitepaper)
resources.why: The original description of a transaction as a chain of digital signatures, the first row of the chapter's table of terms.

resources.title: Bitcoin Transaction Malleability and MtGox (Decker and Wattenhofer, 2014)
resources.why: The measurement behind the Mt. Gox story: 302,000 BTC ever involved in malleability attacks, 1,811 before the exchange's press release.

resources.title: Pizza for bitcoins? (bitcointalk, 2010)
resources.why: The thread in which 10,000 BTC bought two pizzas: the 131-input transaction this page parses.

resources.title: Strange block 74638 (bitcointalk, 2010)
resources.why: The report of the value overflow and the five-hour timeline of the patch, as the forum recorded it.

resources.title: Value overflow incident - Bitcoin Wiki
resources.why: The community's account of block 74,638, the 0.3.10 fix and the reorganisation at block 74,691.

resources.title: Lightning Network Explained (Wikimedia Commons, CC licence on the file page)
resources.why: A short video on the payment channels that the sequence field's original scheme and BIP68's timelocks exist to make possible.
